# Undra documentation

Undra owns the part of your app that is not pixels: domain logic, reactive state, the data layer, persistence and the dev loop. These pages take you from an empty directory to a running app, then explain how the pieces work.

## Where to start

- **New here?** [Getting started](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/getting-started.html) installs the toolchain and CLI, scaffolds a project, runs the live dev loop and puts an app on each platform.
- **Want a working example of a login, a paged list or an offline queue?** The [cookbook](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/) has each as a tested recipe, and [Fieldbook](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/sample.html) puts them together in one app.
- **Writing a core?** [Core concepts](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/concepts.html) covers stores, signals, computeds and keyed lists. [Queries & mutations](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/queries.html) covers the data layer, and [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/ports.html) covers everything that touches the outside world. [Objects](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/objects.html), [host callbacks](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/callbacks.html), [types](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/types.html) and [generic functions, objects and stores](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/generics.html) cover what else crosses the boundary.
- **Data that arrives or grows?** [Paging and lazy lists](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/paging.html), [polling](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/polling.html), [WebSocket and server-sent events](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/realtime.html) and the [local database](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/db.html).
- **Testing, shipping, running?** [Testing your app](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/testing.html), [Shipping an update](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/updates.html), [Reviewing generated code](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/reviewing-generated-code.html), [workers and crash recovery](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/web.html) on the web, [Operating in production](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/production.html) (crash reports, background runs, the size of the shipped core), and [one core or several](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/several-cores.html).
- **Fitting it into what you have?** [Bazel](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/bazel.html) builds the core and its bindings in your graph, and [your network stack](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/network-stack.html) (OkHttp, URLSession, fetch) carries the core's requests.
- **Moving an existing app?** The guides [from Kotlin Multiplatform](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/from-kmp.html) and [from UniFFI](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/from-uniffi.html), and [supporting iOS 15 and 16](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/ios-15-16.html).
- **Looking something up?** [The CLI](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cli.html) lists every command and flag. [Architecture](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/architecture.html) explains the schema, the generators, the wire and the twelve rules. The API overviews show what a record, error, store or port looks like in [Swift](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-swift.html), [Kotlin](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-kotlin.html) and [TypeScript](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-typescript.html).

## The idea in four sentences

You write your domain in Rust and mark it with a handful of attributes. Undra generates idiomatic Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript from the schema those attributes produce, so the UI stays SwiftUI on iOS, Jetpack Compose on Android, React on the web, and React Native. Each platform keeps a local mirror of your state, so reads never cross the language boundary. A write crosses once per transaction, and the core answers with one compact binary change-set that patches every mirror.

**Where these pages come from.** Everything here is digested from the repository: the README, the specification in `docs/SPEC.md`, the onboarding guide, the benchmark results and the playground app. When a page and the spec disagree, the spec wins; the [repository](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra) is the record.

## A note on numbers

Performance figures on this site are measured on an Apple M5 Pro host, in release builds, and guarded by budgets in CI. The device rows come from the iPhone simulator, the Android emulator and headless Chromium on that machine; none is from a physical phone, and nothing on this site claims a per-device target as met. The results are in [bench/RESULTS.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/getting-started.html

# Getting started

Three commands put the to-do app that every new project starts with on your screen, running on its Rust core. Then the live loop, the native apps, and what you ship.

## In five minutes

With Rust (and its `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target) and Node installed:

bash

```bash
curl -fsSL https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/install.sh | sh   # the CLI; cargo is the other way, below
undra init myapp                                               # a core, its bindings, and an app per platform
cd myapp/web && npm install && npm run dev                     # the web app on the core: http://localhost:5173
```

`undra init` prints `Created …/myapp (… files, bindings for schema hash 0x…)` and what to run next; nothing is downloaded, the templates are part of the binary. `npm run dev` starts Vite, whose `undra()` plugin builds the core to WebAssembly first (`==> Building the core for web`, then a table with the module's size against its budget; the first build compiles the Undra crates and takes a minute or two). The page at `http://localhost:5173` is a to-do list whose state lives in the Rust core in `core/src/lib.rs`. Edit that file and save: the plugin rebuilds the core and reloads the page.

That is the whole loop on the web. The rest of this page installs what each platform needs, shows [`undra dev`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/getting-started.html#4-start-the-live-loop) (one core served to every app, its state kept across a rebuild), and runs the iOS and Android apps. `undra doctor` says what your machine is missing, with the command that fixes each gap.

## What you need

Install only what your target platforms need. `undra doctor` checks all of it and prints the fix for each gap.

| You want | You need |
| --- | --- |
| Any core (everything in `crates/`) | Rust stable, plus the cross targets Undra ships to |
| Web | Node 20+, and `binaryen` (for `wasm-opt`, optional: it makes the wasm core smaller) |
| Android | JDK 17, Kotlin, Gradle, the Android SDK and NDK r27, `cargo-ndk` |
| iOS (macOS only) | Full Xcode from the App Store, plus an iOS simulator runtime |

## 1. Install the toolchain

Rust comes first, with the targets Undra builds for.

bash

```bash
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown \
  aarch64-apple-ios aarch64-apple-ios-sim \
  aarch64-linux-android x86_64-linux-android
```

Then the platform pieces you need.

bash

```bash
# Web and the TypeScript runtime
brew install node binaryen

# Android: JDK, Kotlin, Gradle, then the SDK and NDK
brew install openjdk@17 kotlin gradle
brew install --cask android-commandlinetools
cargo install cargo-ndk
```

For iOS, install Xcode from the App Store (the Command Line Tools alone have no XCTest and no simulators), then:

bash

```bash
sudo xcode-select -s /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer
sudo xcodebuild -license accept
xcodebuild -downloadPlatform iOS        # simulator runtime, one time, large
```

The Android SDK needs a few packages (platform 35, build-tools 35, NDK 27.2, the emulator and a system image). The [onboarding guide](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/ONBOARDING.md) has the exact `sdkmanager` line and an `avdmanager` line that creates the `undra` emulator used throughout the project.

## 2. Install the CLI

Pick one channel. The installer puts a prebuilt `undra` binary on your machine (macOS and Linux, arm64 and x86_64); cargo builds it from source with Rust 1.85 or newer.

| Channel | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Installer | `curl -fsSL https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/install.sh \| sh` |
| cargo | `cargo install --git https://github.com/shreypdev/undra undra-cli` |

The installer detects your OS and architecture, verifies the download against the release checksums, installs to `~/.undra/bin` and prints the line to add to your `PATH`. It never uses `sudo`.

bash

```bash
undra --version
undra doctor      # prints what is missing, with the fix
```

`undra doctor` exits with status 1 when something the project needs is missing, so it works in CI too. Inside a project it only checks the platforms named in `undra.toml`. Each finding says what it found (`ok`, `missing` or the wrong version), the value it saw, the exact command that fixes it and the heading of the onboarding guide that explains it; `undra doctor --fix` prints every fix as one block to read and paste (it runs nothing) and `--json` prints the report for tools.

### From a checkout (contributors)

bash

```bash
git clone https://github.com/shreypdev/undra.git && cd undra
cargo install --path crates/undra-cli    # the `undra` command
source scripts/env.sh                   # PATH, JDK and Kotlin jars, Xcode fallback, per shell
```

## 3. Create a project

bash

```bash
undra init myapp                        # core + shells: SwiftUI on iOS, Jetpack Compose on Android, React on the web
undra init myapp --platforms ios,web    # only some of them
undra init myapp --id dev.acme.myapp    # application id / bundle identifier
cd myapp
```

Nothing is downloaded: the templates are part of the `undra` binary. The project you get is a directory with a `undra.toml` and:

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `core/` | The Rust core: a working to-do store with `#[undra::store]` and `#[undra::api]` |
| `generated/` | Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript bindings for that core, already generated ([how to review them](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/reviewing-generated-code.html)) |
| `ios/` `android/` `web/` | One minimal, real app per platform, using the generated bindings |

The project depends on the release of the `undra` that made it, and on nothing but the Undra repository on GitHub: no registry account, no token. With `undra` 1.0.0 the lines are:

| Where | The dependency |
| --- | --- |
| `core/Cargo.toml` | `undra = { git = "https://github.com/shreypdev/undra", tag = "v1.0.0" }` |
| iOS (the Xcode project, and `generated/swift/Package.swift`) | `.package(url: "https://github.com/shreypdev/undra", from: "1.0.0")`, product `UndraRuntime` |
| `android/app/build.gradle.kts` | `implementation("com.github.shreypdev.undra:runtime:v1.0.0")` and `:android-adapters:v1.0.0`, from `https://jitpack.io`, which `settings.gradle.kts` declares for that group only |
| `web/package.json` | `"@undra/runtime": "https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/releases/download/v1.0.0/undra-runtime-1.0.0.tgz"` |

Swift Package Manager reads the repository's tags, JitPack builds the Kotlin modules from the tag, and npm installs the release's tarball by its URL. `undra upgrade` moves all of them to a newer release together. Pass `--undra-path ~/src/undra` (or set `UNDRA_PATH`) to use a checkout's crates and runtimes instead.

## 4. Start the live loop

bash

```bash
undra dev                          # serves the core on ws://127.0.0.1:7443
undra dev --addr 0.0.0.0:7443      # reachable from a phone on your network
```

`undra dev` builds your core for this machine and serves it over a WebSocket. A simulator, a phone or a browser tab connects with the `remote` transport of its runtime and uses this core instead of a built-in one. The banner says how each platform connects:

text

```
Undra dev server is running.

ws://127.0.0.1:7443

  schema hash   0x…
  devtools      http://127.0.0.1:7443/devtools?token=…
  web           … or ?undra=<url> in the page URL
  iOS           launch the app with UNDRA_DEV_URL set to the URL above
  Android       emulator  ws://10.0.2.2:7443
```

Edit Rust and save: the core is rebuilt and restarted with its state, the connected apps reconnect by themselves and stay on the screen they were on, and the terminal says so (`Restarted: ws://127.0.0.1:7443 (schema hash 0x…); state kept (1 store, 1 KiB, restored in 157 µs)`). An edit that changes the API, a field or an error's message, changes the schema hash: the server says so, and an app built from the old bindings reports the mismatch and stops until you run `undra bindgen` and rebuild it. Development log records (a line per transaction commit, port call and panic) print in the terminal; the devtools address opens a timeline of every change-set.

On the web, open the page with the server's address: `http://localhost:5173/?undra=ws://127.0.0.1:7443` (development builds only). Vite's plugin watches `core/src` too and rebuilds the wasm core; it reloads the pages that run that core and leaves a page opened with `?undra=` alone, so the page stays on the served core with its state.

**No authentication.** The server has none. Keep the default loopback address unless a device has to reach it, and never expose it beyond a network you trust.

## 5. Run each platform

Each shell is a plain native project wired to your core, and its own README says how to run it. The short version:

### Web

bash

```bash
cd web && npm install && npm run dev
```

The page runs the core in the browser as a wasm module, which the `undra()` Vite plugin builds. With `?undra=ws://127.0.0.1:7443` in its URL it uses the core that `undra dev` serves instead; `web/src/undra.ts` does that with one call:

ts

```ts
await UndraMyappCore.load({ mode: "remote", url: devUrl });
```

### iOS

Open `ios/` in Xcode and run on a simulator. Xcode resolves the Swift package `undra` from `https://github.com/shreypdev/undra` at the project's release the first time (it clones the repository, about 47 MiB). There is no `undra build` to run first: the *Build the Undra core* Run Script phase of the Xcode project builds the core before the app compiles, a Debug build with a debug core and a Release build with a release one, and Xcode skips it while the core is unchanged. In debug builds the generated app reads `UNDRA_DEV_URL` (for example `ws://<your Mac>:7443`) and attaches to `undra dev` when it is set.

### Android

Build and install from `android/` with Gradle (`./gradlew :app:installDebug`); the runtime's modules come from JitPack, built from the release's tag. There is no `undra build` to run first, because the `undraBuild` Gradle task builds the core before everything else and Gradle skips it while the core is unchanged. A release variant (`assembleRelease`, `bundleRelease`) gets a release core, anything else a debug one: a debug core is tens of megabytes per ABI. Debug builds can run against `undra dev` instead (no native build needed; `-PundraSkipBuild=true` leaves the task out): `./gradlew -PundraDevUrl=ws://10.0.2.2:7443 :app:installDebug` for an emulator, or `adb reverse` (`undra dev --android`) and `ws://127.0.0.1:7443` for a USB device.

## 6. Build what you ship

In a project made by `undra init` the app builds do this for you: Gradle's `undraBuild` task, Xcode's build phase and the `undra()` Vite plugin (`@undra/runtime/vite`) run `undra build` before each app builds, and skip it while the core is unchanged. They find `undra` on `PATH`; `undra doctor` checks that it is there. A repository built by Bazel uses [the Bazel rules](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/bazel.html) instead, which call the same CLI. The explicit form is for packaging and for CI steps that build the core once:

bash

```bash
undra build --release        # every platform in undra.toml
undra build --platform ios,android,web --release
```

| Platform | Artifact, below `build/`, named after the core's namespace |
| --- | --- |
| iOS | `ios/MyappCore.xcframework` (device and simulator slices) |
| Android | `android/jniLibs/<abi>/libmyapp_core.so`, arm64-v8a and x86_64, 16 KB page aligned |
| Web | `web/myapp_core.wasm`, release profile then `wasm-opt -Oz` |
| Host | `host/libmyapp_core.{dylib,so}`, for JVM tests and `undra bindgen` |

`undra init` also writes `.github/workflows/undra.yml`: a job for the core (format, clippy, tests, `undra bindgen --check`) and one per app, each installing `undra` at the version pinned once at the top of the file. When a newer Undra is out, `undra upgrade` moves every pin of the project (the core's dependency, the runtimes, the workflow) in step, regenerates the bindings and prints the migration notes of every release it crosses; `undra upgrade --dry-run` shows the lines first.

Sizes are printed at the end next to the design's budgets. On the reference build the hello-world web core is 113.1 KB gzipped (budget 120 KB, gated in CI) and the arm64-v8a Android `.so` is 898.2 KB (budget 1.2 MB per ABI, gated in CI). To trade speed for size, or size for speed, set `opt_level` in `undra.toml`: [Operating in production](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/production.html#size) has the numbers for each setting.

## Prefer to explore first?

Try it in your browser first: the [live playground](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/playground/) is the real Rust core running as WebAssembly. The [playground source](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/tree/main/examples/playground) is the same thing, fully built: a to-do list, a counter, a 10,000-row keyed list and remote queries with an offline switch, on Chrome, an iPhone simulator and an Android emulator. It uses only public APIs, and proof screenshots are committed in its `.proof/` folder.

bash

```bash
undra build -C examples/playground --platform web
cd examples/playground/web && npm install && npm run dev
```

## If you are contributing

Every suite runs locally and nothing needs the network after install. The table is the same one the CI matrix follows.

| Suite | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Rust workspace | `cargo test --workspace` |
| Lints | `cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` |
| TypeScript runtime | `cd runtimes/ts/@undra/runtime && npm ci && npm test` |
| Kotlin runtime | `runtimes/kotlin/undra-runtime/scripts/test-local.sh` |
| Swift runtime | `cd runtimes/swift/UndraRuntime && swift test` |
| wasm ABI | `bash crates/undra-ffi/tests/wasm/run.sh` |
| Contract scenarios, three platforms | `bash contract-tests/run-all.sh` |
| Benchmark budget gate | `cargo test -p undra-bench --test budgets --release` |

Read `CLAUDE.md` (the constitution) and `docs/SPEC.md` before you write code; the [architecture page](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/architecture.html#constitution) digests the rules. Changes land one piece per worktree, with an adversarial review before merge; `docs/AGENT_WORKFLOW.md` describes the loop for humans and agents alike.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/concepts.html

# Core concepts

State in Undra lives in the Rust core as signals inside stores. Platforms hold a local mirror, reads never cross the boundary, and a write crosses once per transaction.

## The building blocks

Everything a platform can see is one of eight kinds of thing, each declared with an attribute. They cross the boundary in one of two ways: by value (copied) or by handle (a reference to something that stays in the core).

| Concept | Declared with | Crosses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Record | `#[undra::api]` on a `struct` | by value |
| Enum | `#[undra::api]` on an `enum`, unit or data variants | by value |
| Error | `#[undra::error]` on an `enum`; adds `Display` and `std::error::Error` | by value |
| Object | `#[undra::api]` on an `impl` block; methods are sync or async | by handle |
| Store | an object whose struct has `#[undra::store]`; its signals are mirrored | by handle |
| Port | `#[undra::port]` on a trait; implemented by the platform or by a Rust fake | the core calls out to it |
| Query, mutation | `#[undra::query]`, `#[undra::mutation]` on an `async fn` | managed by the query client |
| Function | `#[undra::api]` on a free `fn` | like a method with no receiver |

The rest of this page is about stores, because that is where reactive state lives.

## Stores

A store is a struct of signals with an `impl` block that says what the platforms can call. The to-do list from the playground is a complete example:

core/src/todos.rs

```rust
#[undra::store(restore = "Self::assemble")]
pub struct Todos {
    next: AtomicU64,                       // private state: not a signal
    #[undra(key = "id")]
    todos: Signal<Vec<Todo>>,              // signal 0
    filter: Signal<Filter>,                // signal 1
    #[undra(key = "id")]
    visible: DerivedList<Todo>,            // signal 2, a view of todos
    remaining: Computed<u32>,              // signal 3, derived
}

#[undra::api(store)]
impl Todos {
    pub fn new(ctx: Ctx) -> Self { /* … */ }
    pub async fn add(&self, title: String) -> Result<Todo, TodoError> { /* … */ }
    pub fn toggle(&self, id: Uuid) { /* … */ }
    pub fn set_filter(&self, filter: Filter) { self.filter.set(filter); }
}
```

A few rules worth knowing up front:

- **Signals are the fields of type `Signal<T>`, `Computed<T>` and `DerivedList<T>`**, numbered in declaration order (0, 1, 2, …). Other fields are private state: a `Ctx`, a counter, configuration.
- **A store needs a constructor**, a `pub fn` returning `Self` or `Result<Self, E>`. Generated code calls it to create the object in the core and gets back a handle.
- **Receivers are `&self`.** Objects are shared, so mutation goes through signals or a lock. `&mut self` is rejected with a teaching error (`E0020`).
- **Method arguments and results are wire types**: numbers, strings, bytes, options, vectors, maps, your records and enums, and `Result<T, E>` where `E` is a `#[undra::error]` enum.

## Signals

A `Signal<T>` holds a value. You read it with `get()` (a clone) or `with(|v| …)` (a borrow), and write it with `set(value)` or `update(|v| …)`.

rust

```rust
self.filter.set(Filter::Done);                       // replace
self.todos.update(|list| list.retain(|t| !t.done));  // edit in place
let open = self.todos.with(|list| list.iter().filter(|t| !t.done).count());
```

A write outside a transaction is an implicit single-write transaction, so the change is committed and delivered at once. Inside `update`, the closure holds the value's write lock: it must not read or write the same signal, or read a computed derived from it. A violation panics with a clear message instead of deadlocking.

## Computeds

A `Computed<T>` is a value derived from signals. You name its inputs and give it a function of them:

rust

```rust
let parity = Computed::new(&count, |n| if n % 2 == 0 { Parity::Even } else { Parity::Odd });
let summary = Computed::new((&count, &changes), |(n, changes)| format!("{n} after {changes} changes"));
```

Inputs are `&Signal<A>` or `&Computed<A>`, or a tuple of up to six of them, and the closure receives references. A computed is recomputed in the core, in dependency order, and **pushed in the same change-set as the write that caused it**. The UI never derives anything itself, so it cannot disagree with the core about, say, how many items are left.

A computed list is recomputed and sent whole on every change of its inputs. For a filtered or sorted view of a keyed list, use a [derived list](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/concepts.html#derived-lists), which costs the change instead.

Because a store with computeds cannot be rebuilt from its plain signals automatically, you name a function that assembles it: `#[undra::store(restore = "Self::assemble")]`. The macro tells you when you forget (`E0013`).

## Transactions

When several signals change together, group the writes. Everything inside `ctx.txn` commits as one transaction, so observers see one consistent change-set and never a half-applied state. The playground's counter changes two signals and derives a third:

core/src/counter.rs

```rust
pub fn add(&self, amount: i32) {
    self.ctx.txn(|| {
        self.count.update(|c| *c = c.saturating_add(amount));
        self.changes.update(|n| *n = n.saturating_add(1));
    });   // one change-set carries count, changes and parity
}
```

Transactions nest: an inner `txn` joins the outer one. A change-set is never split, and change-sets are delivered in commit order; for one store they reach the platform one at a time with strictly increasing transaction ids.

## Change-sets and observation

A platform does not receive everything. It **observes** signals, and only observed signals that changed are sent. Two details follow from that:

- **Observing sends the current value right away**, before the call returns in-process, so a store's initial state arrives as an ordinary change-set. A signal written while unobserved is remembered as pending and sent when someone starts observing it.
- **Only what changed is sent.** Writing `filter` in the to-do store ships `filter` and the rows that entered or left `visible`, and nothing else, because `todos` did not change.

A signal marked `#[undra(no_coalesce)]` is delivered on every commit instead of being folded into the latest value. A change-set is a compact binary structure, described on the [architecture page](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/architecture.html#the-wire).

For side effects that belong in the core, `Effect::new(deps, f)` runs `f` after each commit that dirtied one of its dependencies, and is cancelled when dropped.

## Keyed lists

A `Signal<Vec<T>>` marked `#[undra(key = "field")]` is a **keyed list**. The key is the identity of a row, and the core sends changes to it as a patch of positional operations instead of the whole list.

| Operation | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Insert { index, item }` | put the item at `index` |
| `Remove { index }` | take the row at `index` out |
| `Update { index, item }` | replace the row at `index` |
| `Move { from, to }` | take the row at `from`, then place it so it ends at `to` |
| `Clear` | empty the list |

The platform applies the operations in order to its own copy of the list. If a patch ever disagrees with that copy (an index out of bounds), the platform treats the signal as out of sync and observes it again, which resends the full value.

### Why a list write costs the change, not the list

How the core produces the patch decides the cost. There are two ways.

**Recorded operations** are the fast path. `Signal<Vec<T>>` has `push`, `insert`, `remove`, `update_at`, `move_item` and `clear`. Each one mutates the list and appends the operation it performed to a log; at commit, that log *is* the patch. No key is hashed and no item is compared, so the cost is the change, not the length of the list.

examples/playground/core/src/biglist.rs

```rust
/// Inserts a new row so that it ends at `index`. One keyed `Insert`.
pub fn insert_at(&self, index: u32, label: String) -> Result<u32, ListError> {
    // …check the index…
    let id = self.next_id.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
    self.items.insert(index as usize, Item { id, label, version: 0 });
    Ok(id)
}
```

**Raw writes** (`set`, `update`, `replace`) are the fallback. They are always correct, but the core cannot know what you did, so at commit it diffs the new list against what the platform has: hash every key, compare the surviving rows. That is O(list). It also falls back to sending the whole value when the two lists share no key, a key occurs twice, or more than half of the old rows were removed.

The difference is measured. On a 10,000-row observed list, median times from the benchmark suite (host-measured, Apple M5 Pro):

| One change to 10,000 rows | Diffed | Recorded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Insert | 536.16 µs | **6.31 µs** |
| Update | 532.32 µs | **272.3 ns** |
| Move | 702.95 µs | **9.74 µs** |

What remains at 10,000 rows is the memory move of the vector's tail, which `Vec::insert` needs in the core and which is paid twice (the list and its baseline): about 0.6 ns per row. The same insert into 100 rows is 359 ns and into 1,000 rows is 770 ns. The decision record is [ADR-027](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-027-keyed-list-ops-are-recorded-not-diffed.md).

**Rule of thumb.** Inside a store, reach for `push`, `insert`, `remove`, `update_at` and `move_item` when you change one row. Use `set` or `update` when you genuinely replace the list (a refresh from the server) or make an edit no recorded operation can express. A transaction that mixes both is diffed as a whole.

## Derived lists

A `DerivedList<T>` is a filtered, sorted or mapped view of a keyed list, and it costs the change, not the list. You build it from the list with a pipeline:

core/src/todos.rs

```rust
let visible = todos.derive().filter_with(&filter, |filter, todo| filter.matches(todo)).build();
let remaining = todos.derive().filter(|todo| !todo.done).count();   // a Computed<u32>
```

Its value is always the obvious one: the rows that pass, mapped, then sorted stably by key (`filter`, `filter_with`, `map`, at most one `sort_by_key`; equal keys keep the list's order). But it is never recomputed. It replays the list's [recorded operations](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/concepts.html#why-a-list-write-costs-the-change-not-the-list) on an index of its own, O(log n) each, and the platform receives each as at most two patch operations: a row that enters or leaves the filter is an `Insert` or a `Remove`, a row whose sort key changes a `Move` and an `Update` (so lists animate it), a change the filter hides nothing at all. The platforms see a read-only keyed list, generated exactly like a computed list.

| One row changed in 10,000 | Computed list | Derived list |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core, per change | 176.5 µs | **333 ns** |
| Sent to the platform | 352.6 KB | **158 bytes** |
| Applied on the web (TypeScript) | 1.07 ms | **1.6 µs** |

**Rule of thumb.** Write the source list with the recorded operations: a raw write (`set`, `update`, `replace`) rebuilds every view of it and sends them whole. Keep pipeline closures pure functions of the row (debug builds panic when one reads a signal); a value the view depends on besides its rows is a parameter (`filter_with`, `sort_by_key_with`). Host-measured, Apple M5 Pro; the decision record is [ADR-039](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-039-derived-keyed-lists.md).

## What the platforms see

Each platform runtime holds a **mirror**: store handle, then signal id, then the decoded value. Generated code exposes the mirror in the platform's own idiom (an `@Observable` property, a `StateFlow`, a `Signal` with `useSignal`), so reading is a local memory read that never calls into the core.

Every change-set is applied on the main thread, in one hop per transaction: Swift on the `MainActor`, Kotlin on `Dispatchers.Main.immediate`, and TypeScript in a queued flush on the page's main thread. A store is an object with a lifetime: release it explicitly with `close()` (Swift and Kotlin use `deinit` and a `Cleaner` as backstops, TypeScript a `FinalizationRegistry`), and `UndraCore.stats()` shows live handle counts.

## Snapshot and restore

The core can snapshot every store's plain signals (computeds are left out and recomputed) and restore them, which is how a web page recovers after a crash and how tests rebuild state. Restore keeps the same handles valid, so the platform's references keep working, and it cancels calls that were running on the stores it replaced. This is why the `restore` function above rebuilds computeds from signals, and why the to-do store continues its id counter above the largest id in the snapshot.

## Determinism

The core reads no clock and no random source and starts no thread of its own. Time comes from the `Clock` port, delays from `ctx.sleep` (which goes through the `Timer` port), randomness from `Rng`, the network from `Http`. That is rule R12, and it is why every scenario can be driven with deterministic fakes in Rust and with in-memory adapters on each platform. The to-do store's ids come from a counter for the same reason. See [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/ports.html).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/queries.html

# Queries & mutations

Data fetching, caching and offline behaviour are not something each platform reimplements. They live in the core, next to the state they feed, and every platform observes the same cache.

## Why the data layer is in the core

Fetching, caching, retrying, optimistic updates and offline queues are logic, and logic is what Undra writes once. The core never opens a socket: every request goes through the `Http` port, which is `URLSession`, `HttpURLConnection` or `fetch` in an app and a scripted fake in a test. The query client keeps one cache that all platforms observe, so the to-do list on the iPhone and the one in a Chrome tab agree about what is fresh.

## Defining a query

A query is an `async fn` whose first parameter is the `Ctx`, marked with `#[undra::query]`. This is the playground's remote to-do list, a `GET` that is cached per list:

core/src/remote.rs

```rust
/// The items of the server's list `list`: `GET {base}/lists/{list}/todos`.
#[undra::query(key = "remote-todos:{list}", stale = "30s", persist, retry = 1)]
pub async fn remote_todos(ctx: &Ctx, list: String) -> Result<Vec<RemoteTodo>, RemoteError> {
    let url = endpoint(ctx, &format!("/lists/{list}/todos"))?;
    parse(&send(ctx, HttpRequest::get(url)).await?)
}
```

| Argument | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `key = "…"` | the cache key; `{param}` placeholders name parameters, so two lists are two independent entries |
| `stale = "30s"` | how long a successful result stays fresh |
| `persist` | write the entry to the `Kv` port so it survives a restart |
| `retry = 3` | how many times to retry a failed fetch |
| `idempotent` | (mutations) the request is safe to repeat, which makes it eligible for the offline queue |

The signature is checked when you compile: it must be `async`, take `ctx: &Ctx` first, and return `Result<T, E>`. A query whose success value is `()` or an `Option` is rejected, because a query caches a value and effects belong in a mutation (`E0040` to `E0042`).

## Observing a query

Platforms observe a query through a generated **query handle**, which is an ordinary store. For `remote_todos` it is `RemoteTodosQueryHandle`, and it has five signals:

| Signal | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `data` | the latest successful result, or nothing yet |
| `status` | `idle`, `fetching`, `success` or `error` |
| `error` | the error of the latest failed fetch, cleared by the next success |
| `fetching` | whether a request is in flight, also true while refetching stale data |
| `updatedAt` | when `data` last changed |

Constructing the handle registers an observer and starts a fetch if the entry is missing or stale. Releasing it removes the observer; when the last observer goes, the in-flight fetch is cancelled and the entry is kept for five minutes before it is garbage collected. The handle also has `refetch()` (fetch now, even if fresh) and `invalidate()` (mark stale; it refetches while observed).

tsx

```tsx
const inbox = await RemoteTodosQueryHandle.create("inbox");   // observe
const items = useSignal(inbox.data);                          // in a component
const busy = useSignal(inbox.fetching);
```

## Staleness, refetch and dedup

An observed entry refetches when it is stale and something happens:

- an observer is added while it is stale,
- the app becomes `Active` again (the `Lifecycle` port),
- connectivity returns (the `Connectivity` port),
- its optional interval elapses, or
- it is invalidated, by key prefix.

**One fetch per key at a time.** If five screens observe the same list, they share one in-flight request.

**Polling and paging.** `interval = "30s"` refetches an observed query on a schedule ([Polling](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/polling.html)), and `infinite` turns a cursor query into a keyed list that grows by the page ([Paging and lazy lists](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/paging.html)).

## Retry with jitter

A failed fetch is retried `retry` times (three by default) with exponential backoff, `min(1000 × 2ⁿ, 30000)` milliseconds, with plus or minus 20% jitter. The jitter comes from the `Rng` port and the delay from the `Timer` port, so a test with fakes sees exactly the schedule it scripts.

## Mutations

A mutation is an `async fn` marked `#[undra::mutation]`. It shares its cache key with the query it affects. Call it through the context:

rust

```rust
ctx.mutate::<PostRemoteTodoMutation>((list, title))
    .optimistic(move |cache| {
        cache.update::<RemoteTodosQuery>((cached,), |items| items.push(placeholder));
    })
    .invalidates(/* keys to mark stale */)
    .await
```

`optimistic` runs inside a transaction with typed access to cache entries (`get`, `set`, `update`), so the UI shows the new item at once. On success the `invalidates` keys are marked stale and refetched if observed, which replaces the placeholder with the server's item. The playground wraps this in `create_remote_todo` and `set_remote_done`, which are what its three UIs call.

### Precise rollback

If the mutation fails, the optimistic write is undone, but only **the writes that mutation made**. Every cache entry carries a write stamp that changes with each write: an optimistic write, a `set`, or a fetch result. When a mutation fails, each entry it wrote is restored to what it was before, *unless something else has written that entry since*. An entry that was written since keeps that write.

That rule is what makes concurrent mutations safe:

- a later optimistic mutation's placeholder survives an earlier mutation's rollback, even on the same entry;
- a fetch result that arrived in the meantime is newer than the failed closure and is kept;
- a later mutation that wrote directly on top of the failed one inherits its restore point, so if it fails too the entry goes back to before both.

Stamps are compared, never contents, so two writes of equal data are still distinguishable. This behaviour is covered by the optimistic-rollback contract scenario on all three platforms.

## The offline queue

A mutation marked `idempotent` that fails with a network error while the `Connectivity` port says the device is offline is not lost. It is appended to a persisted queue (the `Kv` key `undra.query.queue2`) with its parameters, the fingerprint of their types and an idempotency key, and replayed in order when connectivity returns. The request carries an `Idempotency-Key` header that stays the same across retries and replays, so a server can tell a repeat from a second item.

rust

```rust
#[undra::mutation(key = "remote-todos:{list}", idempotent)]
pub async fn post_remote_todo(ctx: &Ctx, list: String, title: String) -> Result<RemoteTodo, RemoteError> {
    // …
    if let Some(key) = undra::query::idempotency_key() {
        request = request.with_header("Idempotency-Key", key.to_string());
    }
    // …
}
```

A mutation that is not `idempotent` fails immediately when offline. While a queued call waits, the optimistic placeholder stays visible, and the caller's `await` keeps waiting until the network returns and the request is replayed.

A queued call survives an app update: its input is migrated by parameter name, or by a `#[undra::migrate]` hook. One that cannot be migrated is never dropped; it moves to the **dead letters**, which `ctx.query().dead_letters()` lists and `retry_dead_letter` or `discard_dead_letter` settle. [Shipping an update](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/updates.html) has the rules.

## Persistence

Entries marked `persist` are written to the `Kv` port after each successful fetch (debounced, 250 ms) and read back when the core starts. Each entry carries the fingerprint of its type, so an unrelated change to the core keeps the cache, and an entry whose type changed is migrated by name or, if it cannot be, dropped and refetched. At most 1,000 entries are kept (`set_max_persisted_entries`), least recently updated first out.

Storage can fail: a quota runs out, a device is locked. The `Kv` port reports it as a `StorageError`, and the client treats storage as best-effort: a failed write is logged once and retried, a failed read starts the entry empty, and an offline queue that cannot be read is never overwritten or replayed until it can be.

## Testing without a network

Because the network is a port, a query is tested with a scripted fake and no sockets. `FakeHttp` answers from rules and records every request, including a flaky endpoint:

rust

```rust
let http = FakeHttp::new();
// two timeouts, then success for ever after
http.respond_sequence("https://x.test/a", [Err(HttpError::Timeout), Err(HttpError::Timeout)]);
http.respond("https://x.test/a", HttpResponse::new(200, b"ok".to_vec()));
```

Pair it with `FakeClock` to advance time and `ScriptedConnectivity` to go offline. [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/ports.html) lists them all.

## See it run

The playground's **Remote** tab on every platform is this page in motion: a cached query, optimistic adds that roll back when the server refuses, and an **Offline** switch that queues writes and replays them on reconnect. Its source is [`examples/playground/core/src/remote.rs`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/playground/core/src/remote.rs).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/ports.html

# Ports & adapters

The core never touches the outside world directly. Time, randomness, the network, storage and the app's lifecycle all come through ports: traits the platform implements and the core calls.

## What a port is

A port is a Rust trait marked `#[undra::port]`. The platform implements it (an adapter), or a Rust fake does in a test. The core calls it through the context, for example `ctx.http().request(req).await`, and does not know or care what is behind it. That is what keeps the core deterministic (rule R12): it has no wall clock, no random source and no threads outside the `Clock`, `Rng` and `Timer` ports and the runtime.

There are three kinds, and the kind decides how a call travels:

| Kind | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **sync** | the platform answers before the call returns. A port is sync only if every method is sync |
| **async** | the platform answers later; the core's task waits, and can be cancelled |
| **event** | fire and forget from the platform into the core, such as "connectivity changed" |

## The ten standard ports

| Port | Kind | Methods |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Clock` | sync | `now_ms() -> i64`, `monotonic_ns() -> u64` |
| `Rng` | sync | `fill(len) -> Bytes` |
| `Log` | sync | `log(level, target, message)` |
| `Http` | async | `request(HttpRequest) -> Result<HttpResponse, HttpError>` |
| `Kv` | async | `get`, `set`, `delete`, `list(prefix)` |
| `SecureStore` | async | the same shape as `Kv`, for secrets |
| `Fs` | async | `read`, `write`, `delete`, `list`, each returning `Result<_, FsError>` |
| `Timer` | sync | `set(timer_id, delay_ms)`; the platform answers later with a timer-fired event |
| `Connectivity` | event | `changed(online, kind)` with `NetKind` of `Wifi`, `Cellular`, `Wired`, `Unknown` or `None` |
| `Lifecycle` | event | `changed(state)` with `AppState` of `Active`, `Inactive` or `Background` |

They exchange a small set of types: `HttpRequest` (method, url, headers, optional body, optional timeout), `HttpResponse` (status, headers, body), `HttpError` (`Network`, `Timeout`, `Cancelled`, `InvalidUrl`), `Header`, `FsError` (`NotFound`, `Denied`, `Io`), `NetKind` and `AppState`.

These ports and types ship inside each platform runtime and are **not** generated into your app's bindings. Every core links `undra-ports`, so its schema contains them and the schema hash covers them, but the generator leaves them out and the generated code refers to the runtime's own types. That is why your app can have its own record called `Timer` or `Log`.

## Default adapters

Each runtime ships an adapter for every port, so a new app works without adapter code.

| Port | Swift | Kotlin (Android) | TypeScript (browser) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Http` | `URLSession` | `HttpURLConnection` | `fetch` |
| `Kv` | files in Application Support | files in `filesDir` | IndexedDB |
| `SecureStore` | Keychain | AES-256-GCM under an Android Keystore key | IndexedDB with WebCrypto |
| `Fs` | `FileManager` | `Context.filesDir` | OPFS |
| `Clock`, `Rng`, `Log` | Foundation, `SecRandom`, `os_log` | `System`, `SecureRandom`, `android.util.Log` | built in |
| `Timer` | `DispatchQueue` | `ScheduledExecutor` | `setTimeout` |
| `Connectivity`, `Lifecycle` | `NWPathMonitor`, `scenePhase` | `ConnectivityManager`, activity lifecycle callbacks | `navigator.onLine`, `visibilitychange` |

Every default store is per core namespace (`<namespace>/kv` under the app's `undra` directory in Application Support or `filesDir`, a Keychain service or Keystore alias and an IndexedDB database named after it), so two cores of one app never read each other's keys, secrets or files; an adapter you pass yourself keeps the location you gave it.

On Android one call installs all ten, `AndroidPlatformDefaults.install(core, context)`; the runtime alone installs only `Clock`, `Rng`, `Log` and `Timer`. On the JVM without Android, `Connectivity` and `Lifecycle` are stubs. On the web, `Clock`, `Rng` and `Log` are bound to imports of the wasm module, so a web app needs no adapter code for them.

Under React Native, `loadNative` installs all ten too: `Kv`, `SecureStore`, `Fs` and `Connectivity` are native code in `@undra/react-native` (files in the app's private storage, the Keychain or the Android Keystore, `NWPathMonitor` or `ConnectivityManager`, with the Swift and Android adapters' file layouts), `Http` is React Native's `fetch` and `Lifecycle` its `AppState` ([docs/REACT_NATIVE.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/REACT_NATIVE.md)).

## Supplying your own adapter

You replace a default when you load the core. The playground replaces `Http` with an in-memory server (so it needs no backend) and `Kv` with a map:

web/src/undra.ts

```ts
const adapters = { http: server, kv: memoryKv() };
await UndraPlaygroundCore.load({
  mode: "wasm-main",
  wasm: new URL(wasmUrl, location.href),
  adapters,
});
```

ios/PlaygroundApp/UndraBootstrap.swift

```swift
let adapters = Adapters.platformDefault
    .removing(portId: fnv1a32("port.Connectivity"))
    .replacing(PlaygroundNetwork.shared)
    .replacing(KvAdapter(directory: store))
try UndraPlaygroundCore.load(.inproc(adapters: adapters))
```

android/.../UndraApp.kt

```kotlin
val core = UndraPlaygroundCore.load(
    LoadOptions(mirror = MirrorOptions(framePacer = ChoreographerFramePacer())),
)
// Http, Kv, SecureStore, Fs, Connectivity and Lifecycle: the real adapters, nothing faked.
AndroidPlatformDefaults.install(core, this)
```

On Android the playground keeps every default: its Remote tab talks to a small HTTP server on the device's loopback interface, through the real `Http` adapter. To replace one port there, register another implementation after `install` (`core.registerPort(StandardPorts.Http.PORT_ID, impl)`).

Register the ports your core needs when you load it. A core's start-up work (query hydration reads the `Kv` port) runs as soon as the runtime exists. It asks for `Kv` every 100 ms for five seconds, so adapters registered right after the load (Android's `install`) are in time; a port registered later than that is missed, and the cache then starts empty.

## Your network stack inside

The defaults above are the platform's own. If your app has a network stack of its own (a token that is refreshed, interceptors, tracing, certificate pinning), a request the core makes through a default adapter does not go through it: on Android `HttpURLConnection` is OkHttp underneath, but the platform's instance, not your `OkHttpClient`. Hand your stack to the three network ports instead (`Http`, `WebSocket`, `Sse`) and every request the core makes goes through it. You do not write the adapters: the contract the core relies on (typed errors, a timeout that covers the body, cancellation that closes the socket, a size cap, streams that stop the server when the core stops reading) is already implemented, and the same test suites check it on each.

| Platform | You pass | Your stack applies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Android | your `OkHttpClient`, to the optional `okhttp-adapters` module | interceptors, `Authenticator` (a `401` is answered with a refreshed token and the request goes again), event listeners, `CertificatePinner`, `Dns`, proxy, cookie jar, dispatcher (a WebSocket's upgrade is the exception OkHttp makes: your application interceptors see it, your network interceptors and event listener do not) |
| iOS and macOS | your `URLSession`, to `HttpAdapter`, `URLSessionWebSocketAdapter` and `URLSessionSseAdapter` | its configuration and `URLProtocol` classes, its delegate (server trust and pinning, authentication challenges), proxy, cookies |
| Web | your `fetch` and `WebSocket`, to `fetchHttp`, `fetchSse` and `browserWebSocket` | whatever your wrapper does to a request: a token, a retry on `401`, a trace header |
| React Native | nothing: `reactNativeHttp()` is React Native's `fetch` | React Native's own networking module, so what the app configures there |

kotlin

```kotlin
// In place of AndroidPlatformDefaults.install(core, this): the same ten ports, and Http, WebSocket and Sse go through your client.
AndroidPlatformDefaults.installWithOkHttp(core, this, appGraph.okHttpClient)
```

swift

```swift
let adapters = Adapters.platformDefault
    .replacing(HttpAdapter(session: session))
    .replacing(URLSessionWebSocketAdapter(session: session))
    .replacing(URLSessionSseAdapter(session: streamingSession)) // same delegate, a configuration that lets a stream be quiet
```

ts

```ts
const adapters = { ...browserAdapters(), http: fetchHttp({ fetch: appFetch }) };
const ports = {
  [OptInPortIds.WebSocket.portId]: webSocketPort(browserWebSocket({ WebSocket: AppWebSocket })),
  [OptInPortIds.Sse.portId]: ssePort(fetchSse({ fetch: appFetch })),
};
```

The pieces and the places they differ from the defaults are documented where they live: the [okhttp-adapters README](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/runtimes/kotlin/undra-runtime/okhttp-adapters/README.md) (redirects, retries and timeouts are your client's; a WebSocket on OkHttp repairs malformed UTF-8 in a text frame instead of failing the connection, and OkHttp tells neither your event listener nor your network interceptors about a WebSocket's upgrade; a stream is opened on a client derived from yours with no read timeout and HTTP/1.1), and the [cookbook recipe](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/network-stack.html), with the code of all three. The decision is [ADR-060](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-060-app-network-stack-in-ports.md).

## When a port is missing

An unavailable port is a normal outcome, not a bug. A port nobody registered behaves as unavailable, a call can be cancelled, and a host can reply with bytes that do not decode. The core handles all three without panicking:

- If the port method returns `Result<T, E>`, the failure becomes an `E`. `HttpError` and `FsError` implement `From<PortError>`, so an unavailable `Http` port is `Network("the Http port has no adapter registered (E0062: register one, see ..)")`, with the code and the link to the fix. Your own error type needs the same conversion, and the macro checks it at compile time (`E0033`).
- If the method has no error channel, there is no typed way to say "unavailable", so the call panics with a message that names the port and method and says how to bind one (`E0062`, in the shape of every diagnostic: what, why, fix, docs link). The runtime contains that panic at the boundary. Give optional ports a `Result`, or register them.

## Writing your own port

Mark a trait with `#[undra::port]`. The macro registers it in the schema and generates a proxy type, so the core calls your trait like any other, and the platform gets a protocol or interface to implement. This one is made up, to show the shape:

rust

```rust
#[undra::port(sync)]
pub trait Haptics {
    fn tap(&self, strength: u8);
}
```

A port method's parameters must be wire types (`E0030`), and an `event` port's methods cannot return a value (`E0031`).

## Testing with fakes

Every standard port has a deterministic Rust fake in `undra::ports::fakes`. They are all `Send + Sync`, keep state behind a lock, and never read the system clock, a random source or a thread.

| Fake | Port | Behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FakeHttp` | `Http` | scripted replies chosen by a matcher; every request recorded |
| `MemKv`, `MemSecureStore` | `Kv`, `SecureStore` | in-memory ordered maps; operations recorded |
| `MemFs` | `Fs` | in-memory tree with the platform adapters' error semantics |
| `FakeClock` | `Clock` and `Timer` | settable time; `advance` fires due timers |
| `SeededRng` | `Rng` | `xorshift64*`; the same seed gives the same bytes |
| `CaptureLog` | `Log` | keeps every record |
| `ScriptedConnectivity`, `ScriptedLifecycle` | `Connectivity`, `Lifecycle` | push scripted events into a runtime |

`TestRuntime::new()` runs the executor on the test thread and lets you drive it with `run_until(fut)` and `run_pending()`. Installing the fakes binds all of them into it. The doctest of `FakeHttp` shows the style:

rust

```rust
use undra_ports::{Http, HttpError, HttpRequest, HttpResponse};
use undra_ports::fakes::FakeHttp;
use undra_runtime::testing::TestRuntime;

let http = FakeHttp::new();
// A flaky endpoint: two timeouts, then success for ever after.
http.respond_sequence("https://x.test/a", [Err(HttpError::Timeout), Err(HttpError::Timeout)]);
http.respond("https://x.test/a", HttpResponse::new(200, b"ok".to_vec()));

let t = TestRuntime::new();
let get = || HttpRequest::get("https://x.test/a");
assert_eq!(t.run_until(http.request(get())), Err(HttpError::Timeout));
assert_eq!(t.run_until(http.request(get())), Err(HttpError::Timeout));
assert_eq!(t.run_until(http.request(get())).unwrap().status, 200);
assert_eq!(http.call_count(), 3);
```

Time works the same way. `FakeClock` is the single source of time for both `Clock` and `Timer`, so `ctx.sleep` asks for a timer and advancing the fake clock serves it: sleeps wake at exactly their deadline. On a runtime with the fakes installed, advance time with `Fakes::advance`, not `TestRuntime::advance`.

The platforms get the same treatment. The [contract scenarios](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/contract-tests/scenarios.md) run every platform runtime against the real core with a manual clock, an in-memory `Http` server, an in-memory `Kv` and a test that emits connectivity events itself.

The test kit puts these fakes behind the real core in Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript too, with a manual clock, and replays recorded port traffic: [Testing your app](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/testing.html).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/objects.html

# Objects and identity

A method can return an object and take one. The platform gets a class, the same wrapper every time it asks for the same object.

## Returns and parameters

A method returns an object the way Rust already shares one, behind an `Arc`, and takes one by reference. Undra generates a class for it in each language, so you never see a handle.

| In Rust | On the platform |
| --- | --- |
| `Arc<Shelf>`, `Option<Arc<Shelf>>`, `Vec<Arc<Shelf>>` returned, also inside a `Result` or an `async` method | a `Shelf`, an optional one, a list of them |
| `&Shelf`, `Arc<Shelf>`, `Option<&Shelf>`, `Vec<Arc<Shelf>>` as a parameter | a `Shelf` you pass, an optional one, a list |
| a constructor returning `Arc<Self>` | a constructor that gives the same object back while you hold it |

A returned store is a store: observe it and its signals arrive like those of any other.

## One object, one wrapper

Ask for the same object twice and you get the same wrapper while the first is alive. A store returned twice is observed once, a list of shelves is a list you can compare, and in Swift the wrapper is `Hashable` by identity, so `ForEach(shelves, id: \.self)` works.

The reference you hold is given back when the wrapper is closed or collected, once. Hold the wrapper for as long as you use it; `close()` it to let go early.

## What stays out

An object travels as a parameter or a return, and nowhere else.

| Not allowed | Why |
| --- | --- |
| An object inside a record, a variant or a store's signal, in a stream item, a query or a mutation | a value is copied, compared, saved and merged; an object is none of those. Put the object behind a method (`E0064` says so) |
| An object of another core | two cores can issue the same handle numbers, so the generated code refuses it before anything is sent: `UndraCallError.refused` |
| An object in a port's parameter or return | pass a record or an id instead |

## After a restore

An object a method returned is not part of a saved snapshot: after a restore (a web worker crash, `undra dev` reloading the core) its handle is stale, and calling the method again returns it. Constructed stores restore as before, and so do query handles: the snapshot keeps what a handle is made of and the core builds it again when the app first uses it (ADR-059). What a store keeps in a private field is whatever its `restore` hook rebuilds.

## Good to know

- **Passing an object lends it.** The call holds it until it finishes, so closing the wrapper while a call is in flight is safe.
- **A failed call hands nothing out.** An error, a cancel or a panic gives the references it had issued back.
- **A shelf stays alive while you hold it,** even if the core drops its own reference.

The playground's [Workshop](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/playground/core/src/workshop.rs) uses every shape on this page, and the contract scenario S27 checks them on Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/callbacks.html

# Host callbacks

A trait the app implements, so the core can call it: a progress report, a note, a question for the user.

## Declare it

A callback is a trait the app implements. Mark it `#[undra::callback]`, take it as `Arc<dyn Trait>` in a method or function, and call it from the core like any other trait.

| A method on the trait | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `fn note(&self, line: String)` | fire and forget: the core does not wait, and nothing is lost on the way |
| `async fn confirm(&self, q: String) -> Result<bool, E>` | asks the app and awaits its answer, a typed error included |
| `#[undra(coalesce)]` | a listener that has fallen behind gets only the newest call |
| `#[undra::callback(background)]` | runs off the main thread, in order, without waiting for a frame |

A method that returns a value without `async` is refused (`E0071`): the core never blocks waiting for app code.

## Where it runs

By default on the main thread, in the order things happened. A callback joins the same queue as state changes, so a listener sees the stores as they were when the core called it. With `background` each listener has its own serial executor instead. Either way the core never runs app code inside its own call.

## Errors and cancelling

An implementation that throws the method's own error answers the core with it, typed. Any other error is reported through `onError` and the core sees the app as unavailable. A throw from a fire-and-forget method is only reported. None of it unwinds into the core.

When the core stops waiting (the call that was awaiting was cancelled), the task running the implementation is cancelled too: a Swift `Task`, a Kotlin `Job`, a TypeScript `AbortSignal` passed as the last argument.

## How long it lives

The core holds the callback until it lets go, so a listener you create inline lives as long as the core uses it. A core that keeps the listener and an app that keeps the core make a cycle across languages. Two ways out:

- **A subscription object.** Return something the app closes (`watch` above): closing it drops the core's hold.
- **A weak wrapper.** Hand the core a wrapper that forwards while the target lives and does nothing after.

A stream method takes a callback like any other method: the core holds it while the stream runs and lets it go when the stream ends or is dropped. The core never calls a weak wrapper whose target is gone (the question is answered unavailable); if your own code does in Swift, the method throws the error type's `Unavailable`, and an error type without one stops the app with a message.

## Testing

In a Rust test pass an implementation written in Rust: `#[undra::port] impl Reporter for Recorder` records the calls, and an `async` method answers as you set it. See [Testing your app](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/testing.html).

The playground's [Reporter](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/playground/core/src/workshop.rs) is this page's example, and the contract scenario S28 checks ordering, errors, cancelling and release on Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/types.html

# Newtypes, generics and decimals

A newtype crosses as the value it wraps and arrives as a distinct type. A generic type gets a name per use. Money is a `Decimal`, never a float.

## Newtypes

A tuple struct with one field is a newtype. It crosses as the value it wraps, with no length and no tag, so it costs nothing on the wire, and each platform gets a distinct type, so an `AccountId` can never be passed where a `UserId` is wanted.

| In Rust | Swift | Kotlin | TypeScript |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `struct AccountId(pub Uuid)` | `struct AccountId: RawRepresentable, Hashable, Codable` | `@JvmInline value class AccountId(val value: UUID)` | `type AccountId = string & {{ __brand }}` and a function `AccountId(value)` |

The inner type is any value type: another newtype, a record, a `Vec`, an `Option`, a `Decimal`. A newtype can stand anywhere a record can, and as a map key when the type it wraps is a valid key (`String`, an integer, `bool`, `Uuid`); the compiler checks it, so `HashMap<Price, _>` with `struct Price(Decimal)` is an error at the map, not a surprise on a phone. A keyed list may use a newtype as its key field.

Swift and Kotlin add `Comparable` when the wrapped type has an order that means something (numbers, strings, dates, durations, decimals). A `Uuid` gets none: Foundation's `UUID` is comparable only from iOS 17. No literal conformances are generated, because a literal that becomes an `AccountId` is what the type is there to prevent.

Wrapping a field you already persist in a newtype needs no migration code: the bytes are the same, so an old snapshot or cached query result reads back as it was.

## Generics

Generic code crosses as named instantiations: you list the types, the platforms get an ordinary function, record, class or store for each. Data types first; [generic functions, objects and stores](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/generics.html) follow, with the limits.

### Generic data types

The schema describes concrete types, so a generic struct or enum is a *template* that registers nothing, and each use is a named instantiation. The name is yours and stays stable, which is what the generated Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript need.

On every platform `EntrySlice` is an ordinary record and `LoadableEntries` an ordinary enum, byte for byte what you would get by writing them out. Signatures spell the alias; writing `Slice<Entry>` in one is [E0002](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0002) and the message says which alias to declare. An alias lives in the crate of its template (a second one for the same instantiation is [E0070](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0070)), and its arguments are concrete types, other aliases and newtypes included.

### Generic functions, methods, objects and stores

The same shape, one level up (ADR-058). A function lists its types, `#[undra::api(generic(T = [Todo, Note]))]`, and each is one function: Swift and Kotlin overload it, TypeScript takes the type's name first (`newest("Todo", rows)`). An object or a store over a type parameter is a template, `#[undra::api(store, generic)] impl<T: Row> Selection<T>`, and each alias, `#[undra::api] pub type TodoSelection = Selection<Todo>;`, is an ordinary store of that name with its own type id, handles, signals and snapshot. [The guide](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/generics.html) has the Rust and what Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript call, and where to put the alias.

### What is not there

| Refused | Code | Why, and what would lift it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A generic function with no list (an open-ended `T`) | [E0002](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0002) | Callers are on the platforms, so the core must contain what they can call. Nothing lifts it: this is the design. |
| Two type parameters on a function or method | [E0072](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0072) | Each listed type is one function; two parameters need pairs, which need a syntax and names for pairs on the platforms. |
| A scalar, a `String`, a container or an object in a function's list | [E0072](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0072) | An instantiation is presented under the type's name; unnamed types would need naming rules in three languages. Wrap it in a newtype. |
| A generic method inside a generic object | [E0074](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0074) | An instantiation is one class; a second list multiplies it. Tests only: the expansion composes. |
| A generic constructor | [E0002](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0002) | A constructor returns the object, whose type has no such parameter. |
| Generic queries and mutations | [E0002](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0002) | A query is cached, persisted and invalidated under one name and key; instantiations need keys and handle names of their own. |
| Generic ports, callback traits and error enums | [E0002](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0002) | The platform implements a port once, by the trait's name, and an error is thrown by name; named instantiations of traits would lift it. |
| An alias in another crate than its template | [E0070](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0070) | The instantiation implements the boundary traits for the template's type, which only its crate may do. |
| Native generics: `func newest<T>`, `Selection<Todo>` as a generic class | none | The schema would need type parameters and described type sets. The overloads stay source-compatible with that. |

Lifetimes are [E0003](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0003) and const generics [E0002](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0002), as before; bounds and `where` clauses are yours and are checked at the alias, by `rustc`.

## Decimal, for money

`Decimal` is an exact decimal number: a 128-bit mantissa and a scale of at most 38, so `19.99` is `1999` with scale `2`. It never goes through a float. The scale is part of the value, so `1.10` and `1.1` are different values to `==` (and to a map) and the same number to a numeric comparison; `Decimal` is therefore not a map key.

| Platform | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | `undra::Decimal { mantissa: i128, scale: u8 }` | exact `FromStr` and `Display`, `cmp_numeric`; no arithmetic. With the `rust_decimal` feature, `rust_decimal::Decimal` crosses too; a value it cannot hold (more than 96 bits of mantissa, or a scale above 28, which a Swift `1 / 3` has) is a decode error, so round on the platform first |
| Swift | `Foundation.Decimal` | decoding is exact; `==` and hashing are numeric (`1.0 == 1.00`, unlike the other three); a NaN encodes as zero, 2127 or more saturates, digits past the 38th after the point (or past a 127-bit mantissa) are cut off |
| Kotlin | `java.math.BigDecimal` | `equals` is scale-sensitive, `compareTo` is numeric, as Kotlin engineers expect; digits past the 38th after the point (or past a 127-bit mantissa) round half up, a whole part of 2127 or more saturates |
| TypeScript | `Decimal` of `@undra/runtime` | `mantissa: bigint`, `scale`, `parse`, `toString`, `equals`, `compare`; no arithmetic, convert through `toString()` to your decimal library |

A scale above 38 is refused by every decoder, in the core as much as on the platforms. `i128` and `u128` stay out; the error points here, or at a `String` newtype for identifiers.

## Types from other crates

The types most Rust teams already use cross as the wire type they stand for, behind features of the `undra` crate. Each dependency is built without a clock or a randomness feature, so a core that uses them still builds for wasm32, iOS and Android, and still reads no clock of its own.

| Feature | Crosses as |
| --- | --- |
| `uuid` | `uuid::Uuid` as `Uuid` |
| `chrono` | `DateTime<Utc>` as `Timestamp` (milliseconds), `TimeDelta` as `Duration` |
| `time` | `OffsetDateTime` and `UtcDateTime` as `Timestamp` (normalised to UTC), `time::Duration` as `Duration` |
| `rust_decimal` | `rust_decimal::Decimal` as `Decimal` |
| `bytes` | `bytes::Bytes` as `Bytes` |

Precision is documented, not hidden. A `Timestamp` is milliseconds, and a finer value rounds toward negative infinity on its way out. A `Duration` is never negative, so a negative `TimeDelta` encodes as zero. `DateTime<Local>` and `DateTime<FixedOffset>` are [E0001](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0001): convert to `Utc`, offsets do not cross. Spell a type without its feature and the error names the feature to turn on.

The playground's [ledger](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/playground/core/src/ledger.rs) uses every shape on this page, and the contract scenario S31 checks them on Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/generics.html

# Generic functions, objects and stores

Write the code once over a type parameter, and say which types the platforms get. A generic function becomes a set of overloads; a generic object or store becomes one ordinary class for each alias you declare.

Undra's callers are Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript, which cannot call a Rust generic: there is no `T` at run time to dispatch on. So the core lists the types it is generic over where it declares the code, the macro expands the ordinary function, method, object or store once for each, and the platforms see what you would have written by hand. Nothing is generic on the wire, in the schema or in the runtimes; the [playground](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/playground/)'s [selection module](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/playground/core/src/selection.rs) is the example this page follows, and the contract scenario S34 checks it on Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript.

## Functions and methods

List the types after `generic(T = [..])`. The function stays a plain generic Rust function, so the core's own code and tests call it as usual; each listed type is one more function across the boundary, named `newest<Todo>` in the schema, with an id of its own.

Each language gets the shape its own engineers write. Swift and Kotlin overload on the parameter's type, and take the type itself (`Todo.self`, `Todo::class`) when no parameter says which one is meant, as `draft`. TypeScript has no overloading on types, so every generic function takes the type's name as a leading string literal and is one overload set whose signatures the compiler checks; the literal is always there, so every generic function is called the same way. A type that is not listed is the compiler's error in all three, with the candidates beside it.

A method of an object or store takes the same list on the method, `#[undra(generic(T = [Todo, Note]))]`; each listed type is one method, overloaded in the generated class the same way. The documentation, `async`, streams, typed errors and `ctx` work as they do for any function, because each instantiation is one.

The list holds named value types: records, enums, newtypes. A scalar, a `String`, a container or an object in a list is [E0072](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0072), because the platforms would have to invent a name for it. A function has one type parameter; two is [E0072](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0072) too. A type that has no list at all is [E0002](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0002): the callers are on the platforms, and the core must contain what they can call.

## Objects and stores

An object or a store over a type parameter is a *template*: it registers nothing, and each alias that names it is an ordinary object or store of that name. This is the shape of [generic data types](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/types.html#generic-data-types), extended to impl blocks and to a store's struct.

`TodoSelection` and `NoteSelection` are two stores in every sense: two type ids, two handles, two sets of signals, two entries in a snapshot, and each ticks and restores on its own. Toggling a to-do is one keyed insert into the to-do selection's `rows` and nothing for the notes. A generic object that is not a store has no attribute on its struct, only `#[undra::api(generic)]` on its impl block and an alias.

The alias is where the rules are checked, as if you had written the store out: a type argument the position cannot hold is the error you would get there (a `HashMap` key that is not a valid key is [E0006](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0006)), and a keyed list over a row type without the key field is [E0008](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0008) at the alias. A type parameter that stands in a signal needs the bound the signal needs, `SignalValue` (in the prelude), which the example's `Row` has as a supertrait.

### Where to put what

- **Declare the alias next to the template.** A hidden macro carries the template's signatures and expands where the alias stands, so the types they name must be in scope there. Next to the template this is invisible; in another module, a missing `use` is `rustc`'s "cannot find type in this scope", at the signature and in the alias's expansion. A store's instantiation also reads the store's fields and calls its `restore` hook, so in another module those must be visible there too: with private ones, `rustc` says "field `rows` of struct `Selection` is private" and "associated function `assemble` is private", in the alias's expansion. In the template's module both questions go away.
- **The alias lives in the crate of its template, once per instantiation.** A second alias for the same instantiation, or one in another crate, is [E0070](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0070): the instantiation implements the boundary traits for the template's type, which only that crate may do.
- **A store's struct comes first.** The impl block must be below its struct in the same module; the macro says so in a name, `_undra_error_E0011_…`, when it is not.
- **One block per type, for the type applied to its own parameters.** `impl<T> Cache<Vec<T>>` and a method with a list inside a generic block are [E0074](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0074): an instantiation is one class, and a second list would multiply it.
- **Name an instantiation when a signature mentions one.** A function that returns `Arc<Selection<T>>` or `Page<T>` reaches the platforms as the alias's class or record, found by the compiler; spelling `Selection<Todo>` in a hand-written, non-generic signature is still [E0002](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0002), and says which alias to declare.

## What an instantiation is

It is exactly a hand-written definition under another name, so everything that works for those works for it, and nothing was added to the wire, the runtimes or the generated classes of an object.

- **Ids.** A function's id comes from its schema name, `fnv1a32("fn.newest<Todo>")`; an alias's from its own name. A raw call with an id that names no instantiation (`newest<Draft>`) is refused as a bad request and the core carries on, `UndraCallError.refused` on the platforms.
- **The schema.** One definition per instantiation; a function's carries a label (`newest`, `T = Todo`) that the generators read to make overloads, and that is part of the schema's hash only where it is set, so every schema without generics keeps its hash. `undra bindgen --check` and `schema.json` see it like any other change.
- **Persistence and the testing kit.** One restorer and one fingerprint per instantiated store, computed from its concrete signals; a recording is of one schema, so adding an instantiation records again, as any schema change does. Renaming an alias is removing a store type and adding one.
- **Devtools** list a call as `newest<Todo>` and a store under its alias.
- **Two cores** each hold the instantiations of the crates they link; nothing is shared at run time.

## When it goes wrong

The macro's errors are the usual four-part ones: [E0072](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0072) for a list that is wrong (a parameter the function does not have, an empty list, a type listed twice, a type that is not a named value type, two parameters), [E0074](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0074) for a generic block of the wrong shape, [E0002](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0002) for a generic with no list, a generic constructor or a signature that spells an instantiation, and [E0070](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0070) for a second or foreign alias. An error inside one instantiation says which one: "in `newest<Todo>`".

A call with a type that is not listed is the platform compiler's error, naming the overloads that exist: Swift's "no exact matches in call to global function", Kotlin's "none of the following candidates is applicable", TypeScript's "no overload matches this call". One caveat, from Swift 6.3: for an *array literal* of an unlisted type (`newest(rows: [Draft(..)])`) the compiler prints "failed to produce diagnostic for expression" instead of the message it prints for a variable. It is the compiler's wording, only in that case; the call is rejected either way.

An argument that does not say its type picks no overload, as with any overload set: `newest(rows: [])` and a `nil` are Swift's "ambiguous use of", and `newest(emptyList())` is Kotlin's "cannot infer type". Write the type where the value is made, `newest(rows: [Todo]())` or `newest(emptyList<Todo>())` (in Swift, a declared result type, `let latest: Todo? = try newest(rows: [])`, also picks it). TypeScript's leading literal always picks the overload, so `newest("Todo", [])` needs nothing.

In TypeScript the exported function is one overload set whose body switches on the literal, so a bundle that calls `newest("Todo", ..)` also carries the code and codecs of `newest("Note", ..)`: tree-shaking keeps or drops a generic function whole, with every type it is listed for.

## What is not there
