The table is [on the types page](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/types.html#generics-limits), with what would lift each limit. In short: no open-ended `T` (every instantiation is listed), one type parameter per function, no generic queries, ports, callbacks or error enums, and no native generics, because the schema and the platforms' dispatch have no type parameters. A generic `Page<T>` that a function returns is still the named record of [the data types](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/types.html#generic-data-types).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/paging.html

# Paging and lazy lists

A feed from a server grows by the page. A big collection in the core is read a window at a time. Neither ships a whole list across the boundary.

## Two kinds of long list

"Paging" hides two different problems, and they get different tools.

|  | A feed from a server | A big collection in the core |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where the rows are | on a server; the core fetches a page at a time | already in the core (a database, a derived view over 50,000 rows) |
| What the screen shows | every row loaded so far | a window of it |
| Use | an `infinite` query: a keyed list that grows by the page | `Lazy<T>`: the platform pages the core's list on demand |

## Infinite queries

An infinite query is a query with a cursor. The function takes the cursor and returns one page; the handle on each platform shows all the pages loaded so far as one list, keyed by the field you name.

The cursor is not part of the cache key and not a parameter on the platform. The handle has the five signals of every query and two more, `hasNextPage` and `fetchingNextPage`, and `data` is the list itself, empty before the first page rather than optional.

Loading the next page appends with the same recorded `push` a store uses, so the change-set is the new rows and nothing else, however long the list already is. A refetch (a stale entry, `invalidate`, the app coming to the front, the network returning, a poll) fetches the loaded pages again in order from the first, each with the cursor the previous response returned, and sends only what changed. `refetch_pages = N` bounds that: a feed scrolled through fifty pages need not cost fifty requests on every refresh.

A mutation edits the whole list with `CacheView::update_items`, inside the optimistic transaction. `persist` keeps the first `persist_pages` pages (one by default) in the same format as any persisted query, so a cold start shows the first page at once. Not in this version: previous pages (paging backwards) and an upper bound on pages kept in memory; for a list that outgrows memory, feed a store's `Lazy<T>` from the query.

## Lazy lists

A store field of type `Lazy<T>` is a list the core owns and the platform reads a window of. The platform is told how many rows there are and which version of the list that is; it asks the core for the pages it needs.

Use a lazy container to show it (`LazyVStack`, `LazyColumn`, a virtualised list), never one that builds every row up front: SwiftUI's `List` over `0..<count` reads all of them at once and the cache cannot hold that. Reading a row that is not loaded gives `nil`, `null` or `undefined` and asks for its page of 50 rows and one page of prefetch on each side, once. Requests made in one frame go out together. At most 24 pages are kept, least recently touched first out. A change to the list, whatever it is, is one 12-byte entry (the new length and the new version): the platform keeps showing the rows it has and asks again for the pages on screen, so a change costs the window, never the list. A reply carries the version it was read at, so a page that arrives after a newer change is thrown away and asked for again.

|  | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| Observing a list of 100,000 rows | 20 bytes |
| A change of any size | 12 bytes, then the window |
| A page of 50 rows in the core | microseconds (a few hundred nanoseconds on the reference machine) |
| Rows kept on the platform | at most 24 pages |

`Lazy::over(&derived)` is a read-only lazy view of a derived list ([core concepts](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/concepts.html)): its pages come from the derived index in O(log n + page), so a filtered and sorted view over 50,000 rows pages as cheaply as the list itself. A store with a view needs a `restore` hook, because the view is rebuilt from its source rather than saved. A `Lazy` is store state: a snapshot carries its rows, and after a restore the platform gets a new page server and reads its window again.

Rows not yet loaded have no identity, so animations across a re-page follow the index; the loaded rows have their keys. A `PagingSource` adapter over `UndraLazyList` for Jetpack Paging can follow if teams ask. On iOS 15 and 16 the Swift class is `UndraLazyListObject`, an `ObservableObject` you hold with `@ObservedObject`.

The playground's [Library and feed](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/playground/core/src/paging.rs) use both, and the contract scenario S32 checks them on Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript. The [pagination recipe](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/pagination.html) shows the older shape, one query per page number.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/polling.html

# Polling

An `interval` on a query refetches it while it is observed. It runs from the end of the last fetch, pauses when the app is away and resumes when it returns.

## An interval on a query

Add `interval` to a query and the core refetches it while somebody is looking.

The shortest interval is one second; below that the compiler says to use a stream, which is the tool for real-time data ([the opt-in ports](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/db.html) have WebSocket and Server-Sent Events).

## How it polls

The next fetch is scheduled one interval after the *end* of the previous one, whether it succeeded or failed once its retries ran out. A fetch slower than the interval never overlaps the next, and a struggling server is asked less often rather than hammered.

| Situation | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Nobody observes the entry | no timer; the last observer going away cancels it |
| The app is in the background or inactive | paused, unless the query says `poll_in_background` |
| The device is offline | paused |
| The app comes to the front, the network returns | the usual triggers fire (a stale entry refetches, going online refetches everything observed) and polling continues from the end of that fetch |
| Several observers | the entry polls at the shortest interval any of them asked for, each new observer starting from the attribute's |
| A fetch fails | retried with backoff as any query is, then the interval runs from the end; the error shows and the next success clears it |

Time comes from the Clock and delays from the Timer port, so a test under `undra::ports::fakes` advances the clock and sees each poll, background pause included. The contract scenario S33 checks it on every platform with real timers.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/realtime.html

# WebSocket & server-sent events

Live data comes into the core like everything else: through a port. The core reads at its own pace and decides when to reconnect; the platform owns the socket.

## Turn it on

`WebSocket` and `Sse` are opt-in ports: a core asks for them with a cargo feature, and a core that does not keeps the schema hash and the wasm size it had. Each platform answers with its own client: `URLSessionWebSocketTask`, the Kotlin runtime's client on the JVM and Android, the browser's `WebSocket`.

core/Cargo.toml

```toml
[dependencies]
undra = { version = "0.1", features = ["websocket", "sse"] }
```

## A connection

The core connects, sends and reads. Messages arrive as a stream the core pulls: it asks for 16 at a time, so a core that stops reading stops the socket, on the platforms that can pause one.

core/src/chat.rs

```rust
use undra::ports::ws::{WsConnection, WsError, WsMessage, WsOptions};

let conn = WsConnection::connect(&ctx, "wss://chat.example.com/room", WsOptions::default()).await?;
conn.send_text("hello").await?;
let mut messages = conn.messages();
while let Some(next) = undra::ports::next(&mut messages).await {
    match next {
        Ok(WsMessage::Text(text)) => room.push(text),
        Ok(WsMessage::Binary(_)) => {}
        Err(WsError::Closed { code: 1000, .. }) => break, // the server said goodbye
        Err(error) => return Err(error),
    }
}
```

## Every end is typed

| What happened | The stream ends with |
| --- | --- |
| the core called `close` | nothing: it simply ends |
| the server sent a close frame | `Closed { code, reason }` |
| the connection dropped | `Network` |
| the server broke the protocol | `Protocol` |
| the upgrade was refused | `Refused { status }` (from `connect`) |

Browsers cannot send headers with a WebSocket, so the browser adapter refuses a connect that has some instead of dropping them: put the credential in the URL or a subprotocol.

## Reconnecting is yours

The port never reconnects on its own: which close codes to retry, how long to wait and what to resend are your app's rules, and they run in the core, where a test drives them with a fake clock. `Backoff` gives the delay, a weak context sleeps.

rust

```rust
let backoff = Backoff::default(); // 500 ms doubling to 30 s, with jitter from the Rng port
let mut attempt = 0;
while weak.sleep(backoff.delay(attempt, &*ctx.rng())).await.is_ok() {
    attempt += 1;
    // connect again, re-subscribe, reset `attempt` once a message arrives
}
```

## Server-sent events

`sse::subscribe` is a stream of events parsed as the HTML standard says. It ends with `Ended` when the server finishes the response; subscribe again with the last event id to resume.

rust

```rust
let mut events = sse::subscribe(&ctx, "https://api.example.com/feed", vec![], last_id.clone());
while let Some(Ok(event)) = undra::ports::next(&mut events).await {
    last_id = event.id.clone().or(last_id);
    feed.apply(event.data);
}
```

## In tests

`FakeWebSocket` and `FakeSse` are scripted servers: accept or refuse, push, close, drop, echo. They record what the core sent and how much it pulled, so backpressure is an assertion.

rust

```rust
let fakes = fakes::install(&t);
fakes.web_socket.echo(true);
// ... the core connects and sends ...
assert!(fakes.web_socket.delivered(conn) <= consumed + 24);
```

On the web the adapters are an opt-in import, `@undra/runtime/realtime`, so an app that does not use them ships none of them. Design: [ADR-047](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-047-websocket-and-sse-ports.md).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/db.html

# Local database

Structured local data with SQLite, written once in the core. The platform owns the file and the thread; the core sends bound statements and gets typed rows back.

## Turn it on

`Db` is an opt-in port over the SQLite each platform already has: the system library on iOS, `android.database.sqlite` on Android, a JDBC driver on the JVM, `node:sqlite` in Node and wa-sqlite in a worker on the web. The core stays small and never blocks: the platform owns the database and its thread. On the web the files live in the origin private file system, which one tab holds at a time: a second tab of the same app gets `Unavailable`.

core/Cargo.toml

```toml
[dependencies]
undra = { version = "0.1", features = ["db"] }
```

## Open and migrate

Migrations are numbered SQL. The platform runs every one the database has not seen yet, in one transaction: if one fails, none of them happened.

core/src/notes.rs

```rust
const MIGRATIONS: &[Migration] = &[
    Migration::new(1, "CREATE TABLE notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, done INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)"),
    Migration::new(2, "CREATE INDEX notes_done ON notes (done)"),
];

let db = Database::open(&ctx, "notes", MIGRATIONS).await?;
```

## Values are parameters

SQL is a `&'static str`, so a value can only reach a statement as a bound parameter. Cells come back typed.

rust

```rust
db.execute("INSERT INTO notes (title) VALUES (?)", params![title]).await?;
let rows = db.query("SELECT id, title, done FROM notes WHERE done = ?", params![false]).await?;
for row in rows.iter() {
    let id: i64 = row.get("id")?;
    let title: String = row.get("title")?;
}
```

## Transactions

A transaction commits when its body returns `Ok` and rolls back on `Err`, or when its task is dropped half-way.

rust

```rust
db.transaction(|tx| async move {
    for title in titles {
        tx.execute("INSERT INTO notes (title) VALUES (?)", params![title]).await?;
    }
    Ok(())
}).await?;
```

## Errors you can match

| Error | When |
| --- | --- |
| `Constraint { kind, .. }` | a `UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`, foreign-key or `CHECK` constraint failed |
| `Busy` | the database stayed locked past five seconds |
| `Migration { version, .. }` | a migration failed and everything rolled back, or the file is newer than the app |
| `Sql` | a syntax error, a missing table, a cell read as the wrong type |
| `Corrupt`, `Full`, `Unavailable` | the file, the disk, or no database to talk to |

## In tests

`FakeDb` answers by SQL fragment, injects failures and records every statement, migration and transaction, so the core's database logic is tested without a device.

rust

```rust
fakes.db.fail_on("INSERT", DbError::Full);
assert_eq!(notes.add("milk".into()).await, Err(DbError::Full));
```

Design: [ADR-048](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-048-db-port.md).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/testing.html

# Testing your app

The kit runs your real core on fakes and a manual clock, plays a recorded session as a screen state, and replays what a session asked of the platform.

## Pick one

| You want | Use |
| --- | --- |
| a screen that reacts, or a cache that goes stale | `PreviewCore`: the real core, its ports faked, time in your hands |
| a state that is slow to reach | `RecordedCore`: a recorded session under the generated stores, no core |
| a test that fails when the core makes another request | `Replayer`: a recording as the script for the ports |

The same three exist in Swift (`UndraTestKit`, a product of the `UndraRuntime` package), Kotlin (`com.github.shreypdev.undra:testkit`, at the runtime's version), TypeScript (`@undra/testkit`, the release's `undra-testkit-<version>.tgz`, no runtime dependencies) and, for tests of the core itself, Rust (`undra::testing`). They sit beside the runtimes: no generated file, wire frame or C entry point changes.

## Preview a screen

`PreviewCore.load` starts your app&rsquo;s own core in the process with a deterministic fake behind every standard port. A seed fills them; `advance` moves the clock one deadline at a time and lets the core settle between.

**Sleeps in a native core run in real time.** The manual clock moves what the core reads (`Clock`, staleness, timestamps) and timers armed through the `Timer` port. A native core&rsquo;s `ctx.sleep` is waited for, as the C ABI never hands sleeps to the host: `advance(5_000)` does not finish a 5-second sleep, it returns at once and the task still wakes 5 real seconds later. In a native preview, make that delay a parameter the preview sets to a few milliseconds, wait the real duration and then `settle()`, preview the state after the wait with `RecordedCore`, or run the story on the web, where sleeps follow the clock. `advance` stops after `maxTimers` firings with a typed `TimerStormError` (a timer that re-arms itself without time passing never ends).

## Play a recording

`RecordedCore` loads a recording and releases its change-sets with a playhead you move. Calls are answered by the next recorded reply for the same target; a call the recording has no reply for is a typed refusal that names it.

## Record a session

The dev server sees every call, reply, change-set and port call, on iOS, Android and the web alike, so one flag captures a session. A reload starts a new core, so a new file (`session-2.json`).

bash

```bash
undra dev --record session.json
```

A recording holds what the app asked the platform and was answered, so it can hold secrets. `SecureStore` payloads are left out by default (the calls are there, their arguments and replies are empty; `--record-secrets` keeps them). HTTP headers and bodies, `Kv` values and files are recorded as they are: do not share a recording of a real account&rsquo;s session. If the file cannot be written the runner warns once, stops recording and keeps serving.

A recording is one canonical JSON document, `undra.recording` version 1: payloads in hex, handles as strings, times in milliseconds. A recording made on one platform is read by all of them.

## Replay port traffic

A `Replayer` answers a core&rsquo;s port calls from a recording, in order per port. A call that differs is a typed `mismatch`, an extra one is `exhausted`, a recorded call with no reply in the file is `unanswered`, and a recorded call never made is `unconsumed`. A deviation consumes nothing, so one wrong call does not shift every later answer.

## In the playground

- **iOS:** three SwiftUI `#Preview`s, built with the app.
- **Android:** two Compose `@Preview`s over `RecordedCore` (the preview pane cannot load a native core); the kit is a debug-only dependency.
- **Web:** four stories in Component Story Format, rendered by Vite alone. Storybook loads them unchanged and is not a dependency.

The kit uses only public APIs, and CI builds all three. [docs/TESTING.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/TESTING.md) has the full reference: the seed and recording formats, the fakes&rsquo; conformance file, and the limits.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/updates.html

# Shipping an update

An app update changes the core's types while the device still holds data the old version wrote. Undra reads it by name, converts what it can, and refuses the rest out loud.

## What outlives a build

Three things an app writes can be read by the next version of the app: a **snapshot** of its stores (crash recovery on the web, `undra dev`'s reload, an app that saves one), the **cached results** of `persist` queries, and the **offline queue** of idempotent mutations. Each records the *fingerprint* of its types: a hash of exactly the records, enums and fields it holds. A change elsewhere in the core (a new method, a new query, a doc comment) does not move it, so the data is used as it is, with no work at all.

When a fingerprint did change, Undra reads the old bytes with the description that was stored next to them and converts them to the new types **by name**. It never guesses: data that cannot be converted is refused with a typed outcome you can show, never decoded into the wrong values.

## What migrates for free

These changes need no code. They are the ones most updates are made of:

| Change | What the old data becomes |
| --- | --- |
| Fields or signals reordered | matched by name; order is irrelevant |
| A field added as an `Option` | `None` |
| A field added with `#[undra(default)]` | its zero value: `false`, `0`, `""`, empty, the nil UUID, the epoch |
| A store signal added with `#[undra(default)]` | `T::default()` |
| A field, variant or signal removed | dropped |
| Enum variants added or renumbered | matched by name |
| An integer widened (`i32` to `i64`, `u8` to `u32`, `u16` to `i32`), `f32` to `f64` | the same value |
| `T` to `Option<T>`, `Bytes` to `Vec<u8>` or back | the same value |
| Any of these inside a `Vec`, an `Option` or a map | applied to every item |

Anything else is not structural: a narrowing (`i64` to `i32`), a type change (`i32` to `String`), a renamed field, variant or signal, a variant the new type no longer has, or a new field with no default. Those need a hook.

## Writing a hook

A hook is a plain function marked `#[undra::migrate]`. It receives the old value as a `DynValue` (fields and variants by name) and returns the new one, or a `MigrateError` to refuse it. There are three kinds:

rust

```rust
use undra::prelude::*;

// Any persisted `Todo` whose structure changed, wherever it is.
#[undra::migrate(ty = "Todo")]
fn todo_from_name(old: &DynValue) -> Result<Todo, MigrateError> {
    let title = old.field("name").and_then(DynValue::as_str)
        .ok_or_else(|| MigrateError::new("a todo without a name"))?;
    Ok(Todo { title: title.to_owned(), done: false })
}

// One signal of one store in a snapshot (`None`: the snapshot has no such signal).
#[undra::migrate(store = "Profile", signal = "age")]
fn age(old: Option<&DynValue>) -> Result<f32, MigrateError> {
    match old.and_then(DynValue::as_i64) {
        Some(age) if age >= 0 => Ok(age as f32),
        Some(age) => Err(MigrateError::new(format!("{age} is not an age"))),
        None => Ok(18.0),
    }
}

// The queued input of one mutation, by parameter name.
#[undra::migrate(mutation = "add_todo")]
fn add_todo(old: &DynRecord) -> Result<DynRecord, MigrateError> {
    let mut new = old.clone();
    new.rename("name", "title");
    Ok(new)
}
```

Structural migration is tried first, then the hook. Hooks run in the core, under the panic guard: a hook that panics is a failed migration, logged with its name. `from = "0x…"` restricts a hook to one old fingerprint, when you need to tell two older versions apart. A target that does not exist, or a function of the wrong shape, is [E0066](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0066).

## When nothing converts

Each kind of data has its own refusal, and none of them loses data silently:

| Data | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| A snapshot | the restore fails as a whole with `RestoreError::Incompatible { store, signal, reason }` (restore code 7 on the platforms: `UndraRestoreError` / `UndraRestoreException`), the core is unchanged, and the reason is logged. One exception: a store *type* the new build removed is left out (its handles go stale) and reported. |
| A cached query result | deleted, because it can be fetched again; a WARN names the query and the reason |
| A queued mutation | never deleted: it moves to the dead letters, and the rest of the queue replays |

The dead letters are yours to show, export or settle:

rust

```rust
let query = ctx.query();
for letter in query.dead_letters() {
    log::warn!("{} could not be sent: {}", letter.mutation, letter.reason);
    // letter.params: the input by parameter name; letter.raw: the bytes as stored
}
query.retry_dead_letter(key)?;   // after an update that added a hook
query.discard_dead_letter(key);  // for good
```

`ctx.query().persist_stats()` counts what was migrated, dropped and dead-lettered, and the runtime's statistics carry the same numbers under `query.persist`.

## Testing an update

Build the old and the new core, write the data with one and read it with the other. The playground does exactly this in its contract scenarios: `UNDRA_PLAYGROUND_V2=1 undra build` builds a second core whose stores, records and mutations changed the way an update does, and every platform checks that a snapshot and a queue written by the first are read by name by the second, and that an incompatible change is refused or dead-lettered. In Rust, a `TestRuntime` restores a snapshot you build from an edited `Schema` (its `stores_closure` is the description an older build would have written).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/reviewing-generated-code.html

# Reviewing generated code and versioning the API

The Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript that `undra bindgen` writes are an artifact of the core's schema. Review the schema; let CI prove the bindings.

## The rule

- **Do not read the generated files in a review.** GitHub collapses them, and `undra bindgen --check` proves they are exactly what the schema generates.
- **Read the schema diff.** `undra schema diff --against origin/main` lists what changed in the public API, one line per change, each marked `breaking` or `additive`.
- **Version the API as the schema, not as its generated text.** Commit `schema.json` next to `generated/`: an API change is a few lines of JSON, and thousands of lines of bindings move with it.

## What the lines are

The generated code is long because each public item becomes native code: an observable class with typed members, a decoder per signal, a documented wrapper per method, in three languages. That is the price of bindings a Swift, Kotlin or TypeScript engineer would write themselves, so the fix is not to generate less. Here is what the playground, with 15 stores, produces per platform.

|  | Lines | Code | Doc comments | Other comments | Blank |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Swift | 7,787 | 6,626 | 699 | 43 | 419 |
| Kotlin | 7,365 | 5,698 | 1,263 | 18 | 386 |
| TypeScript | 7,692 | 6,121 | 1,170 | 11 | 390 |

Lines of each kind of generated file:

| File | Swift | Kotlin | TypeScript |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Types | 885 | 755 | 785 |
| Errors | 422 | 270 | 462 |
| Objects | 1,490 | 1,650 | 1,902 |
| Stores | 3,737 | 3,430 | 3,268 |
| Ports | 22 | 28 | 27 |
| Queries | 763 | 727 | 744 |
| Callbacks | 91 | 105 | 86 |
| Ids | 286 | 290 | 283 |
| Core | 37 | 77 | 68 |
| Index | – | – | 11 |
| Package and build files | 54 | 33 | 56 |
| **Total** | **7,787** | **7,365** | **7,692** |

Three things stand out. Doc comments are 9 to 17 percent of a tree and the reason the bindings can be used without the Rust source open. `Stores` is almost half of every tree. And one fixture, the `Bench` store (128 counters and a 10,000-row list, there to measure the boundary), is 1,698 of the Swift lines, 1,325 of the Kotlin and 1,082 of the TypeScript; the median of the other fourteen stores is about 125 lines per platform, so one real feature is on the order of 130 to 250 lines on each of the three. `node scripts/generated-weight.mjs [dir]` prints these tables for any generated tree.

## Collapsed in review

Every generated file says what it is on its first line: the generator, the core, the schema hash and "Do not edit". `package.json` has no comments, so it carries the sentence as a `"//"` member, and `tsconfig.json` as a comment line. `undra bindgen` also writes a `.gitattributes` at the root of each tree, `swift/`, `kotlin/` and `ts/`:

swift/.gitattributes

```gitattributes
# Generated by `undra bindgen`: do not edit, it is rewritten with the bindings.
# GitHub collapses these files in a pull request and leaves them out of the language statistics.
# Review the schema (`undra schema diff`), not the bindings: `undra bindgen --check` proves they
# match it. A collapsed file opens to its full diff when you click it.
* linguist-generated=true
```

GitHub reads `linguist-generated` to fold a file in a pull request's diff and to leave it out of the repository's language bar. The diff is not hidden: click a collapsed file to see it, and `git diff` prints it as ever (the rule does not set `-diff`). The pattern covers the whole tree, so a file of your own kept inside one folds too; put a `.gitattributes` with `-linguist-generated` beside it, or keep your files outside the generated trees. Lint exclusions for the trees are a separate matter, handled with the build.

## Review the schema, not the bindings

bash

```bash
undra schema export -o schema.json              # once, and after each API change; commit it
undra schema diff --against origin/main         # what changed since the base
```

text

```
Public API: origin/main:schema.json (schema 0x4d503c0c6414f9bc) -> schema.json (schema 0x53c10651c39d0ca4)

breaking  case Filter.Archived: added (an exhaustive `switch` or `when` over it stops compiling)
breaking  field Todo.due: added (Option<Timestamp>, with a default): Swift and Kotlin initializers default it, but a TypeScript object literal that builds a `Todo` must name it
breaking  field Todo.priority: added without a default (u8): everything that builds a `Todo` must supply it
breaking  method Todos.add: parameter `tags: Vec<String>` added
additive  method Todos.clear: added (fn clear())
breaking  method Todos.toggle: removed (was fn toggle(id: u32))
additive  signal Todos.open_count: added (u32, computed)
additive  function import_all: added (async fn import_all(items: Vec<Todo>) -> u32)
breaking  method Notifier.dismiss: added (fn dismiss()); the app implements it, so its implementation must add it
additive  port Presence: added (an event port: the app sends its events when it has them, and implements nothing)
additive  callback Cancel: added
breaking  mutation add_todo: removed (was async fn add_todo(title: String) -> Result<Todo, TodoError>)
additive  query todo: stale time changed from none to 30000 ms

7 breaking, 6 additive.
```

The old side is the file as committed at the ref (`git show`; nothing is built), the new side is the file in the working tree; name another file after the ref, or give two files and no ref. The order is fixed, so the same two schemas print the same text, and doc comments and wire ids are not compared. The command exits with status 0 whatever it finds, so run it freely; add `--exit-code` to make a breaking line exit 1 in CI.

Nothing is built, so the report is only as current as the file. The bindings beside it say which schema they were generated from, and the command compares: when `schema.json` disagrees with the bindings in the working tree (an API change nobody exported) or at the ref, it prints a warning that names both hashes, and a stale working-tree file fails `--exit-code` too.

The size of a review is the point. The thirteen changes above, on a to-do core small enough to read, change 581 lines of generated code (183 of Swift, 193 of Kotlin, 205 of TypeScript), 77 lines of `schema.json` and print 13 lines of diff. `schema export` writes every type and every small definition on one line, so the playground's whole schema is about 3,300 lines and a field that became optional is one changed line.

The pull request template asks for this output when a core's API changes: paste it, and justify every `breaking` line.

## What breaking means

A line is **breaking** when code an app wrote against the old bindings can stop compiling or change what it means against the new ones, and **additive** when it cannot. A removed or changed signature is breaking; an added function, method, store, object or record is additive. An added record field is breaking even with a default: a TypeScript record is an interface, and an object literal that builds one must name every field (Swift and Kotlin default an appended field of a primitive, string, time, optional or collection type). Items are matched by name.

| Item | Additive | Breaking |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Any item | added | removed |
| Record field | a default gained | added, with or without `#[undra(default)]`; removed; retyped; reordered; a default lost |
| Enum or error case | message changed | added (an exhaustive `switch` or `when` stops compiling); removed; payload or index changed |
| Method, constructor, function | added; `Ctx` taken or not (no generated signature shows it) | removed; a parameter added, removed, renamed, retyped or reordered; return type or `async` changed |
| Store signal | added; `no_coalesce`, `default`, `computed` or `key` changed (every signal is a read-only property) | removed; type changed |
| Query or mutation | added; cache key, stale time, `persist`, `idempotent`, polling changed; a paged query's cursor type | removed; parameters or return type changed; paging added or removed; the item key changed to or from `id` |
| Port (the app implements it) | a standard port added | an opt-in standard port added (a web app registers its adapter); any other port added; a method added, removed or changed; removed |
| Event port (the app sends it) | added; a method added | a method removed or changed; removed |
| Callback (the app implements it) | added | a method added, removed or changed; `background` changed (the calls move on or off the main thread); removed |

"Additive" means compatible, so it includes behaviour that no signature shows, like a query's stale time. A line holds for all three languages: what breaks in any one of them is breaking. The full rules are [SPEC 2.6](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/SPEC.md).

## Keeping it honest in CI

The first step proves the committed bindings, the second proves the committed schema, and the third turns a breaking change into a decision somebody makes on purpose. Without the third, the diff is for the reviewer to read. To skip committing bindings at all, generate them at build time and ignore the trees; the committed bindings are what a native reviewer's IDE and a Swift package see without running `undra`, which is why Undra commits them by default.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/web.html

# Workers & crash recovery

On the web the core is a wasm module. It can run off the main thread, and when a panic traps it, it can come back from its last snapshot.

## Worker mode

`mode: "wasm-worker"` runs the core in a Web Worker, so a heavy call never blocks the UI. The core calls some ports synchronously (Clock, Rng, Log and any `#[undra::port(sync)]`) and cannot wait for the main thread, so those are answered **in the worker**. Clock, Rng and Log need nothing from you. Ports with asynchronous methods (Http, Kv, SecureStore, Fs and your own async ports) run on the main thread, exactly as in `wasm-main`.

## Your own synchronous ports

Put them in a small module the worker imports before the core starts, and pass its URL. The same module overrides Clock, Rng or the core's timers in this mode:

ts

```ts
// main.ts
const core = await UndraCore.load({
  mode: "wasm-worker", wasm, expectedSchemaHash: UndraIds.schemaHash,
  worker: { ports: new URL("./worker-ports.js", import.meta.url) },
});

// worker-ports.ts: runs inside the worker
export default {
  [UndraIds.Ports.Locale.portId]: localePortImpl({ hello: () => "Bonjour" }),
};
export const adapters = { timer: myTimer }; // optional: clock, rng, timer
```

A synchronous port registered on the main thread in this mode is refused when the core loads (`UndraError("options")`, naming the port), not at its first call. With a bundler, make the module a worker entry.

## Recovering from a crash

A native core contains a panic and keeps going. A wasm core cannot: the panic traps the instance. With `recovery: crashRecovery()` (imported from `@undra/runtime`, so an app without it ships none of this code), the runtime keeps a snapshot of your stores (at most once a second while they change, in an idle moment, in the worker in worker mode) and restarts from it:

ts

```ts
import { UndraCore, crashRecovery } from "@undra/runtime";

const core = await UndraCore.load({
  mode: "wasm-main", wasm, expectedSchemaHash: UndraIds.schemaHash,
  recovery: crashRecovery(), // or crashRecovery({ snapshotEveryMs, maxSnapshotBytes, maxRestarts, perMs })
  onPanic: (report) => crashReporter.send(report),
  onCoreRestarted: (e) => configureRemote(core, settings), // re-apply core state that is not in a store
});
```

| On a trap | What your app sees |
| --- | --- |
| Calls and streams in flight | fail with `UndraCallError.Unavailable`, reason `restarted`; they may or may not have run and are never retried for you |
| Stores | keep their handles and show the snapshot's values |
| Query handles | keep their handle and their wrapper (the core re-issues them from the snapshot, and builds each one again when the recovery observes it), then fetch again; one created after the last snapshot goes stale |
| Other objects | go stale: calls on them are refused |
| Store writes after the last snapshot, running tasks and timers, configuration a call set | lost; re-apply configuration in `onCoreRestarted` |

Persisted queries and the offline queue live in `Kv` and are not affected. Past `maxRestarts` within `perMs` (default 3 a minute) the core stays down and `onClose` reports the crash, so a panic that recurs on every restart cannot loop. Recovery is off by default: it costs a snapshot up to once a second (about 0.04 ms for 100 KB of state; a restart takes about 1.6 ms).

## Randomness

A wasm core needs WebCrypto. Without `crypto.getRandomValues`, `load` rejects with `UndraTransportError("unsupported")` rather than run with predictable idempotency keys.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/production.html

# Operating in production

Four things a shipped app needs that nobody should write for themselves: a crash report that names the Rust frame, the symbol files to read it with, a way to finish the offline queue while the app is not on screen, and a core that is as small as a native release build can make it.

## Crash reports

A panic in the core never crashes the app: the call that was running fails with `UndraCallError.panicked` and the core goes on. Your crash reporter still wants to know. Set `onPanic` when you load the core and it receives one structured report for every panic the core contained (a call, a detached task, a computed, a background task, an init or migration hook), once, in order, on the main thread. Nothing is linked for you: forward the report to the reporter you already use. Without `onPanic` the runtime logs one line, so a panic is never silent.

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| The panic | `message` and `location` (`file:line:column`; release builds remap your home directory to `~`, so no path names your machine). |
| The context | `operation`, what was running (`Todos.add`, `task`, `computed Todos.visible`), and the Rust `thread`. |
| The backtrace | `frames`, innermost first, at most 48. Always the `address` of each instruction as an offset into the core's image; a debug build also has `symbol`, `file` and `line`. |
| The build | `namespace`, `coreVersion` and `schemaHash`: which core. |
| The image | `imageId`: the Mach-O UUID, ELF build id or wasm SHA-256 of the image the addresses belong to, which is what symbol files are keyed by. |

Crashlytics takes the frames as `StackFrame(address:)` on iOS and as synthetic stack trace elements on Android, Sentry as an event whose frames carry `instruction_addr` and whose debug image is `imageId`. The recipes are three lines each and Undra links no reporter.

On the web a panic traps the module, which cannot call out of its last moments. The runtime builds the same report from what the core logged before it trapped and the trap's stack, and calls `onPanic` before it restarts anything ([crash recovery](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/web.html#recovering-from-a-crash)). A wasm frame's `address` is the module offset in the stack line (`wasm-function[41]:0x1a2b`), its `symbol` the function name when the build has one. The generated entry passes `namespace`; the module carries no version, so pass `coreVersion` in the load options if you want it in the report. In tests, `CaptureDiagnostics` (the Rust fakes and each testing kit) records the reports.

## Symbol files

A release build keeps line tables and nothing else: the code, the optimisation and the size of what ships are the same with or without them. `undra build --release` strips the copies it ships, keeps the unstripped ones below `build/symbols/` and writes `manifest.json` there (per image: namespace, core version, schema hash and the image id a report carries). `--no-symbols` skips all of it.

| Platform | Ships | Symbols to keep (and upload) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| iOS | `build/ios/<Ns>Core.xcframework` | The **app's own dSYM**: Xcode's Release configuration already asks for one, and it now contains the Rust frames. Crashlytics and Sentry upload it as for Swift. A static library has no dSYM of its own. |
| Android | `build/android/jniLibs/<abi>/lib<ns>.so`, stripped | `build/symbols/android/<abi>/lib<ns>.so`, and `native-debug-symbols.zip` in the Play Console layout (Crashlytics: `unstrippedNativeLibsDir`). The libraries carry a GNU build id. |
| Web | `build/web/<ns>.wasm` | `build/symbols/web/<ns>.debug.wasm` (the same code with its names), `<ns>.wasm.functions.txt` (the function map) and `<ns>.dwarf.wasm` for the browser's debugger. |
| Host (JVM, macOS) | `build/host/lib<ns>.{dylib,so}` | A `.dSYM` or `.debug` file next to it. |

The generated CI workflows upload `build/symbols/` next to the app build, so every release keeps the files its crashes need. To read a report by hand, give it to `undra symbolicate`:

sh

```sh
undra symbolicate report.json              # a report as onPanic received it, serialised
undra symbolicate --platform android --image-id <build id> 0x2f3a1c
undra symbolicate --dsym App.app.dSYM report.json     # iOS: the app's dSYM
```

It finds the image by `imageId` in the manifest and prints one line per frame, `address symbol (file:line)`: `atos` with the dSYM on Apple platforms, `llvm-symbolizer` on the Android twin, the function map and the debug module on the web.

## Background runs

The OS gives an app a window to work in while it is not on screen: iOS `BGTaskScheduler`, Android WorkManager, a page about to hide. The core spends it on what is worth finishing: the offline queue replays, stale queries refetch, and what waits to be written is written. The platform calls `runInBackground` with the window it was given; the core runs its background tasks inside it and reports back.

| Report | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Finished | `finished`: every task was done in time and nothing is pending. Tell the OS it succeeded only then. |
| Work done | `replayed` queued mutations sent, `refetched` queries fetched again. |
| Work left | `stillPending`: queued mutations and unfinished fetches. |

A run returns when its tasks are done, or half a second before the deadline so you can still tell the OS. Whatever a task did stays done: the queue persists per item, a request in flight is the client's and goes on, so a run that is cut short, or cancelled when the OS takes the window back, loses nothing and sends nothing twice. Offline, a run ends at once and says what is pending; it does not hold the window for a network that may not return.

On iOS the identifiers are `<id>.processing` and `<id>.refresh`; `undra init` writes them to `Info.plist` with the `processing` and `fetch` background modes. **BackgroundTasks does not run in the simulator**: test the handler with the fakes in the Swift package, and on a device with the debugger command Apple documents. On Android the worker returns `retry()` while work is pending, and the web has no background beyond the page's own life yet: Background Sync in a service worker needs the core inside the worker and is a follow-up.

Your own work joins the run with `undra::background::register(ctx, name, pending, run)` in Rust: `pending` says cheaply how much is waiting, `run` does it and reports progress to the `Deadline` as it goes. The core's statistics carry `background.pending`, which is what the platforms read to decide whether a window is worth asking for.

## Size of the shipped core

`undra build --platform ios,android --release` builds the core with the `release-mobile` profile of the generated crate: the release profile with the optimiser asked for size (`opt-level = "s"`), except for the crates the call path runs through (the wire codec, the signals, the runtime and the C ABI), which stay at `opt-level = 3` so that a call is not slower. Nothing else changed. The panic strategy is not on the list: a native panic must unwind so the core can contain it and report it (the report above), so `panic = "abort"`, the biggest size lever Rust has, is not used. Line tables stay (the symbol files above), the shipped copies are stripped as before, and the host build, which runs your core's tests and `undra bindgen`, keeps `opt-level = 3`.

| Hello-world core | Before (`opt-level = 3`) | Now (`release-mobile`) | Gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Android arm64-v8a `.so` | 966.0 KB | 898.2 KB | at most 1.2 MB, and 5% over the record |
| Android x86_64 `.so` | 1,028.2 KB | 960.8 KB | at most 1.2 MB, and 5% over the record |
| iOS arm64, added to an app | 838.1 KB | 784.1 KB | at most 900 KB, and 5% over the record |

The Android numbers are the stripped, 16 KB aligned file Gradle packages. The iOS number is what the device slice of the XCFramework adds to an app once its link has kept what is reachable and dropped the local symbols; the `.a` file itself is larger and is not a measure. A bigger core is bigger: the playground, with queries, persistence and several stores, is 2.49 MB for arm64-v8a (2.84 MB at `opt-level = 3`, 12% less).

When a byte budget is hard, choose size over speed per platform with `opt_level` in `[android]` or `[ios]` of `undra.toml`. `"z"` optimises every crate for size, the call path included; `"3"` is the speed profile, for an app whose own hot code (it is optimised for size by default, like everything outside the call path) should not be. A panic unwinds in all three, and the Xcode and Gradle builds pick the setting up with no flag.

| `opt_level` | Hello world, arm64-v8a | Playground, arm64-v8a | Playground, added to an iOS app | A synchronous call (Android emulator / iOS simulator) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `"3"` | 966.0 KB | 2.84 MB | 2.62 MB | 1x |
| `"s"` (the default) | 898.2 KB | 2.49 MB | 2.31 MB | 0.99x / 0.99x |
| `"z"` | 766.5 KB | 2.02 MB | 1.65 MB | 1.58x / 1.33x |

At `"z"` a 1 KB record or a change-set of 100 signals also costs 13% to 18% more; the default is within the noise on every row the device bench measures. A core of 1.6 MB at the old speed profile is about 1.42 MB at the default and about 1.18 MB at `"z"`. Measure your own: `undra build --release` prints the size.

The sizes are gated in CI (`scripts/native-size.sh`: over the design's budget, or more than 5% over the recorded size, fails). To measure your own core, `undra build --release` prints each library's size at the end. To see where the bytes are, the NDK's tools read the unstripped twin that `--release` keeps in `build/symbols/android/<abi>/`:

sh

```sh
NDK_BIN=$ANDROID_HOME/ndk/27.2.12479018/toolchains/llvm/prebuilt/<host>/bin
$NDK_BIN/llvm-size -A build/android/jniLibs/arm64-v8a/lib<ns>.so            # sections: .text, .eh_frame, .rela.dyn, ...
$NDK_BIN/llvm-nm --print-size --size-sort -C --defined-only \
  build/symbols/android/arm64-v8a/lib<ns>.so | tail -40               # the largest functions
```

What is left is mostly the runtime, your core and Rust's standard library: a Rust library that does nothing but catch a panic is about 260 KB stripped, because the standard library's panic and backtrace support comes with it, and the unwind tables that make a contained panic possible are about a tenth of a core. Two linker options save more and are not applied for you: `-Wl,--pack-dyn-relocs=android` (about 3%; the loader of every Android version you support has to read the packed format, so that is your call) and `-Wl,--icf=all` (about 0.5%, merges functions with equal bodies, which changes function addresses); set them with `RUSTFLAGS` if your app can take them.

## Debugging into Rust

| Where | How |
| --- | --- |
| Xcode | A debug build keeps full DWARF in the core: step from a Swift call into Rust, and set breakpoints by `breakpoint set -f todos.rs -l 42`. `undra init` writes an `.lldbinit` that loads the toolchain's Rust formatters; `undra doctor` checks it. |
| Android Studio | The *Dual (Java + Native)* debugger with the unstripped debug `.so` (the generated Gradle module keeps its symbols in debug); `build/symbols/android` is the symbol directory for a release reproduction. `doctor` checks the NDK's LLDB. |
| Chrome | The C/C++ DevTools Support (DWARF) extension reads the debug module the dev build serves; breakpoints in `.rs` files. A browser extension is not something `doctor` can check, so it prints the link. |
| Host tests | `rust-lldb` or CodeLLDB on `cargo test`. |

The same panic that reaches your crash reporter is in the console during development: with `undra dev` the report goes to the app attached to the dev server like any port call.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/several-cores.html

# One core or several

Most apps need one core. When a second one arrives, a vendor's SDK or a module another team ships, the two load into the same app side by side, each under its own namespace.

## One core first

Put the app's domain in one core and split it into crates inside it. Add a second core only for code that ships on its own.

|  | One core, several crates | Several cores |
| --- | --- | --- |
| State and transactions | shared: one store graph, one order of writes | separate: each core has its own |
| Releases | together | each on its own schedule |
| Cost | one runtime | a runtime, its threads and a copy of Undra per core |

## The namespace

A core's namespace names everything it exports, so two cores never collide. By default it is the core's package name in snake case; set it in `undra.toml` (lowercase letters, digits and `_`, at most 32 characters).

undra.toml

```toml
[core]
path = "core"
namespace = "acme_pay"
```

| What | Named |
| --- | --- |
| The C symbol, which returns the core's table | `acme_pay_undra_api` |
| iOS | `AcmePayCore.xcframework`, one prelinked `libacme_pay.a` per slice |
| Android | `libacme_pay.so` |
| Web | `acme_pay.wasm` |
| The bindings' entry, in Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript | `UndraAcmePay` |

`undra build` refuses a namespace that a sibling project already uses, and every runtime refuses to load two cores with one.

The namespace also keeps the default storage apart: each core's `Kv`, `SecureStore`, `Fs` and `Db` live under `undra/<namespace>/` on every platform, so two cores that use the defaults never see each other's data unless you hand them one adapter of your own.

## Loading two cores

Load each core once, through its own entry. Every generated type defaults to the core of its own package, so a call never reaches the wrong one.

On iOS each slice exports one symbol, so the two libraries link next to each other with no `-force_load`. On Android each core registers its natives on its bindings' own class. In React Native, `loadNative(UndraAcmePay)` installs one module per namespace.

## Good to know

- **Pass values between cores, not objects.** An object belongs to the core that made it, and two cores can issue the same handle numbers.
- **Each core closes on its own.** Shutting one down leaves the other running; a closed core can load again.
- **Two local Swift packages need two directory names.** SwiftPM names a local package after its directory.

The [two-core test apps](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/tree/main/examples/two-cores) load one core under two namespaces on iOS, Android, the JVM and Node, and CI runs them on every change.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/bazel.html

# Bazel

Undra's build is a command line, and a Bazel repository can call it as one: the rules run `undra build` and `undra bindgen` in hermetic, offline actions, so the core, its bindings and the code that uses them are targets in your graph.

## What you get

| Rule | Produces | With |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `undra_core` | per platform: `lib<ns>.dylib` or `.so` (host), `<ns>.wasm` (web), the XCFramework (iOS), `jniLibs/<abi>/` (Android), and the symbol files | `undra build`, the profiles of every other build |
| `undra_bindings` | the Swift package, the Gradle module and the npm package, as outputs, never committed, never stale | `undra bindgen --library`, read from the host build |
| `undra_kt_jvm_library` | the Kotlin bindings over the Kotlin runtime | `rules_kotlin` |
| `undra_ts_library` (`ts.bzl`) | the TypeScript bindings, type-checked and compiled against the runtime, linked into `node_modules` | `aspect_rules_ts`, `aspect_rules_js` |
| `undra_swift_library` | the Swift bindings and the C module of the core's entry over the Swift runtime | `rules_swift` (macOS) |
| `undra_android_library` (`android.bzl`) | the Kotlin bindings as an Android library | `rules_kotlin`'s `kt_android_library`, the Android SDK |

## Set up

Pin Bazel in `.bazelversion` (8.8.1 is what the rules are tested with) and put the rules and the toolchain in `MODULE.bazel`. The core is an ordinary Cargo crate that depends on `undra`; `undra.toml` stays the project file.

If you use `undra_ts_library`, add `common --repo_env=DO_NOT_TRACK=1` to your `.bazelrc`. The TypeScript rules it loads (`aspect_rules_js`) report which rulesets and versions your build uses to Aspect unless that variable is set, and only your repository can set it: a module cannot do it for you. The other rules never load them.

`bazel test //...` in [examples/bazel](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/tree/main/examples/bazel) builds the to-do core for the host and the web, generates the bindings, and runs Kotlin tests against the real core through JNI, TypeScript tests against the wasm module under Node, and, on macOS, a Swift test that loads it in process. CI runs it on Linux for every change, and the Swift test and the iOS core on macOS.

## Why it is hermetic

The rules call the CLI rather than copy its build: the shim, the release profiles, the `wasm-opt` pipeline, the path remapping and the symbol files stay in one place, so the web size gate and the schema hash are the CLI's. What makes an action that runs Cargo safe to cache:

- **The compiler is Bazel's.** `rustc`, `cargo` and each target's standard library come from your `rules_rust` toolchain, pinned by checksum. No `rustup`.
- **The crates are the lock file's.** `undra_vendor` downloads each crates.io package once, by the checksum `Cargo.lock` records, and an action unpacks them into a Cargo directory source with the network off.
- **The CLI is built the same way,** from the checkout the core is built against.
- **The build sees only what the target declares.** The action copies `undra.toml`, `srcs` and `workspace` into a private directory and builds there, with any spawn strategy, sandboxed or not; a file missing from `srcs` is a build error, not a silent read of your tree.
- **The build directory is named by the target,** because Cargo and `undra build` put the build's path into symbol names: the same target builds in the same place in every checkout, so the same inputs give the same bytes (two clones on one Mac produced byte-identical cores).

The C linker, and for iOS and Android Xcode, the NDK and `cargo-ndk`, are the machine's: no Bazel rule distributes them for Rust.

## Platforms

| Platform | Needs | Where it is built |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `host`, `web` | nothing outside the rules | Linux and macOS, in CI on every change |
| `ios` | Xcode, and `apple_support` first in your `MODULE.bazel` | macOS, in CI on every change; the target is `manual` |
| `android` | the NDK and `cargo-ndk` on the machine, and a C++ toolchain registered for the Android platforms (`rules_android_ndk`), which the rules do not set up | declared, not built anywhere yet: without that toolchain, analysis stops at `Unable to find a CC toolchain`, even with the NDK installed |

`undra_android_library` needs the Android SDK only (`rules_android` reads `ANDROID_HOME`), not the NDK. The example's (`bazel build //android:hello --config=android`) was built by hand on macOS; CI does not build it, because `rules_android` then downloads its own tools, one of them an archive without a checksum.

## Generated code and your linters

A repository that lints everything reports the bindings, because they are the output of a generator. `undra bindgen` now writes the exclusions beside each tree and lists them in its manifest, so `--check` keeps them honest:

| Tree | File | Read by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kotlin | `.editorconfig`, and `@file:Suppress("ALL", "ktlint")` in every file | ktlint 1.x; detekt and IntelliJ read the annotation too |
| Swift | `.swiftlint.yml`, an `excluded:` list to merge into yours | SwiftLint |
| TypeScript | `.eslintrc.json`, and `eslint.config.undra.mjs` to spread into a flat config | ESLint 8 and 9 |

ktlint 1.8 reports 90 findings on the example's generated Kotlin without them and none with either one; `bazel test //kotlin:lint_test` in the example runs that comparison. The annotation does not silence the Kotlin compiler: its warnings about the generated code still show. The detekt, IntelliJ, SwiftLint and ESLint readings follow each tool's documentation and are not run in CI.

## Good to know

- **Bazel caches a core as a whole.** A change to the core rebuilds its dependencies inside the action (seconds for a small core); a remote cache makes that cost the author's alone.
- **Swift needs its files listed.** `rules_swift` compiles files, not a directory, so `undra_bindings(swift_files = [..])` names them; a wrong list fails the build and prints the right one.
- **Telemetry.** Only `ts.bzl` loads `aspect_rules_js`, whose telemetry is on unless your `.bazelrc` sets `--repo_env=DO_NOT_TRACK=1` (Set up, above); the example sets it.
- **The scratch directory.** Each core builds in `/tmp/undra-bazel-<key>`, removed when the action ends. On Linux the sandbox's `/tmp` is private; on macOS two builds of the same target take turns, and another user's build of it goes to a directory of its own.
- The decision, its alternatives and what was measured are in [ADR-061](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-061-bazel-support.md).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/

# Cookbook

Recipes for what every app does. Each is a module of one Rust crate that is compiled and tested, with the lines that call it from Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript.

## How these are made

- **Every Rust sample is compiled and run.** The recipes are one crate, `examples/cookbook`, a module each, and every page quotes it. `cargo test -p cookbook` runs each against the test runtime and the fakes, so a recipe is a test, not a paragraph.
- **Every platform line compiles.** The Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript on these pages are checked in CI against the bindings generated from that crate: `swift build` in Swift 6 mode, `kotlinc -Werror` and `tsc --strict`.
- **Code is collapsed.** Each page says the idea in a few lines and keeps the code one click away.

## Where to start

- **An app with a login?** [Auth](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/auth.html), then [offline-first](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/offline.html).
- **An existing codebase?** [From Kotlin Multiplatform](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/from-kmp.html) or [from UniFFI](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/from-uniffi.html): three steps, the first one small.
- **Want it all in one place?** [Fieldbook](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/sample.html), field notes with photos, uses the recipes together on the web, iOS and Android.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/auth.html

# Auth

Where a token lives, when it is refreshed and what logging out forgets are rules of the app, not of three UIs. Written once in the core, they hold on iOS, Android and the web.

## The recipe

- **The session is a signal.** `Auth.session` is `SignedOut` or `SignedIn`. The root view switches on it; nothing else decides which screen shows.
- **Tokens are secrets, not state.** They go to the `SecureStore` port (Keychain, Android Keystore, WebCrypto) and never into a signal, because every signal is mirrored into each platform's memory.
- **A 401 is not an error.** `authed` adds the token and, on a `401`, refreshes once and retries. A second request that meets the same `401` waits for the refresh in flight. A refresh the server refuses signs the user out, wherever the request came from.
- **Queued writes use today's token.** An offline write replayed an hour later goes through `authed` too, so it carries the token that is current then.
- **Logout forgets.** Both tokens, the persisted cache, the session. It is refused with a typed `PendingWrites` while writes wait in the offline queue: they would go out as whoever signs in next.

## On the platform

The root view switches on the session, and a failed sign-in is a case, not a string to parse.

## What the tests prove

- Sign-in puts the tokens in `SecureStore` and nothing in plain storage.
- A `401` costs exactly one refresh and the caller never sees it; a refused refresh clears both tokens, the persisted cache and the screen.
- A request that meets a refresh in progress waits instead of refreshing again.
- A session left by the last run resumes (refreshing on the way); sign-out is refused while a write is queued.

## Limits

- The query client has no `clear()` yet. Sign-out deletes the persisted entries and the recipe keys cached data by user (`profile:{user}`), so the next person never reads the last one's entry; in-memory entries leave with their observers.
- The core cannot show a login web view or an OAuth sheet: that is the platform's. It hands the code to `sign_in` like any other value.

Source: [`examples/cookbook/core/src/auth.rs`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/cookbook/core/src/auth.rs). The sample app, [Fieldbook](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/sample.html), uses it.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/pagination.html

# Pagination and infinite lists

An infinite list is a keyed list that grows. The core owns the pages, the cursor and the filter, so a page crosses as one-row inserts however long the list already is.

## The recipe

- **One keyed list.** `posts` is appended with the recorded list operations, so a page of twenty rows is twenty one-row inserts in a single change-set (SPEC 3.8), not the whole list.
- **A derived view.** `visible` is a `DerivedList` of it, filtered by `topic`. Typing in a search box sends the rows that entered or left the view.
- **The cursor is a signal.** It is the server's opaque next-page token, so it survives a restore (a crash recovery, an `undra dev` rebuild) and a screen can show "end of list" from `exhausted`.
- **`load_more` is safe to call from a scroll view on every frame.** It does nothing while a page is in flight or after the last page, and a call cancelled mid-flight (the screen went away) does not leave the store stuck loading.
- **Refresh starts a generation.** A page still on its way from before the refresh is dropped when it arrives. A row the server repeats between two pages is added once.

## On the platform

The view is a plain array on the platform. Asking for the next page is a call the list makes when its last row appears.

## What the tests prove

- Pages append until the server says there are no more, and then a scroll view's calls send nothing.
- A failed page keeps the cursor, so the retry continues from the same place.
- A page reaches the platforms as one change-set of inserts, for the list and for the view (decoded from the wire, as a platform sees it).
- The topic filters the view, and pages loaded later join it.

## Limits

- This recipe is the shape that needs nothing new: one query handle per page, stitched together in the core. For a feed that grows by the page, an `infinite` query keeps the pages, the cursor and the refetch order in the core, and `Lazy<T>` lets a platform read a window of a list that is too big to send; both are in [Paging and lazy lists](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/paging.html). Here, every page you load stays in memory on each platform that observes the list.
- Prepending (a chat's older messages) is a `insert` at index 0 of the same list; the recipe appends only.

Source: [`examples/cookbook/core/src/paging.rs`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/cookbook/core/src/paging.rs).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/forms.html

# Forms and validation

Validation rules written three times drift. Written once in the core, a form is a few signals and one command, and every platform draws the same errors.

## The recipe

- **A signal per field.** Each text field binds to a setter (`set_email`); the core holds the value, so a rotation or a restore loses nothing.
- **Errors are derived.** `errors` is a `Computed` of the fields: recomputed when one changes, never by the UI, and sent to the platforms only when it changed. It shows the problems of the fields the user has left, so an empty form is not an angry form.
- **The rules are plain functions.** `problems` takes values and returns problems: testable without a runtime, and the one place a rule is written.
- **The command refuses typed.** `submit` on an invalid form returns `Invalid` before any request, shows every problem from then on, and the server's "taken" is a case (`EmailTaken`), not a message to parse.

## On the platform

A field is a binding to a setter; the errors and the button state are signals.

## What the tests prove

- Nothing is shown until a field is left; the error goes as soon as the field is right.
- An invalid submit makes no request and shows all three problems; a second submit while one runs is refused.
- A valid submit sends the trimmed email; a `409` is `EmailTaken`, a `500` is a network case, and the form can be submitted again.

## Limits

- Messages are plain English strings from the core. For several languages return a code (an enum) and let each platform localise it, or ask a synchronous port the way the playground's `Locale` does.
- The server must still validate: this is the client's half, written once instead of three times.

Source: [`examples/cookbook/core/src/forms.rs`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/cookbook/core/src/forms.rs).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/upload.html

# File upload

The core reads the file through `Fs`, sends it in parts through `Http` and shows progress as a signal. The offline queue does the retrying, so no part of the recipe asks whether the network is up.

## The recipe

- **A part is a mutation.** `put_part` is `idempotent`, so while the device is offline it waits in the persisted queue and is replayed when the network returns, with the same `Idempotency-Key`. The upload just `await`s it.
- **Progress is a patch.** `uploads` is a keyed list; every acknowledged part is a one-row update of `sent` and `total`, which is a progress bar.
- **One part in the queue at a time.** The queue stores a part's bytes, so memory and disk cost one part, not the file.
- **Retry resumes.** A part the server refuses fails the upload with the reason in its row. `retry` reads the file again and continues from the first part the server has not acknowledged.
- **The server's name for the upload comes from the `Rng` port:** random in an app, seeded in a test.

## On the platform

A row per upload; progress and a retry button are plain reads and one call.

## What the tests prove

- A 150,000-byte file goes up as three parts and the screen sees 0, 64 KiB, 128 KiB, then all of it.
- Offline, the upload waits with one part in the queue; when the network returns it finishes, and the queue is empty.
- A refused second part fails the upload at 64 KiB; `retry` sends parts 1 and 2 and never part 0.

## Limits

- The `Http` port has no streaming body and `Fs` reads a file whole, so the recipe suits photos and documents, not a multi-hundred-megabyte video.
- The queue replays while the app runs, and in the windows the OS gives a [background run](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/production.html#background) (`BGTaskScheduler`, WorkManager). Undra does not hand the transfer itself to the OS, so a part is sent only while the app or one of those windows is alive.
- Progress is per acknowledged part, not per byte on the wire.

Source: [`examples/cookbook/core/src/upload.rs`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/cookbook/core/src/upload.rs).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/realtime.html

# Real-time

The platform owns the socket; the core owns the policy. Which close to retry, how long to wait and what to resend are written once, in Rust, and tested with a fake clock.

## The recipe

- **One task.** `Live::start` spawns it. It connects, reads, and when the connection ends sleeps `Backoff` (500 ms doubling to 30 s, jitter from the `Rng` port) on the `Timer` port, then connects again.
- **Every end is typed.** A refused upgrade with `401` or `403` stops for good, because the credentials are the problem. A normal close (`1000`) is a goodbye. Anything else is retried.
- **A server that accepts and drops** keeps backing off: the attempt count resets when a message arrives, not when the socket opens.
- **Fallback.** Every third failed attempt the core tries server-sent events (`Fallback`), resuming from the last event id, for networks that cut WebSockets.
- **Backpressure is the core's pace.** Messages are a stream the core pulls, sixteen at a time: a core that stops reading stops the socket, on the platforms that can pause one.

## On the platform

The UI observes `link` (idle, open, reconnecting, fallback, stopped) and the keyed list `messages` like any store. It never sees a socket. The platform's job is the adapter: `URLSessionWebSocketTask`, the Kotlin runtime's client, the browser's `WebSocket`.

## What the tests prove

- A dropped connection shows `Reconnecting` and opens again after the backoff; the wait doubles while the server stays down.
- Refused credentials stop for good (two minutes of fake time, no new connection); a `1000` close is a goodbye.
- A network that cuts WebSockets reaches the event stream on the third attempt, and the next stream resumes with the last event id.
- `send` needs an open connection; `stop` closes with `1000` and does not come back; the list keeps the last hundred.

## Limits

- WebSocket and Sse are opt-in ports ([WebSocket & server-sent events](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/realtime.html)): the module is behind the cookbook's `realtime` feature.
- A message sent while the link is down is not queued: presence and chat are facts about now. Anything that must arrive is a mutation.
- A browser cannot send headers on a WebSocket, so a credential goes in the URL or a subprotocol.

Source: [`examples/cookbook/core/src/realtime.rs`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/cookbook/core/src/realtime.rs).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/offline.html

# Offline-first

Offline-first is three decisions the core makes once: reads come from disk, writes queue, and an update never loses what the last build left on the device.

## The recipe

- **Reads come from disk.** `notes` is a `persist` query: the list is on screen from the first frame of the next launch, and refreshed in the background.
- **Writes queue.** `add_note` is `idempotent`: offline it goes into a persisted queue and is replayed in order when the network returns, after a restart too. `create_note` shows the note at once and takes it back if the server refuses.
- **The outbox is data.** `outbox()` says how many writes wait and which ones an update could not carry over (dead letters), with the reason.
- **An update is two rules.** Build 2 renamed a field and added another. `#[undra(default)]` fills the new field in old data. A `#[undra::migrate]` hook handles the rename in cached lists and queued writes. Whatever a hook refuses is never lost: a queued write becomes a dead letter.

## On the platform

A cached list, a write that returns when the server has it, and a count for the "waiting to sync" line.

## What the tests prove

- A note created offline shows at once; when the network returns the server gets it and the placeholder gives way to its note.
- The app is killed with a write queued: the new process finds it on disk and replays it with the same `Idempotency-Key`.
- A refused write takes its placeholder back; sign-out is refused while a write is queued.
- Both hooks turn build-1 data (`body`) into build-2 data (`text`), and refuse what is not a note.

## Limits

- Only a failure while the `Connectivity` port says offline queues a write. A `500` is returned to the caller like any error.
- A migration across two builds needs two builds to prove end to end. The recipe tests the hooks directly; the playground's contract scenarios run build A's data under build B on all three platforms ([Shipping an update](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/updates.html)).

Source: [`examples/cookbook/core/src/offline.rs`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/examples/cookbook/core/src/offline.rs).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/network-stack.html

# Your network stack

Your app already has one: a token it refreshes, interceptors, tracing, certificate pinning. Hand it to the core's network ports and every request the core makes goes through it, with nothing Undra-specific to configure.

## The problem

The core never makes a request; the platform does, through the `Http` port (and `WebSocket` and `Sse` where the core asks for them). The default adapters use the platform's own client. That is not *your* client: on Android `HttpURLConnection` is OkHttp underneath, but the platform's instance, so a request from the core carries no token, shows in no trace and is not pinned. The fix is not an adapter of your own (the contract is hundreds of lines: typed errors, a timeout that covers the body, cancellation that closes the socket, streams that stop the server when the core stops reading). It is passing your client to the adapter that already is that contract.

## The recipe

- **Android:** add the optional `okhttp-adapters` module (`com.github.shreypdev.undra:okhttp-adapters`, at the runtime's version) and call `AndroidPlatformDefaults.installWithOkHttp(core, context, client)` in place of `install`. `Http`, `WebSocket` and `Sse` go through your `OkHttpClient`: its interceptors, its `Authenticator` (a `401` is answered with a refreshed token and the request goes again), its event listeners, its `CertificatePinner`. One exception is OkHttp's own: a WebSocket's upgrade is seen by your application interceptors, not by your network interceptors or your event listener.
- **iOS:** pass your `URLSession` to `HttpAdapter`, `URLSessionWebSocketAdapter` and `URLSessionSseAdapter`. Its configuration, its delegate (server trust and the pinning built on it, authentication challenges) and its `URLProtocol` classes apply. Give event streams a session with the same delegate and a configuration that lets a stream stay quiet.
- **Web:** pass your `fetch` and `WebSocket` to `fetchHttp`, `fetchSse` and `browserWebSocket`. Whatever your wrapper does to a request, it does to the core's.
- **React Native:** nothing to pass. `reactNativeHttp()` is React Native's `fetch`, which is the app's networking module, so what the app configures there applies.

## What goes through your stack, and what is yours

| Port | Kotlin on OkHttp | Swift on URLSession |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Http` | the whole call, as the app's own requests go | the whole task |
| `WebSocket` | the upgrade request (OkHttp gives its listener no WebSocket events) | the upgrade: the connection is a task of your session |
| `Sse` | the request, on a client derived from yours with no read timeout and HTTP/1.1 | the request, on the session you give the Sse adapter |

What your client decides stays yours: redirects, retries, the timeouts when a request has none of its own, compression, caching, how many calls run at once (the core's requests wait their turn with yours). The core's contract holds on top: an error status is a response, a failure is a typed error, the request's own timeout bounds the whole exchange, cancelling the call closes the socket.

## What the tests prove

- **Kotlin:** the Http, WebSocket and Sse contract suites that run on the default adapters run on OkHttp's too, on the JVM and on a device. An interceptor sees every request and changes a header, an `Authenticator` refreshes a token and the request, its body included, goes again, an event listener sees each call, and the recipe's client above is run against a local server.
- **Swift:** the WebSocket suite runs a second time on an app's session, and Http, Sse and WebSocket are shown to carry the session's configuration and to reach its delegate.
- **TypeScript:** a wrapped `fetch` sees every request, adds a header and answers a `401` with a refreshed token; an app's `WebSocket` constructor adds a token to the upgrade.

## Limits

- OkHttp's WebSocket repairs malformed UTF-8 in a text frame (U+FFFD) where the default adapter fails the connection with close code 1007; keep `ClientWebSocketAdapter` for the port if you need the check.
- The default OkHttp client follows redirects from `https` to `http`; the other adapters never do. `followSslRedirects(false)` gives the same rule.
- The Kotlin lines are compiled and tested with the `okhttp-adapters` module (they need OkHttp, which the other modules never carry); the Swift and TypeScript lines are checked like the rest of the cookbook.

Source: [`okhttp-adapters/README.md`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/runtimes/kotlin/undra-runtime/okhttp-adapters/README.md) and [ADR-060](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-060-app-network-stack-in-ports.md). The ports: [Your network stack inside](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/ports.html#your-network-stack-inside).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/from-kmp.html

# Moving from Kotlin Multiplatform

You do not move the domain on a Monday. Undra loads next to your Kotlin and your Swift, and takes over one piece at a time.

## Three steps

| Step | What moves | What it removes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **L1** side by side | A few pure functions (parsing, pricing, validation). The KMP module, Ktor, SQLDelight and your state holders stay. | For those functions: an Objective-C header or Alpha Swift export on the Swift side, and exceptions that end the process (KMP-1 to KMP-4). |
| **L2** one feature | One screen's state and requests become a store, a query and a mutation. | The `Flow` collectors, the collection copies and the assembled data layer, for that feature (KMP-5, KMP-14, KMP-15). |
| **L3** whole domain | `expect`/`actual` code becomes ports; persistence and the offline queue move in. | One shared framework per module, the CocoaPods dependency, and a dev loop that rebuilds the app (KMP-9, KMP-11, KMP-13). |

Row ids are those of the [limitations catalogue](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/specs/2026-10-01-competitive-limitations.md), as of October 2026. [Undra vs Kotlin Multiplatform](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-kotlin-multiplatform/) compares the two and says where KMP is ahead.

## What maps to what

| Kotlin Multiplatform | Undra |
| --- | --- |
| `expect` / `actual` | a port (`#[undra::port]`): the platform implements it, tests use a fake |
| `StateFlow`, a ViewModel | a store's signals: a `StateFlow`, an `@Observable`, a hook |
| Ktor client | the `Http` port, with queries and mutations over it |
| SQLDelight, Room | `Kv`; a `Db` port over SQLite behind a feature |
| `suspend` functions | Rust `async`, generated as `suspend`, `async throws`, `Promise` |
| sealed class errors | `#[undra::error]` enums |
| Compose Multiplatform | not applicable: the UI stays SwiftUI, Compose and React |

## Start

`undra adopt ../MyApp` writes a core crate and the exact steps for your project files, and edits none of them ([the CLI](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cli.html)). Move one function, call it from Kotlin and Swift, ship. [Auth](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/auth.html) and [offline-first](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/offline.html) are what L2 looks like.

## What does not carry over

- **Shared UI.** Compose Multiplatform has no counterpart, on purpose.
