- **Android has a boundary.** Shared Kotlin is plain Kotlin there; Undra crosses JNI. Device numbers are not published yet.
- **Generic classes** do not cross as generics: generic records, enums, functions, objects and stores cross as [the instantiations you list](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/generics.html), each a named type, an overload or a class of its own, and a type parameter with no list is [E0002](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0002).
- **Rust** is no longer your Android team's daily language.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/from-uniffi.html

# Moving from UniFFI

You already have a Rust core. Undra adds what sits above the bindings: state the UI observes, a data layer, ports with fakes and a dev loop. The move is mostly attributes.

## Three steps

| Step | What moves | What it removes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **L1** side by side | A new Undra crate beside your UniFFI one. Plain-data functions first: `#[uniffi::export]` becomes `#[undra::api]`. | Cancellation from either side, panics as typed values, a typed error for a mismatched library (UNI-3 to UNI-5). |
| **L2** one feature | State a screen polls, or is pushed through callbacks, becomes a store; its fetches a query and mutations. | The state-sync glue, and the cache, retry and offline logic you did not have (UNI-1, UNI-9). |
| **L3** whole domain | Platform services reached through callbacks become ports. | The test doubles you wrote by hand (UNI-12). |

Row ids are those of the [limitations catalogue](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/specs/2026-10-01-competitive-limitations.md), as of October 2026. [Undra vs UniFFI and Crux](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-uniffi-and-crux/) compares the two and says where UniFFI is ahead.

## What maps to what

| UniFFI | Undra |
| --- | --- |
| `#[uniffi::export] fn`, `async fn` | `#[undra::api] fn`, `async fn` |
| `uniffi::Record`, `uniffi::Enum` | `#[undra::api] struct`, `enum` (payloads in all three languages) |
| `uniffi::Error` | `#[undra::error]` |
| an `Object` with methods | `#[undra::api] impl`; a `#[undra::store]` if the UI observes it |
| a callback that pushes state | a signal the UI observes |
| a foreign trait for a platform service | a port (`#[undra::port]`), one per platform |
| a callback interface passed as an argument | a `#[undra::callback]` trait, taken as `Arc<dyn Trait>` |

## What does not map yet

- **Open-ended generics** ([E0002](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0002)). Generic records, enums, functions, methods, objects and stores cross as [the instantiations you list](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/generics.html); a type parameter with no list does not, and there are no native generic types.
- **Other hosts.** Undra targets SwiftUI, Compose, the web and React Native; UniFFI also serves Python and Ruby.

Objects, callbacks and newtypes map: an object crosses as a parameter or a return value, as itself ([objects](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/objects.html)), a `#[undra::callback]` trait taken as `Arc<dyn Trait>` is an argument the core calls back ([callbacks](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/callbacks.html)), and a one-field tuple struct crosses as the value it wraps and arrives as a type of its own ([newtypes](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/types.html#newtypes)). L1 still starts with plain data, because it moves without touching the platform code. [Several cores](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/several-cores.html) load side by side, so the rest can wait. [Auth](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/auth.html) and [offline-first](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/offline.html) show what L2 adds.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/ios-15-16.html

# Supporting iOS 15 and 16

Undra's Swift output is iOS 17 by default, because a generated store is `@Observable`. Lower the deployment target and the same store becomes an `ObservableObject`: the core, the wire and the commands do not change, only how SwiftUI is told to redraw.

## Turn it on

undra.toml

```toml
[ios]
deployment_target = "15.0"   # 15.0 or later; below 17.0 the stores are ObservableObjects
```

Run `undra bindgen`. A new app starts there with `undra init todo --ios-deployment-target 15.0`. `[bindings] swift_observation = "observable-object"` (or `--swift-observation`) picks the shape on any floor; `"observation"` with a target below 17.0 is an error that names both settings. Below iOS 16 the wire `Duration` is the runtime's `UndraDuration` (exact nanoseconds), because `Swift.Duration` is iOS 16.

## Your views

|  | iOS 17+ (observation) | iOS 15 and 16 (observable-object) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| owning view | `@State private var todos = try! Todos()` | `@StateObject private var todos = try! Todos()` |
| child view | `let todos: Todos` | `@ObservedObject var todos: Todos` |
| environment | `.environment(todos)` | `.environmentObject(todos)` |
| outside SwiftUI | `withObservationTracking` | `todos.$visible.sink { … }` |
| connection state | `core.connection.state` | `core.connectionObject` with `@ObservedObject` |

Reading a signal is still a plain property read and a command is still a method call. The `$property` publishers are a gain for UIKit and Combine code on every floor.

## What degrades

- **Granularity.** Observation redraws a view when a property it read changes; an `ObservableObject` redraws every view that observes the store when any of its properties changes. SwiftUI coalesces the events of one drain into one update. Split a big store, or observe a smaller one.
- **A big list is copied on every patch.** `@Published` has no in-place accessor, so a keyed patch to a list copies the array once, where Observation mutates it in place. Measured on an Apple M5 Pro (release build, 32-byte rows): about 5 µs for 1,000 rows, 48 µs for 10,000 and 0.5 ms for 100,000, against 0.2 µs at any size under Observation. It is linear in the list and paid once per applied patch, not per op (the mirror merges a frame's patches into one apply, so 100 ops cost about what 1 does). It is invisible for lists of thousands; for 100,000 rows that change every frame, [page the list](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/pagination.html) or observe a smaller store.
- **One name.** A store member called `objectWillChange` is [E0051](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0051) in this mode, because `ObservableObject` declares it.
- **SQLite change counts.** The built-in `SQLiteDbAdapter` counts changes with `sqlite3_changes`, a C `int` (the 64-bit one needs iOS 15.4): a single statement that changes more than 2,147,483,647 rows reports an undefined count.
- **Nothing else.** The mirror, keyed patches, `no_coalesce` and the error channel are the same code in both modes.

## Raising the floor later

Set `deployment_target = "17.0"`, run `undra bindgen` and make the mechanical edits in the table. No core change, no wire change. The repository's `examples/ios15-sample` is an iOS 15.0 app over a store, a keyed list and a query; [docs/IOS_15_16.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/IOS_15_16.md) says how CI proves the floor.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/sample.html

# Sample app: Fieldbook

A small but real app on one Rust core: field notes with photos, on the web, iOS and Android.

## What it is

Fieldbook is a small but real app: field notes with photos, for a team that works where there is no signal. One Rust core, three apps (web, iOS, Android) that use only the public API, and a test suite that runs the core with no device. The cookbook's recipes, in one product.

## What it demonstrates

| Feature | In the core |
| --- | --- |
| Sign-in with a team code, tokens in the secure store, one re-auth on a 401 | `auth.rs` |
| A note is on the device before the screen shows it, and is sent when there is a network, even after a kill | `notes.rs`: `Kv`, an idempotent `push_note` |
| Search, tag chips, pinned first, newest first | a keyed list, a `DerivedList` and a `Computed` |
| Photos kept in the app's files and uploaded in the background | `Fs` and the queue |
| An update that renames a field and adds three, without losing data | `#[undra(default)]`, `#[undra::migrate]` |
| Who else is in the notebook | `presence.rs`: a reconnecting WebSocket (feature `presence`) |
| State kept across a rebuild under `undra dev` | every store has a `restore` function, tested |

## Run it

Tick **offline** in the web app, write two notes, reload, untick it: the notes were on the device the whole time, and the core sends them when the network returns.

## How far it goes

- The web, iOS and Android apps build in CI (`vite build`, `xcodebuild`, `assembleDebug`); the screens are small on purpose.
- Notes are stored in `Kv`. The `Db` port (SQLite) is the next step for a notebook that grows; it is an opt-in port.
- SwiftUI previews and the web stories run the real core on the [testing kit](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/testing.html)'s fakes, and so do the web tests, with a manual clock. Android's Compose previews are not in the sample: they play a recording, and none was made.

Source: [`examples/fieldbook`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/tree/main/examples/fieldbook), with a README that says how to run each platform. [The cookbook](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/) has the recipes it is made of.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cli.html

# The CLI

One binary runs the whole loop: scaffold a project, generate bindings, build the core for each platform, serve it live, and check your machine. Every command teaches through its own help.

## Overview

text

```
undra [-C <dir>] <command>

  init      create a new project: a core crate and an app shell per platform
  bindgen   generate Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript bindings from the core's schema
  schema    compare the public API of two schemas (breaking or additive), or export the core's schema
  build     build the core for iOS, Android, the web or this machine
  dev       serve the core over a WebSocket to running apps, rebuilding on change
  doctor    check toolchains and SDKs against what the project needs, with the fix for each gap
  adopt     add an Undra core to an existing app, without touching its project files
  upgrade   move a project to this undra's version: every pin, the bindings, the migration notes
```

An Undra project is a directory with a `undra.toml`. Commands find it from the current directory upwards, or you can point at it with the global `-C <dir>` (long form `--project-dir`). `undra <command> --help` prints what the command does, what it needs, what it writes, and examples.

Exit status is `0` on success, `1` for a failed command or a failed `undra doctor`, and `2` for a bad command line.

## undra init

bash

```bash
undra init todo                              # all three platforms
undra init todo --platforms ios,web          # only those shells
undra init todo --id dev.acme.todo           # application id / bundle identifier
undra init todo --undra-path ~/src/undra       # use a local checkout of Undra
undra init todo --ios-deployment-target 15.0   # an iOS app that supports iOS 15 and 16 (ObservableObject stores)
```

Creates a project directory with `undra.toml`, `core/` (a working to-do store), `generated/` (bindings, already generated), one minimal, real app per platform in `ios/`, `android/` and `web/`, and a CI workflow (`.github/workflows/undra.yml`: a job for the core and one per app, installing `undra` at the version pinned at the top of the file). Nothing is downloaded: the templates are part of the binary. Without `--undra-path` the project depends on the release of this `undra`, all from `github.com/shreypdev/undra`: the crates by tag, the Swift package at the repository's root, the Kotlin modules from JitPack and `@undra/runtime` as the release's asset ([the lines](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/getting-started.html#3-create-a-project)). `UNDRA_DIST_GIT_URL`, `UNDRA_DIST_RELEASE_URL` and `UNDRA_DIST_MAVEN_REPO` replace those three addresses, for a rehearsal of a release or a mirror (an `https://`, `http://` or `file://` URL; anything else is `error[undra::C0009]`); `undra bindgen`, `adopt` and `upgrade` read them too. A project that uses a checkout gets no workflow, since CI cannot see the checkout.

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `<name>` | project name: letters, digits, `-` and `_` |
| `--platforms <list>` | `ios`, `android`, `web`, comma separated; default all three (alias `--targets`) |
| `--id <id>` | application id and iOS bundle identifier; default `com.example.<name>` |
| `--undra-path <dir>` | use the crates and runtimes of an Undra checkout (or set `UNDRA_PATH`) |
| `--dir <dir>` | create the project inside this directory instead of the current one |

## undra bindgen

bash

```bash
undra bindgen                          # build the core, extract the schema, write <project>/generated
undra bindgen --out ../shared/bindings
undra bindgen --schema schema.json     # no build: generate from a schema file
undra bindgen --check                  # exit 1 if the generated files are stale (for CI)
undra bindgen --docs                   # include the core's doc comments
```

Reads the core's schema and writes the bindings the app shells import: a Swift package (`<out>/swift/`), a Gradle module (`<out>/kotlin/`) and an npm package (`<out>/ts/`). By default the schema comes from the core itself: the core is built as a host library, loaded, and asked for its schema. With `--schema` it is read from a file instead and nothing is built. Files an earlier run wrote and this one does not are removed; files you added next to them are never touched. Every generated file says it is generated (the generator, the schema hash, "Do not edit"), and each tree gets a `.gitattributes` that marks it `linguist-generated`, so GitHub collapses it in a pull request: [review the schema, not the bindings](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/reviewing-generated-code.html).

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--schema <file>` | generate from this schema JSON instead of building the core |
| `--out <dir>` | write below this directory (default `[paths] generated` in `undra.toml`) |
| `--release` | extract the schema from a release build of the core |
| `--platforms <list>` | only these platforms' bindings (`ios` is Swift, `android` is Kotlin, `web` is TypeScript) |
| `--check` | write nothing; exit with an error if the generated files differ from what would be written |
| `--docs` | keep the core's doc comments in the bindings |
| `--crate-name <name>` | the core crate's name, for a schema file that has none |
| `--swift-observation <mode>` | `observation` (`@Observable`, iOS 17 and later) or `observable-object` (iOS 15 and later); overrides `[bindings] swift_observation`, which follows `[ios] deployment_target` |
| `--ios-deployment-target <version>` | generate the Swift for this iOS floor instead of `[ios] deployment_target` (see [supporting iOS 15 and 16](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/ios-15-16.html)) |

The schema a library exports is the whole schema, doc comments included. `--docs` keeps them in the generated code, so every type, field, variant, method and port carries the text of its `///` comment; without it the generated code has no doc comments. The schema hash covers neither, so both outputs have the same hash and the same wire.

## undra schema

bash

```bash
undra schema export -o schema.json               # write the core's API as a file; commit it
undra schema export --check                      # fail when schema.json is not the core's schema (CI)
undra schema diff --against origin/main          # what changed since the base, each line breaking or additive
undra schema diff --against origin/main --exit-code   # ... and exit 1 when a line is breaking (CI)
undra schema diff old.json new.json              # two schema files
```

The schema is the API: the generated Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript are an artifact of it. `schema export` builds the core as a host library, loads it and writes its schema as JSON (without doc comments unless `--docs`, so fixing a comment is not an API change). `schema diff` compares two schemas and prints one line per change an app can notice, each marked `breaking` (code written against the old bindings can stop compiling) or `additive`; the rules are in [Reviewing generated code](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/reviewing-generated-code.html#what-breaking-means). The order is fixed, so the same two schemas print the same text.

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `diff <old> <new>` | two schema JSON files, old then new (any form `undra bindgen --schema` reads) |
| `diff --against <ref> [file]` | the file as committed at a git ref (`git show`; nothing is built) against the file in the working tree; the file is `schema.json` in the project directory unless named |
| `diff --exit-code` | exit with status 1 when any line is breaking, or when the schema file disagrees with the bindings beside it; without it the exit status is 0 whatever the diff says |
| `export -o <file>` | write the schema to a file (default: standard output) |
| `export --docs`, `--release` | keep the doc comments; extract from a release build |
| `export --check` | write nothing; exit with an error when the file (`-o`, or `schema.json` in the project directory) is not what the export would write |

`diff --against` builds nothing, so it checks the file instead: the generated bindings carry the hash of the schema they were made from, and when `schema.json` disagrees with them, in the working tree or at the ref, a warning names both hashes. Errors are the usual ones: `C0009` for a ref that does not have the file (it says to commit one with `schema export`) or a file outside a repository, `C0002` for a file that is not a schema, `C0003` without `git`, and `C0007` from `export --check` for a file that is not the core's schema.

## undra build

bash

```bash
undra build                                   # every platform in undra.toml, debug
undra build --release                         # optimized: what you ship
undra build --platform web --release
undra build --platform android,host
```

Builds the core for each platform and puts the result where the app shells look for it, below `build/`, named after the core's namespace (`[core] namespace`, by default the core's package name; `hello_core` below):

| Target | Output |
| --- | --- |
| `ios` | `build/ios/HelloCore.xcframework`, device and simulator slices, each one prelinked `libhello_core.a` |
| `android` | `build/android/jniLibs/<abi>/libhello_core.so`, arm64-v8a and x86_64, 16 KB page aligned |
| `web` | `build/web/hello_core.wasm`, release profile, then `wasm-opt -Oz` if installed |
| `host` | `build/host/libhello_core.{dylib,so}`, for the JVM tests and `undra bindgen` |
| `rn` | the `ios` and `android` outputs, plus `build/ios/HelloCore.podspec` for a React Native app's Podfile ([docs/REACT_NATIVE.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/REACT_NATIVE.md)); the iOS half only on macOS |

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--platform <list>` | `host`, `ios`, `android`, `web`, `rn`, comma separated; default every platform in `undra.toml` |
| `--release` | optimized build (LTO, one codegen unit); the web build is always optimized |
| `--configuration <name>` | an Xcode build configuration, as the generated build phase passes it (`$CONFIGURATION`): a name that contains `Release` builds release, any other debug; after an iOS build it writes the stamp Xcode uses to tell which configuration the XCFramework is for |

**Not a manual step.** In a project made by `undra init` the app builds run `undra build` for you, each only when the core changed: Gradle's `undraBuild` task (`preBuild` depends on it; a release variant builds a release core), Xcode's *Build the Undra core* Run Script phase (before Compile Sources, with input and output file lists) and the `undra()` Vite plugin from `@undra/runtime/vite` (on start, and under `vite dev` on every change of `core/src`, followed by a reload). They find `undra` on `PATH`, or in `~/.undra/bin` and the other usual places, and say how to install it when it is missing (`error[undra::C0003]`).

`--release` turns on LTO and one codegen unit. The web build is always optimized. On iOS and Android the release build is also tuned for size (the `release-mobile` profile of the generated crate: `opt-level = "s"`, and a panic still unwinds so the core can contain it), and the host build keeps `opt-level = 3`. `opt_level` in `[ios]` or `[android]` of `undra.toml` chooses the smallest library (`"z"`, calls about 1.5x slower) or the fastest (`"3"`) instead; the [production page](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/production.html#size) has the numbers. Sizes are printed at the end next to the design's budgets. A debug Android core is tens of megabytes per ABI, so package with `--release`. The library is your core plus the Undra C ABI, built from a small crate generated under `target/undra/`; you never write that crate.

**No `-force_load`.** Each iOS slice is one prelinked object whose only global symbol is the core's entry, `hello_core_undra_api`, which the generated bindings call. It links like any other static library, in debug and release, and [another core](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/several-cores.html) can sit next to it.

## undra dev

bash

```bash
undra dev                          # listen on 127.0.0.1:7443
undra dev --android                # also adb reverse the port to every attached Android device
undra dev --addr 0.0.0.0:7443      # reachable from a phone on your network
undra dev --no-watch               # build once and serve
undra dev --no-keep-state          # every rebuilt core starts fresh
undra dev --record session.json     # also write the session as a recording
```

Runs the core on this machine and serves it over a WebSocket. A simulator, a phone or a browser tab connects with the `remote` transport and uses this core instead of a built-in one: edit Rust, save, and the core is rebuilt and restarted. The apps reconnect by themselves, with backoff, whenever the connection drops (a rebuild, a phone that slept, a restarted adb); the core's state is carried across a rebuild (it is snapshotted in this process's memory, never on disk, and restored into the new core), so an app comes back to the screen it was on and its dev bar says "Reloaded, state kept"; a changed schema, or `--no-keep-state`, starts the new core fresh and says so. Logs, including the development records (a line per transaction commit, port call and panic) and a line for each client that connects, reconnects or leaves, print here. Clocks, randomness and logging are answered by this machine, because a remote client cannot answer a synchronous port. The banner also prints the address of the devtools page (behind a per-run token): the stores and their live values, a timeline of every change-set with its diff, a scrubber that restores the core to an earlier step (the app follows, and its dev bar says `time travel: step 3`), the port-call and query-cache logs, and the counters.

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--addr <addr>` | address to listen on; port 0 picks a free one (default `127.0.0.1:7443`) |
| `--no-watch` | build once and serve; do not rebuild on change |
| `--log-level <n>` | log records below this level (0 trace to 5 fatal) are not printed; default 1 |
| `--android` | run `adb reverse` for the server's port on every attached Android device or emulator (only the one in `ANDROID_SERIAL`, when set) |
| `--no-keep-state` | start every rebuilt core from fresh state instead of carrying the running core's state over |
| `--record <file>` | write the session as an `undra.recording` (calls, replies, change-sets, port traffic, with times), rewritten twice a second; a rebuilt core starts `NAME-2.json`. See [Testing your app](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/testing.html) |
| `--record-secrets` | keep `SecureStore` values in the recording (by default the calls of that port are recorded with empty arguments and replies) |
| `--devtools <auto\|on\|off>` | serve the devtools page at `/devtools`: `auto` (default) on a loopback address only, `on` always, `off` never |

How each platform connects (the banner prints these with the real port):

| Platform | How |
| --- | --- |
| Web | `UndraHelloCore.load({ mode: "remote", url: "ws://127.0.0.1:7443" })`, or `?undra=ws://127.0.0.1:7443` in the page URL |
| iOS | set `UNDRA_DEV_URL=ws://<your Mac>:7443`; the generated app reads it in debug builds |
| Android | an emulator uses `ws://10.0.2.2:7443`; a USB device runs `adb reverse tcp:7443 tcp:7443` (or `--android`) and uses `ws://127.0.0.1:7443`. The generated app takes it from the `undra_dev_url` launch extra or `./gradlew -PundraDevUrl=...`, in debug builds only |

Every platform runtime exposes what the connection is doing (`connecting`, `connected`, `reconnecting(attempt)`, `closed(reason)`) and observes its stores again after a reconnect. A call made while the connection is down fails at once with `UndraCallError.Unavailable` instead of waiting, and a command that fails that way is not handed to `onError`, because the connection state already reports the drop. [docs/DEV_LOOP.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/DEV_LOOP.md) has the details and a troubleshooting table.

**No authentication.** The server has none. Keep the loopback default unless a device has to reach it.

## undra doctor

bash

```bash
undra doctor
undra doctor --platform ios
undra doctor --fix       # the commands that close every gap, as one block to paste (nothing is run)
undra doctor --json      # the report for tools
```

Checks every prerequisite that `undra init`, `build`, `dev` and the device benchmarks use, and prints one line per finding. Each finding says what was found (`ok`, `missing`, or the wrong version), the value it observed, the exact fix command and the heading of `docs/ONBOARDING.md` that explains it. It covers rustup, stable Rust at the minimum version and the Rust targets of the platforms (`wasm32`, the iOS device and simulator targets, the Android ABIs of `undra.toml`); full Xcode against the command line tools and a simulator runtime; the Android SDK, `platform-tools`, NDK r27, `ANDROID_HOME` and `ANDROID_NDK_HOME`, `cargo-ndk`, JDK 17, `adb` and whether a device or emulator is attached, and the Gradle wrapper; Node 20+ and npm; `wasm-opt` (optional: it makes the wasm core 10-20% smaller); free disk space (a warning under 10 GB); and whether `undra` is on `PATH`, since the build integrations run it by name. Checks that matter only to people working on Undra (the Kotlin compiler, the `undra` emulator) are marked *for contributors*.

Inside a project only the platforms named in `undra.toml` are checked; elsewhere it checks all of them. It exits with status 1 when something the project needs is missing. `--fix` prints the fix commands as one block with a comment per finding and runs nothing; `--json` prints each finding with its id, state, severity, observed value, fix commands and documentation link.

## undra upgrade

bash

```bash
undra upgrade                  # move the project to this undra, regenerate the bindings, print the notes
undra upgrade --dry-run        # show the lines that would change; write nothing
undra upgrade --no-bindgen     # move the pins only
undra upgrade --docs           # keep the core's doc comments in the regenerated bindings
```

Reads every place a project pins its Undra version (the core's `undra` dependency in `Cargo.toml`, which a `rev` or `branch` pin leaves pinned by the release's tag, `[undra] version` in `undra.toml`, `@undra/runtime` (and `@undra/react-native`, `@undra/testkit`) in `package.json`, the runtime's Kotlin modules (`com.github.shreypdev.undra:runtime`, `:android-adapters` and the optional ones) in the Gradle scripts, the Undra Swift package in the Xcode project, and `UNDRA_VERSION` in the CI workflow), moves them all to the version of this `undra` in the shapes `undra init` writes (one release, all from the Undra repository on GitHub: the release's tag, its npm asset's URL; the JitPack repository is added to `settings.gradle.kts` when a project's Kotlin pins move to it), regenerates the bindings and prints the migration notes of every release the project crosses: what you have to do, what behaves differently, what is new. Only the version text changes, so comments and formatting stay, and the files are written all or none; a version held in a Gradle variable is left and named. Your app's own project files are not edited. A project that depends on a checkout of the Undra repository is on whatever that checkout is: the command says so and changes nothing. A project newer than this `undra` is refused (`error[undra::C0014]`): update the CLI first.

## undra adopt

bash

```bash
undra adopt ../MyApp                          # detect platforms, write ../MyApp/undra/
undra adopt . --platform ios                  # only the iOS steps
undra adopt ../MyApp --undra-path ~/src/undra   # use a local checkout of Undra
```

Adds an Undra core to an app you already have, the conservative way. It writes one new `undra/` directory (a core crate, a `undra.toml` and a `UNDRA_ADOPT.md`) and a list of the exact steps to wire it into the app, with the paths already filled in. The app's own project files are never modified; you make the few edits yourself.

It detects iOS from `*.xcodeproj` or `Package.swift`, Android from `settings.gradle(.kts)` plus `AndroidManifest.xml`, and web from a `package.json` (Vite, webpack, Next and so on). Flags: `--platform <list>`, `--name <name>` (the core's name; default the directory's name) and `--undra-path <dir>`.

## undra.toml

`undra init` writes every setting that matters, with comments.

undra.toml

```toml
[project]
name = "todo"
id = "com.example.todo"        # Android applicationId, iOS bundle id, Kotlin package base
platforms = ["ios", "android", "web"]

[core]
path = "core"                  # the crate bindgen, build and dev work on
# namespace = "todo_core"      # names the core's symbol, libraries and entry; default: its package name

[paths]
generated = "generated"        # written by `undra bindgen`; commit it or check it in CI
build = "build"                # written by `undra build`; do not commit

[undra]
version = "1.0.0"              # the release every dependency names; path = "…" points at a checkout instead

[bindings]
# swift_module = "TodoCore"
# kotlin_package = "com.example.todo.core"
# ts_scope = "app"
# ts_js_number = false         # i64/u64 as `number` instead of `bigint`
# swift_typed_throws = true    # port requirements: `throws(E)`; false emits plain `throws`
# swift_observation = "observable-object"   # Swift stores: "observation" (@Observable, iOS 17+) or "observable-object" (iOS 15+)

[ios]
deployment_target = "17.0"     # 15.0 or later; below 17.0 the Swift stores are ObservableObjects
# opt_level = "s"              # release builds: "s" small (the default), "z" smallest (calls about 1.5x slower), "3" fastest

[android]
abis = ["arm64-v8a", "x86_64"]
min_sdk = 26
# opt_level = "s"              # the same choice for the Android libraries
```

Commit `generated/` or regenerate it in CI, and gate on `undra bindgen --check` so a stale binding cannot ship.

## Errors

CLI errors print as `error[undra::C00NN]` with what happened, why, and what to do. Macro errors in your Rust use the same teaching shape with `E00NN` codes; the catalogue is on the [architecture page](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/architecture.html#diagnostics).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/architecture.html

# Architecture

One schema feeds three generators. Three runtimes hold the mirrors. A small binary wire carries writes in and change-sets out. This page is the tour, and the specification in the repository is the contract.

## The shape of it

Undra is a Rust core, a schema extracted from it, three code generators, and three platform runtimes. Your screens sit on generated bindings; the bindings sit on a runtime package; the runtime talks to the core through a transport that is an ABI, not a framework.

*Figure: Each platform has the same four layers; only the bottom one is platform-specific machinery. React Native shares the web's two middle layers.*

The core is one codebase. On each platform it is linked the way that platform expects: a prelinked static library in an XCFramework on iOS, a `.so` over JNI on Android, a wasm module on the web, each named after the core's namespace and reached through one table of entry points, so an app can carry [more than one core](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/several-cores.html). A React Native app links the iOS and Android builds as they are and reaches them from JavaScript through JSI, under the same generated package and `@undra/runtime` as the web ([React Native](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/REACT_NATIVE.md)). During development the same core can instead run on your machine behind a WebSocket (`undra dev`).

## From Rust to native code

*Figure: Everything is derived from the schema. Bindgen emits three trees that depend only on the matching runtime package.*

Everything starts with the macros. `#[undra::api]`, `#[undra::store]`, `#[undra::port]` and friends validate your code and register a description of each public type and function. Collected together, those descriptions are the **schema**: records, enums, objects, stores with their signals, functions, ports and queries. The CLI builds your core as a host library, loads it, asks for the schema, and hands it to `undra bindgen`, which writes a Swift package, a Gradle module and an npm package. Generated code depends only on the matching runtime package.

Three properties of this design are worth stating plainly:

- **Names become ids at compile time.** A type id is a hash of its name, a method id a hash of `Type.method`, a port id a hash of `port.Trait`, and a signal id is its position among the store's signal fields. Every platform agrees without a registry lookup. The hash is FNV-1a.
- **The schema has a hash.** It is the FNV-1a hash of a canonical form: lists sorted by name, no whitespace, doc comments excluded, so two cores with the same public surface hash the same. Each binding carries the hash it was generated from, and the runtime compares it with the core's when it attaches.
- **Generated code is reviewed like hand-written code.** Golden files lock the output for all three languages, and the output is compiled and run in tests. A record becomes a Swift `struct`, a Kotlin `data class` and a TypeScript `interface`; an error becomes a typed-`throws` enum, a sealed class and an `Error` subclass. See the API overviews for [Swift](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-swift.html), [Kotlin](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-kotlin.html) and [TypeScript](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-typescript.html).

The standard ports and their types are in every schema but are not generated into your bindings, because each runtime already implements them; see [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/ports.html).

## The crates

Twelve Rust crates, and only one of them may contain `unsafe`.

| Crate | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `undra-meta` | the schema model, canonical JSON, the hash, the FNV helpers and registration |
| `undra-wire` | the binary codec, envelope and patches; no `unsafe`, proptested and byte-fuzzed |
| `undra-macros` | the attribute macros and their teaching diagnostics |
| `undra-signals` | `Signal`, `Computed`, `Effect`, transactions, change-set building, keyed patches |
| `undra-runtime` | the executor, core lock, object table, ports, timers, snapshots and panic guard |
| `undra-ports` | the ten standard ports, their records and the deterministic fakes |
| `undra-query` | the query client, mutations, retry, persistence and the offline queue |
| `undra-ffi` | the C ABI, the JNI shim and the wasm exports: **the only `unsafe`** |
| `undra-transport` | the WebSocket server and framing behind `undra dev` |
| `undra-bindgen` | the Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript generators |
| `undra-cli` | the `undra` command |
| `undra` | the facade you depend on: prelude, macros, runtime, ports, query |

The runtimes are `runtimes/swift/UndraRuntime`, `runtimes/kotlin/undra-runtime` and `runtimes/ts/@undra/runtime`. The Kotlin runtime depends on the standard library and kotlinx-coroutines only, and the TypeScript core package has no runtime dependencies.

## The wire

The wire is small on purpose. It is little-endian throughout, with no alignment and no padding. All lengths are `u32`. Decoders never panic on malformed input; they return a typed error.

| Type | Encoding |
| --- | --- |
| integers, floats | fixed width, two's complement or IEEE 754 |
| `bool` | one byte, 0 or 1 (other values are rejected) |
| `String`, `Bytes` | `u32` length, then the bytes (strings validated as UTF-8) |
| `Option<T>` | a tag byte, then the value if present |
| `Vec<T>` | `u32` count, then the items |
| `Map<K, V>` | `u32` count, then pairs, sorted by encoded key so the bytes are deterministic |
| `Duration`, `Timestamp` | `i64` nanoseconds, `i64` milliseconds since the Unix epoch |
| `Uuid` | 16 raw bytes |
| record | its fields in declaration order |
| enum, error | `u16` variant index, then that variant's fields |
| `Result<T, E>` | a tag byte, then `T` or `E` |
| object handle | `u64`: low 32 bits slot, high 32 bits generation |

Transports that cross a real pipe (the WebSocket and worker transports) wrap every message in a 23-byte envelope. In-process calls skip it and carry only the payload.

*Figure: The envelope frames every message on the WebSocket and worker transports. In-process calls carry only the payload.*

The `kind` byte says what the payload is:

| Kind | Name | Direction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1, 2 | Call, Reply | host to core, core to host |
| 3 | ChangeSet | core to host |
| 4, 5 | PortCall, PortReply | core to host, host to core |
| 6, 7 | Cancel, StreamCredit | host to core |
| 8 | StreamItem | core to host |
| 9, 10 | Observe, Release | host to core |
| 11 | Event | host to core (connectivity, lifecycle) |
| 12 | Hello | both: Undra version, schema hash, platform, mode |
| 13 | Log | core to host |
| 14 | TimerFired | host to core |
| 15, 16 | Snapshot, Restore | core to host, host to core |

A **call** carries a target (free function, object method, constructor or lazy page), the object handle, the method id, a call id the host chose, and the arguments encoded in order. The **reply** carries the call id and a status: `0` ok, `1` a typed error, `2` a panic (message and backtrace), `3` cancelled, `4` a stream was opened, `5` a bad request such as an unknown method or a schema mismatch. A failure is always a typed value; nothing escapes as an abort.

A **change-set** is how state comes back. It carries a transaction id and one entry per dirty observed signal.

*Figure: Entries are ordered by signal id. A keyed patch inside an entry is a count and a list of operations.*

An entry's `op` is `0` for a full value, `1` for a keyed patch, and `2` for "lazy list invalidated". A keyed patch is a count and a list of operations (`Insert`, `Remove`, `Update`, `Move`, `Clear`) applied in order to the host's copy; see [Core concepts](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/concepts.html#keyed-lists). The `len` field lets a host skip an entry it cannot decode.

**Streams** use credit-based backpressure. A host grants credit and the core sends at most that many items beyond what has been credited; generated bindings grant 16 on subscribe and top up when consumption drops below 8. A cancel closes the stream.

## The boundary

The native boundary is a C ABI of C-compatible types only. Each core exports one symbol named after its namespace, `<namespace>_undra_api`, which returns a table: its version and size, the schema hash, the namespace, and seventeen entry points (parameter lists abridged here). Two cores in one process are two tables, and nothing of one can bind to the other ([ADR-044](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-044-per-core-symbol-namespacing.md)).

c

```c
const UndraApi *playground_core_undra_api(void);

typedef struct UndraApi {
    uint32_t    abi_version;                       // 2
    uint32_t    size;                              // sizeof(UndraApi), for later additions
    uint64_t    schema_hash;
    const char *name_space;                        // "playground_core"
    UndraBuf  (*schema_json)(void);
    uint32_t  (*init)(cfg, len, reply_cb, changeset_cb, stream_cb, user);
    void      (*shutdown)(void);
    uint32_t  (*call)(ptr, len);                   // async reply arrives on reply_cb
    UndraBuf  (*call_sync)(ptr, len);              // reply returned directly
    void      (*cancel)(call_id);
    void      (*stream_credit)(call_id, credit);
    void      (*observe)(handle, signal_id, on);
    void      (*release)(handle);
    void      (*port_register)(port_id, cb, user);
    void      (*port_reply)(ptr, len);
    void      (*event)(port_id, method_id, ptr, len);
    void      (*timer_fired)(timer_id);
    UndraBuf  (*snapshot)(void);
    uint32_t  (*restore)(ptr, len);
    UndraBuf  (*stats_json)(void);
    void      (*buf_free)(UndraBuf buf);
} UndraApi;
```

Android reaches the same functions through a JNI shim that registers its natives once at load on the bindings' own class, so there is no per-call lookup and two cores never share one. The web has its own module per core, so it needs no table, and no wasm-bindgen: the module exports and imports use only `i32`, `i64` and `f64`, a 64-bit handle is passed as two halves, and `undra_poll()` drives the executor. `Clock`, `Rng` and `Log` are bound to wasm imports, so a web app needs no adapter code for them.

Callbacks are where hosts get hurt, so the contract is explicit and enforced. A callback runs on whichever thread produced the event, possibly with the core lock held, so it must be short, thread-safe and must not throw. It must not call back into the core except the few entries that never take the lock (freeing a buffer, replying to a port call, granting stream credit, firing a timer, reading stats). Every other re-entry is refused with `E_REENTRANT` instead of deadlocking, in every build.

The synchronous call path is allocation-free once warm. A per-thread reply slot lets a synchronous method encode its whole reply into one reusable buffer, which is what moves a call through the C ABI to 49.8 ns ([ADR-028](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-028-synchronous-reply-slot.md)); a counting allocator in the tests holds the lending entry to zero allocations and a C ABI call to exactly one, the buffer it hands back.

## Threading

- **One mutator.** The core has one lock. Whoever holds it *is* the core loop. A synchronous call from the host runs on the caller's thread holding that lock, so it costs a mutex acquire, not a thread hop.
- **Async work.** Async calls are tasks on a small executor with no tokio, polled by the core thread, one task per in-flight call. Cancelling a call drops its future.
- **A blocking pool** runs blocking work off the lock. It must not write signals, and debug builds refuse such writes.
- **wasm is single threaded.** The host calls `undra_poll()` on the next microtask whenever the core asks to be scheduled.
- **Shutdown is orderly.** Every call still in flight is answered as cancelled and every stream ends, each exactly once, before the threads are joined.

## Transports and modes

| Mode | Where the core runs | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| in-process | linked into the app (C ABI on iOS, JNI on Android) | shipping |
| `wasm-main` | a wasm module on the page's main thread | simple web apps |
| `wasm-worker` | the same module in a worker | web apps that want the main thread free |
| `remote` | your machine, behind a WebSocket | `undra dev` |

Platform runtimes do the same jobs everywhere: load the core, allocate call ids, map replies to continuations, hold the mirror and apply change-sets on the main thread, implement observe and release, provide default adapters, implement the codecs, and **refuse a mismatched core** with a clear error that names both hashes.

## Compatibility

A UI and a core that were not built from the same schema must not talk. The schema hash is checked when the runtime attaches and surfaces as a typed mismatch error, and `undra bindgen --check` catches stale bindings at build time. Breaking the wire is a major version and needs an ADR; evolving a schema across a hash mismatch is deliberately not in v1.

## Diagnostics

Every macro mistake is an error with a stable code and a fixed shape: what happened, why, how to fix it, and where to read more. The same shape is used by schema validation and the runtime. This one is verbatim from the test suite:

text

```
error[undra::E0012]: `Vec<Box<dyn Any>>` cannot cross the boundary
  = note: trait objects have no wire representation
  = help: make `items` a concrete `#[undra::api]` type, or an enum listing the cases you need
  = docs: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0012
```

The catalogue, by family:

| Codes | What they catch |
| --- | --- |
| E0001 to E0008 | unsupported types, generics, lifetimes, trait objects, misplaced `Result` or `Stream`, bad map keys, unsupported item shapes, unknown attributes |
| E0010 to E0013 | error enums without messages, a store and its impl block that disagree, trait objects in fields, a store that cannot be restored automatically |
| E0020 to E0022 | `&mut self` or `self` receivers, non-`Send` async futures |
| E0030 to E0033 | port methods with non-wire parameters, invalid port shapes, an error type that cannot represent an unavailable port |
| E0040 to E0042 | query and mutation keys, signatures and return types |
| E0050 to E0052 | schema validation: duplicate names, names that collide after case conversion, clashes with the standard library |
| E0060 to E0064 | look-alike built-in names, aliased types, runtime port failures, `Option<Option<T>>`, objects used as values |

The CLI has its own `C00NN` codes with the same shape; [the error-codes page](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html) lists all of them, each with real messages from the test suite.

## The constitution

Twelve rules, enforced in review, not aspirational. They are the reason the project reads the way it does.

| Rule | In short | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **R1** | The schema is the only truth. A public type or function exists only if the schema can describe it. | Three languages cannot drift from each other if all three are derived from one description. |
| **R2** | `unsafe` lives in `undra-ffi` only, plus one schema loader in the CLI. Every block has a `// SAFETY:` comment; every other crate forbids it. | The audit surface is one crate, and it is the one reviewed under ASan and Miri. |
| **R3** | Generated code must pass native review: a Swift, Kotlin or TypeScript engineer who has never seen Rust would write it that way. Golden files lock it. | Adoption depends on the output feeling native, not generated. |
| **R4** | Every feature lands whole: unit tests, contract scenarios, a benchmark if the boundary is touched, docs on every `pub` item. | No half-features and no untested boundary. |
| **R5** | Reads never cross the boundary; writes cross once per transaction. No generated getter calls into the core. | This is the performance model. Everything else serves it. |
| **R6** | Nothing escapes as a panic or an abort. Every boundary entry is guarded; every error is a typed value. | A bug in the core must never take the app down with an unwinding crash. |
| **R7** | Compatibility is checked at load (schema hash) and at build. Breaking the wire is a major version and an ADR. | Mismatched halves are refused loudly instead of misdecoding quietly. |
| **R8** | Macro errors teach: a code, what, why, fix, docs link. | The Rust-side learning curve is the adoption risk. |
| **R9** | Budgets are tests. Benchmarks live in `bench/` and regressions fail CI. | Performance claims are kept true by the build, not by memory. |
| **R10** | We ship on it first: `examples/playground` uses only public APIs. | If the reference app needs a private door, the public API is wrong. |
| **R11** | Boundary changes need an ADR before code. | The wire, the runtime model, the threading model and generated shapes are expensive to change later. |
| **R12** | The core is deterministic: no wall clock, randomness or threads outside the Clock, Rng and Timer ports and the runtime. | Deterministic cores are testable with fakes and replayable. |

The engineering standards behind them: Rust 2024 edition with MSRV 1.85, `clippy -D warnings`, no `anyhow` in library crates, no `println!` in library code (logs go through the `Log` port), and no dependency that does not build for wasm32, iOS and Android.

## Decisions on record

The big decisions are written down as ADRs before the code. The ones in the tree today:

| ADR | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| [018](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-018-query-handles-and-dispatch-layer.md) | Query handles and the dispatch layer |
| [019](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-019-signals-transactional-delivery.md) | Signals: transactional delivery |
| [020](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-020-signals-delivery-order-and-round-cap.md) | Signals: delivery order and the round cap |
| [021](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-021-signals-contained-misuse.md) | Signals: contained misuse |
| [022](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-022-handle-generations-and-the-snapshot-floor.md) | Handle generations and the snapshot floor |
| [023](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-023-runtime-delivery-reentry-restore-and-shutdown.md) | Runtime delivery, re-entry, restore and shutdown |
| [024](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-024-standard-library-not-generated.md) | The standard library is not generated |
| [025](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-025-ports-typed-outcomes-and-schema-identity.md) | Ports: typed outcomes and schema identity |

| [027](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-027-keyed-list-ops-are-recorded-not-diffed.md) | Keyed list operations are recorded, not diffed |
| [028](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-028-synchronous-reply-slot.md) | The synchronous reply slot |

## What v1 leaves out

By design, v1 has no sync engine, no hosted services and no shared UI of any kind. Kv is a foreign port rather than Rust-owned SQLite. Lazy lists are reserved and rejected. Those are choices recorded in the specification, not gaps.

## Read the source of truth

- [`docs/SPEC.md`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/SPEC.md): the binding specification for the wire, the ABI, the schema, the runtime model and the generated shapes. Code that disagrees with it is wrong.
- [`bench/RESULTS.md`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md): every benchmark row, the machine, and what is still waiting for devices.
- [`.10x/reviews/`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/tree/main/.10x/reviews): the adversarial reviews: the four core crates (signals, runtime, macros, ffi) first, then every feature before it merged.
- [`contract-tests/scenarios.md`](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/contract-tests/scenarios.md): the 35 scenarios that define "the platforms agree".

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html

# Error codes

Every diagnostic Undra raises, from a macro at compile time, from schema validation, from the runtime or from the `undra` command, has a stable code, a fixed shape and a fix. The link at the end of each message lands on its code below.

## How to read one

A diagnostic says what is wrong, why the rule exists and how to fix it. This one is verbatim from the macro test suite:

text

```
error[undra::E0004]: callback `Arc<dyn Listener>` cannot be a field of a record or enum (`Listener` is a callback interface)
  = note: a callback is an instance with a lifetime, not a value: it cannot be copied, compared, stored in a record or mirrored from a signal
  = help: keep an id or a record here, and take the callback as a parameter of the method that needs it
  = docs: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0004
```

## All codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| [`C0001`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#C0001) | no `undra.toml` from `start` up to the filesystem root |
| [`C0002`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#C0002) | a configuration or schema file is unusable |
| [`C0003`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#C0003) | a tool is not installed |
| [`C0004`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#C0004) | a build tool exited with a failure |
| [`C0005`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#C0005) | the core crate is missing, or is not an Undra core |
| [`C0006`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#C0006) | the schema could not be extracted from the built core |
| [`C0007`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#C0007) | the schema cannot be turned into bindings (bindgen diagnostics) |
| [`C0008`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#C0008) | the command would overwrite something it must not |
| [`C0009`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#C0009) | an argument is unusable |

| [`E0010`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0010) | invalid `#[undra::error]` variant |
| [`E0011`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0011) | store and `#[undra::api(store)]` impl block disagree |
| [`E0012`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0012) | trait object in a record field |
| [`E0013`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0013) | store cannot be restored automatically |
| [`E0020`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0020) | `&mut self` receiver |
| [`E0021`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0021) | `self` by value |
| [`E0022`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0022) | non-`Send` future in an async method: `rustc`'s own error, pointed at the method by an assertion named after this code |
| [`E0030`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0030) | port method with a non-wire parameter |
| [`E0031`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#E0031) | event port method that is not a plain `fn(..)` returning `()` |
