### Wire failures

A `WireError` says its code and fields in a production build (`wire: code=unexpected_eof at=12 needed=3; see link`); the development build says the sentence below, with the values in braces.

| Code | The development build says |
| --- | --- |
| [`unexpected_eof`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#wire-unexpected_eof) | unexpected end of input at offset {at}: needed {needed} more byte(s) |
| [`invalid_utf8`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#wire-invalid_utf8) | invalid UTF-8 in string at offset {at} |
| [`invalid_tag`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#wire-invalid_tag) | invalid {ty} tag {tag} at offset {at} |
| [`length_too_large`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#wire-length_too_large) | length {len} at offset {at} exceeds the available input |
| [`trailing_bytes`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#wire-trailing_bytes) | {count} trailing byte(s) after the end of the message |
| [`bad_magic`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#wire-bad_magic) | bad magic: envelope does not start with 554e4452 |
| [`unsupported_version`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#wire-unsupported_version) | unsupported wire version {version} |
| [`schema_mismatch`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#wire-schema_mismatch) | schema mismatch: expected 0x{expected}, got 0x{got} |
| [`duplicate_key`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#wire-duplicate_key) | duplicate map key at offset {at} |
| [`negative_duration`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#wire-negative_duration) | negative duration ({nanos} ns) |
| [`unsafe_integer`](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#wire-unsafe_integer) | integer {value} at offset {at} is outside the JS safe integer range |

Generated by `site/scripts/build-errors.mjs` from `docs/SPEC.md` section 12, the compile-fail tests of the macros crate and the message goldens of the other crates. To change a message, change the code that raises it and regenerate its golden; to change the catalogue, change the specification.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-swift.html

# API overview, Swift

Generated Swift is written the way a Swift engineer would write it by hand: value types, error enums you catch by case, async/await, AsyncSequence and an @Observable store. Swift 6 language mode, strict concurrency, no Objective-C.

`undra bindgen` writes a Swift package (`Sources/<Module>/Generated/*.swift` and a `Package.swift`) that depends only on `UndraRuntime`. The shapes below come from the playground's generated code and the specification (§10.1).

**Reference.** Every declaration the playground generates, with its docs, is in the [Swift reference](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/reference/swift.html).

## Loading the core

Load the core once, before any store is created, through the entry generated for it: `Undra` and the core's namespace (`[core] namespace` in `undra.toml`, by default the core's package name), here `UndraPlaygroundCore`. It checks the core's schema hash against the one the bindings were generated from and throws a clear error if they differ.

UndraBootstrap.swift

```swift
import UndraRuntime
import PlaygroundCore

@MainActor
static func start() throws {
    let adapters = Adapters.platformDefault              // URLSession, Keychain, files, …
        .replacing(PlaygroundNetwork.shared)             // swap one port
    try UndraPlaygroundCore.load(.inproc(adapters: adapters))
}
```

In debug builds you can attach to the core that `undra dev` serves instead, with `UndraPlaygroundCore.load(.remote(url: url, adapters: adapters))`. After loading, every generated type defaults to its entry's core: `try Todos()` is `try Todos(ctx: UndraPlaygroundCore.core)`. Before the core is loaded, or after `shutdown()`, that is a shut-down placeholder: constructors throw `UndraCallError.unavailable(.closed)` instead of stopping the app, and the first use logs what to do. The core links like any static library, with no `-force_load`, so an app can carry [more than one](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/several-cores.html).

## Type mapping

| Rust | Swift |
| --- | --- |
| `bool`, `f32`, `f64` | `Bool`, `Float`, `Double` |
| `i8` … `i64`, `u8` … `u64` | `Int8` … `Int64`, `UInt8` … `UInt64` |
| `String`, `Bytes` | `String`, `[UInt8]` |
| `Duration`, `Timestamp`, `Uuid` | `Duration`, `Date`, `UUID` |
| `Option<T>`, `Vec<T>` | `T?`, `[T]` |
| `Map<K, V>` | `[K: V]` |
| record, enum, error | `struct`, `enum`, `enum` conforming to `Error` |

Names follow the platform: Rust `snake_case` becomes `camelCase` for methods and fields and `PascalCase` for types, and enum variants become `lowerCamel` cases.

## Records

A record is a `struct`: `Sendable`, `Hashable` and `Codable`, with a memberwise initializer.

swift

```swift
/// One item of the to-do list.
public struct Todo: UndraRecord, Sendable, Hashable, Codable {
    public var id: UUID
    public var title: String
    public var done: Bool

    public init(id: UUID, title: String, done: Bool)
}
```

The wire codec (`undraEncode`, `undraDecode`) is generated beside it and is not something you call.

## Enums

A unit enum is a `UInt16`-backed `enum` that is also `CaseIterable`, so it works directly in a `Picker`. A data enum carries its fields as associated values.

swift

```swift
public enum Filter: UInt16, UndraEnum, CaseIterable, Sendable, Codable {
    case all = 0, active = 1, done = 2
}

public enum Figure: UndraEnum, Sendable, Hashable {
    case circle(radius: Double)
    case rect(width: Double, height: Double)
    case label(String)
    case empty
}
```

## Errors

A Rust `#[undra::error]` becomes a Swift `enum` conforming to `Error` (and `LocalizedError`, with the message from `#[error("…")]`). A generated call that can fail is `throws` (or `async throws`) and fails with exactly one of three things: its own error, thrown as the enum itself; `CancellationError`, when the calling task was cancelled; or `UndraCallError`, for anything else that went wrong with the call. The method's `- Throws:` documentation names its error.

swift

```swift
public enum TodoError: UndraError, Error, Sendable, Hashable {
    case emptyTitle            // "the title cannot be empty"
    // a variant that wraps another error carries it: case http(HttpError)
}

do {
    _ = try await todos.add(title: draft)
} catch TodoError.emptyTitle {
    problem = "Enter a title"
} catch is CancellationError {
    // the view went away; nothing to do
} catch {
    problem = error.localizedDescription   // an UndraCallError: panicked, refused, …
}
```

`UndraCallError` is `Sendable`, `Equatable` and `LocalizedError`, so `localizedDescription` reads well in an alert. Generated Swift never stops the app: no reply, cancellation, lost connection or undecodable byte reaches `fatalError`, in debug or release.

| Case | When |
| --- | --- |
| `.cancelledByCore` | The core cancelled the call: a restore replaced the object it ran on, or the core shut down. Not a `CancellationError`, because your task was not cancelled and the write did not land. |
| `.panicked(message:backtrace:)` | The core panicked while running the call. It caught the panic and keeps working. |
| `.refused(reason:)` | The core would not run the call: the object was closed or replaced by a restore, the call came from inside one of the core's callbacks (`E_REENTRANT`), or its arguments did not decode. |
| `.unavailable(UndraTransportError)` | The core cannot be reached: it was shut down or never loaded, or the remote connection closed or timed out. The `UndraTransportError` says which: `.closed`, `.timedOut` or `.connectionLost`. While `undra dev` is reconnecting, every call fails with it at once (`.connectionLost`); so does every call on a core that a rebuild closed for good. |
| `.malformed(String)` | The core answered with something the bindings cannot read. After a successful schema check this is a bug in Undra; report it with the text. |

**Commands report instead of throwing.** A synchronous method that returns nothing and has no error type, such as `todos.toggle(id:)`, stays non-throwing, so a `Button` action or a `Binding` setter calls it directly. If it fails, the runtime logs the failure at error level, passes an `UndraUnhandledError` to `LoadOptions.onError` and returns. A store's properties change only from the core's change-sets, so a refused command leaves the screen showing exactly what the core holds. A store that cannot decode a change from the core skips it and reports it the same way.

swift

```swift
try UndraPlaygroundCore.load(.inproc(
    onError: { unhandled in
        // "Todos.toggle failed: the Undra core refused the call: …"
        logger.error("\(unhandled.description, privacy: .public)")
    }
))
```

The handler runs on the thread that made the call (the main actor for a store), so keep it short, and it must not call into Undra. To stop at the failing line in debug builds, install `onError: { assertionFailure("\($0)") }`.

**A lost connection is not an `onError` event.** Over `undra dev`, a command tapped while the dev server is away fails with `.unavailable` too, and the connection state (`connectionState` on the core `load` returned, or `LoadOptions.onConnectionChange`) already says so, once. A failure that is the connection being down (`.connectionLost`) is therefore logged at warning level and not handed to `onError`; a crash reporter would otherwise get one event per tap for as long as the laptop sleeps. Everything else `.unavailable` is still reported: a command on a core you shut down yourself, and a timeout.

**Typed throws are for ports.** A port requirement keeps `throws(E)`, because your app implements it and `E` tells it which errors the core understands; `swift_typed_throws = false` in `undra.toml` emits plain `throws` there. Calls never use typed throws: Swift's own cancellation (`Task.checkCancellation()`, `Task.sleep`) throws an untyped `CancellationError`, which a `throws(E)` function cannot pass on.

## Objects and functions

An object is a `final class` holding a handle into the core. Sync methods that return a value are `throws`, async methods are `async throws`, a sync method that returns nothing is a command (it reports instead of throwing, see [Errors](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-swift.html#errors)), and stream methods return an `AsyncThrowingStream` that ends with the same three failures. A free Rust function is a free Swift function that takes the core last.

swift

```swift
public final class Probe: UndraObject, @unchecked Sendable {
    public init(ctx: UndraCore = UndraPlaygroundCore.core) throws   // the constructor `new`
    public func counters() throws -> ProbeCounters         // sync
    public func wait(ms: UInt32) async throws -> UInt32    // async
    public func ticks(count: UInt32) -> AsyncThrowingStream<UInt32, Error>   // stream
    public func reset()                                     // a command
}

public func add(a: Int32, b: Int32, ctx: UndraCore = UndraPlaygroundCore.core) throws -> Int32
public func area(_ figure: Figure, ctx: UndraCore = UndraPlaygroundCore.core) throws -> Double   // throws LabError
```

Sync methods on an in-process core call straight into the core (the `call_sync` entry of its table). Streams apply real backpressure: the generated code grants credit as your loop consumes items, and dropping the stream stops it in the core.

Release an object with `close()`, which is idempotent. `deinit` is only a backstop for objects that go out of scope without it, so hold an object for as long as you need its state.

## Stores

A store is an `@Observable` class on the `MainActor`. Every signal is a `public private(set) var`, so SwiftUI tracks reads and re-renders when a change-set is applied. Computed signals are read-only properties the core keeps up to date.

swift

```swift
@MainActor @Observable
public final class Todos: UndraStore {
    public private(set) var todos: [Todo]
    public private(set) var filter: Filter
    public private(set) var visible: [Todo]        // computed by the core
    public private(set) var remaining: UInt32      // computed by the core

    public init(ctx: UndraCore = UndraPlaygroundCore.core) throws
    public func setFilter(_ f: Filter)                       // a command
    public func add(title: String) async throws -> Todo     // throws TodoError
}
```

Reading `todos.visible` is a plain property read: it never calls into the core. The initial values are decoded from the change-set the core emits when the store starts observing during `init`. Commands such as `toggle(id:)` do not throw, so a `Button` calls them without `try`:

swift

```swift
struct TodosScreen: View {
    let todos: Todos
    var body: some View {
        List(todos.visible, id: \.id) { todo in
            Button(todo.title) { todos.toggle(id: todo.id) }
        }
        .toolbar { ToolbarItem(placement: .principal) { Text("\(todos.remaining) left") } }
    }
}
```

## Query handles

A `#[undra::query]` becomes a store with five signals: `data`, `status`, `error`, `fetching` and `updatedAt`, plus `refetch()` and `invalidate()`. Construct one to observe the query; it fetches when the data is missing or stale.

swift

```swift
let inbox = try RemoteTodosQueryHandle(list: "inbox")
// inbox.data: [RemoteTodo]?, inbox.status, inbox.fetching, inbox.error, inbox.updatedAt
```

See [Queries & mutations](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/queries.html) for what the core does behind it.

## Ports

The ten standard ports are implemented by `UndraRuntime` (`URLSession`, Keychain, `FileManager`, `NWPathMonitor` and so on) and are not generated into your module. A port you define yourself becomes a protocol your app implements and registers with the adapters:

swift

```swift
public protocol Http: UndraPort {
    func request(_ req: HttpRequest) async throws(HttpError) -> HttpResponse
}
```

See [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/ports.html) for the defaults and for swapping one.

## Threading and lifetime

- Change-sets are applied on the `MainActor`, in one hop per transaction, so observable properties only ever change on the main thread.
- Stores and objects release their handle on `close()`, with `deinit` as the backstop. `UndraCore.stats()` exposes live handle counts for tests.
- Swift 6 strict concurrency is on. Generated stores are `@MainActor`; objects are `@unchecked Sendable` because the core serializes access behind its lock.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-kotlin.html

# API overview, Kotlin

Generated Kotlin is what a Kotlin engineer would write by hand: data classes, sealed hierarchies, suspend functions, Flow, and StateFlows you read with collectAsState(). The runtime needs only the standard library and kotlinx-coroutines.

`undra bindgen` writes a Gradle module (`src/main/kotlin/<package>/*.kt`, a `build.gradle.kts` and a `.gitignore`) that depends only on `undra-runtime`. The shapes below come from the playground's generated code and the specification (§10.2).

**Reference.** Every declaration the playground generates, with its docs, is in the [Kotlin reference](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/reference/kotlin.html).

## Loading the core

Load the core once per process, before any store is created, typically in `Application.onCreate`, through the entry generated for it: `Undra` and the core's namespace (`[core] namespace` in `undra.toml`, by default the core's package name), here `UndraPlaygroundCore`. It checks that the native library was built from the same schema as the bindings.

UndraApp.kt

```kotlin
class UndraApp : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        UndraPlaygroundCore.load(
            LoadOptions(adapters = mapOf(StandardPorts.Http.PORT_ID to myHttp.portImpl())),
        )
    }
}
```

The core is `libplayground_core.so`, named after its namespace, which `undra build --platform android` writes to `build/android/jniLibs/<abi>/`; it registers its natives on the bindings' own `UndraCoreNative`, so [two cores](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/several-cores.html) load side by side. On Android the runtime installs the adapters that need nothing from the platform (Clock, Rng, Log, Timer); pass the others you want to replace. After loading, every generated type defaults to its entry's core: `Todos()` is `Todos(ctx = UndraPlaygroundCore.core)`. Before the core is loaded, or after it was closed, that is a closed placeholder: constructors and calls on it fail with `UndraCallError.Unavailable` instead of crashing, and the first use logs what to do.

## Type mapping

| Rust | Kotlin |
| --- | --- |
| `bool`, `f32`, `f64` | `Boolean`, `Float`, `Double` |
| `i8` … `i64` | `Byte`, `Short`, `Int`, `Long` |
| `u8` … `u64` | `UByte`, `UShort`, `UInt`, `ULong` |
| `String`, `Bytes` | `String`, `ByteArray` |
| `Duration`, `Timestamp`, `Uuid` | `Duration`, `Timestamp`, `UUID` |
| `Option<T>`, `Vec<T>` | `T?`, `List<T>` |
| `Map<K, V>` | `Map<K, V>` |
| record, enum, error | `data class`, `enum class` or `sealed interface`, `sealed class` |

Names follow the platform: Rust `snake_case` becomes `camelCase` for functions and properties and `PascalCase` for types. Unit enum variants become `UPPER_SNAKE` constants; data enum variants become `PascalCase` classes. Undra does not support `Option<Option<T>>` because Kotlin cannot express nested optionality (`E0063`).

## Records

kotlin

```kotlin
/** One item of the to-do list. */
data class Todo(
    val id: UUID,
    val title: String,
    val done: Boolean,
) : UndraRecord
```

## Enums

A unit enum is an `enum class` with its wire index. A data enum is a `sealed interface` whose variants are data classes, `data object`s for the ones without fields.

kotlin

```kotlin
enum class Filter(val index: UShort) : UndraEnum {
    ALL(0u), ACTIVE(1u), DONE(2u);
}

sealed interface Figure : UndraEnum {
    data class Circle(val radius: Double) : Figure
    data class Rect(val width: Double, val height: Double) : Figure
    data class Label(val value: String) : Figure
    data object Empty : Figure
}
```

`when (figure)` over a sealed interface is exhaustive, so adding a variant in Rust is a compile error in every `when` that forgot it.

## Errors

A `#[undra::error]` becomes a `sealed class` extending `UndraException`, with the message from `#[error("…")]`. A generated call that can fail throws exactly one of three things: its own error, thrown as the sealed class itself, so `catch (e: TodoError)` and `when (e)` work; `CancellationException`, when the calling coroutine was cancelled; or `UndraCallError`, for anything else that went wrong with the call. The method's `@throws` documentation names its error.

kotlin

```kotlin
sealed class TodoError(message: String) : UndraException(message) {
    data object EmptyTitle : TodoError("the title cannot be empty")
    // a variant wrapping another error carries it: data class Http(val cause: HttpError)
}

viewModelScope.launch {
    try {
        store.add(draft)
    } catch (e: TodoError) {
        problem = when (e) {
            TodoError.EmptyTitle -> "Give it a title first."
        }
    } catch (e: UndraCallError) {
        problem = e.message   // Panicked, Refused, Unavailable, …
    }   // a CancellationException ends the coroutine as usual
}
```

`UndraCallError` is a sealed class under `UndraException`, so one `catch (e: UndraException)` shows either kind of failure to the user, and `e.message` reads well in a dialog. Every failure of the call is a typed value: no reply status, lost connection or undecodable byte reaches you as a bare `UndraException`.

| Case | When |
| --- | --- |
| `CancelledByCore` | The core cancelled the call: a restore replaced the object it ran on, or the core shut down. Not a `CancellationException`, because your coroutine was not cancelled and the write did not land. |
| `Panicked(panicMessage, backtrace)` | The core panicked while running the call. It caught the panic and keeps working. |
| `Refused(reason)` | The core would not run the call: the object was closed or replaced by a restore, the call came from inside one of the core's callbacks (`E_REENTRANT`), or its arguments did not decode. |
| `Unavailable(transport)` | The core cannot be reached: it was closed or never loaded, or the remote connection closed or timed out. `transport` is an `UndraTransportException` whose `reason` says which: `CONNECTION_LOST`, `CLOSED`, `TIMEOUT` or `INTERRUPTED`. While `undra dev` is reconnecting, every call fails with it at once (`CONNECTION_LOST`); so does every call on a core that a rebuild closed for good (`transport.cause` is an `UndraSessionLostException`). |
| `Malformed(detail)` | The core answered with something the bindings cannot read. After a successful schema check this is a bug in Undra; report it with the text. |

**Commands report instead of throwing.** A synchronous method that returns nothing and has no error type, such as `store.setFilter(f)`, stays non-throwing, so a Compose `onClick` calls it directly. If it fails, the runtime logs the failure at error level, passes an `UndraUnhandledError` to `LoadOptions.onError` and returns. A store's flows change only from the core's change-sets, so a refused command leaves the screen showing exactly what the core holds. A value the wire cannot represent is reported as `Malformed`, not thrown into the handler. A store that cannot decode a change from the core skips it and reports it the same way, and so does a malformed change-set (dropped whole) or a port implementation that failed.

kotlin

```kotlin
UndraPlaygroundCore.load(
    LoadOptions(
        onError = { unhandled ->
            // "Todos.toggle failed: the Undra core refused the call: …"
            Log.w("app", "${unhandled.operation} failed: ${unhandled.error.message}")
        },
    ),
)
```

The handler runs on the thread that made the call (the main thread for a click), so keep it short, and it must not call into Undra. To crash at the failing line in debug builds, install `onError = { throw AssertionError(it) }`.

**A lost connection is not an `onError` event.** Over `undra dev`, a command tapped while the dev server is away fails with `Unavailable` too, and the connection state (`connectionState` on the core `load` returned, or `LoadOptions.onConnectionChange`) already says so, once. A failure that is the connection being down (`CONNECTION_LOST`) is therefore logged at warning level and not handed to `onError`; a crash reporter would otherwise get one event per tap for as long as the laptop sleeps. Everything else `Unavailable` is still reported: a command on a core you closed yourself, and a timeout.

## Objects and functions

An object is a class holding a handle into the core. Sync methods that return a value are plain functions, async methods are `suspend`, a sync method that returns nothing is a command (it reports instead of throwing, see [Errors](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-kotlin.html#errors)), and stream methods return a `Flow` that fails with the same errors while you collect it. A free Rust function is a top-level Kotlin function that takes the core as its last, defaulted parameter.

kotlin

```kotlin
class Probe private constructor(core: UndraCore, handle: Long) : UndraObject(core, handle) {
    fun counters(): ProbeCounters                       // sync
    suspend fun wait(ms: UInt): UInt                    // async, cancellable
    fun ticks(count: UInt): Flow<UInt>                  // stream
    fun reset()                                         // a command
    companion object { fun create(ctx: UndraCore = UndraPlaygroundCore.core): Probe }
}

fun add(a: Int, b: Int, ctx: UndraCore = UndraPlaygroundCore.core): Int
suspend fun createRemoteTodo(list: String, title: String, ctx: UndraCore = UndraPlaygroundCore.core): RemoteTodo
```

Cancelling the coroutine cancels the call in the core, and a `Flow` applies backpressure: the runtime grants credit as your collector consumes items. The runtime contains core panics at the boundary: a bug in the core fails the call with `Panicked`, not a crash.

## Stores

A store extends `UndraStore`. Every signal is a read-only `StateFlow`; computed signals are updated by the core. Read them in Compose with `collectAsState()`, no extra module needed.

kotlin

```kotlin
class Todos : UndraStore {
    val todos: StateFlow<List<Todo>>
    val filter: StateFlow<Filter>
    val visible: StateFlow<List<Todo>>        // computed by the core
    val remaining: StateFlow<UInt>            // computed by the core

    constructor(ctx: UndraCore = UndraPlaygroundCore.core)
    fun setFilter(f: Filter)                  // a command
    suspend fun add(title: String): Todo      // throws TodoError
}
```

kotlin

```kotlin
@Composable
fun TodosScreen(vm: TodosViewModel = viewModel()) {
    val visible by vm.store.visible.collectAsState()
    val remaining by vm.store.remaining.collectAsState()
    Text("$remaining left")
    LazyColumn {
        // the list is keyed by id in the core, so Compose moves and animates rows
        items(visible, key = { it.id }) { todo -> TodoRow(todo) }
    }
}
```

**Hold on to the store.** The runtime's mirror holds a store weakly. A `StateFlow` on its own does not keep the store, and the core object behind it, alive. Keep the store in a `ViewModel` and close it in `onCleared()`.

## Query handles

A `#[undra::query]` becomes a store with five `StateFlow`s (`data`, `status`, `error`, `fetching`, `updatedAt`) plus `refetch()` and `invalidate()`. Constructing it observes the query and fetches when the data is missing or stale.

kotlin

```kotlin
val inbox = RemoteTodosQueryHandle.create("inbox")
val items by inbox.data.collectAsState()        // List<RemoteTodo>?
val busy by inbox.fetching.collectAsState()
```

See [Queries & mutations](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/queries.html).

## Ports

The ten standard ports are implemented in `dev.undra.runtime.adapters` and, for Android, in the `android-adapters` module (`HttpURLConnection`, files, an Android Keystore key, `ConnectivityManager`, activity lifecycle callbacks and so on; `AndroidPlatformDefaults.install(core, context)` registers them all) and are not generated into your module. You replace one by passing an implementation in `LoadOptions.adapters`, keyed by its port id, or by registering it after the load with `core.registerPort`. A port you define yourself becomes an `interface`:

kotlin

```kotlin
interface Http : UndraPort {
    suspend fun request(req: HttpRequest): HttpResponse     // throws HttpError
}
```

See [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/ports.html) for the defaults. Android-specific adapters live in the `android-adapters` module, not in the runtime.

## Threading and lifetime

- Signals are updated on `Dispatchers.Main.immediate`, in one hop per transaction. On a JVM without Android the runtime falls back to a single-thread executor, which is what the JVM test suite uses.
- `UndraStore` and `UndraObject` implement `AutoCloseable`. Call `close()` to release the handle (a `use { }` block works); a `Cleaner` releases leaked handles as a backstop. `UndraCore.stats()` exposes live handle counts.
- Over JNI, callbacks arrive from core threads and are decoded immediately; you never see a raw buffer.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-typescript.html

# API overview, TypeScript

Generated TypeScript is strict-mode ESM with no any in exported types: plain interfaces and unions for data, promises for calls, signals for state, and hooks for React. The core package has no runtime dependencies.

`undra bindgen` writes an npm package (`src/*.ts`, `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`) that imports only from `@undra/runtime`. The shapes below come from the playground's generated code and the specification (§10.3).

**Reference.** Every declaration the playground generates, with its docs, is in the [TypeScript reference](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/reference/typescript.html).

## Loading the core

Load the core once, before you create a store, through the entry generated for it: `Undra` and the core's namespace (`[core] namespace` in `undra.toml`, by default the core's package name), here `UndraPlaygroundCore`. It compares the core's schema hash with the one the bindings were generated from and rejects a mismatch with `UndraSchemaMismatchError`.

web/src/undra.ts

```ts
import { UndraPlaygroundCore, Todos } from "@playground/core";
import wasmUrl from "../../build/web/playground_core.wasm?url";

await UndraPlaygroundCore.load({
  mode: "wasm-main",                       // the core runs in a wasm module on this thread
  wasm: new URL(wasmUrl, location.href),
  adapters: { http, kv },                  // optional: replace a default adapter
});

const todos = await Todos.create();        // uses UndraPlaygroundCore.core
```

| `mode` | Where the core runs |
| --- | --- |
| `"wasm-main"` | a wasm module on the page's main thread |
| `"wasm-worker"` | the same module in a worker, keeping the main thread free (synchronous ports run in the worker: [Workers & crash recovery](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/web.html)) |
| `"remote"` | the core that `undra dev` serves, over a WebSocket: `{ mode: "remote", url: "ws://127.0.0.1:7443" }` |

Before the core is loaded, or after it was closed, `UndraPlaygroundCore.core`, the default core of every generated constructor and function, is a closed placeholder: constructors and calls on it reject with `UndraCallError.Unavailable`. The module is named after the namespace too, so [two cores](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/several-cores.html) load side by side.

## Type mapping

| Rust | TypeScript |
| --- | --- |
| `bool` | `boolean` |
| `i8` … `i32`, `u8` … `u32`, `f32`, `f64` | `number` |
| `i64`, `u64` | `bigint` (or `number` with `#[undra(js_number)]` / `ts_js_number`) |
| `String`, `Bytes` | `string`, `Uint8Array` |
| `Duration`, `Timestamp`, `Uuid` | `Duration`, `Timestamp`, `string` |
| `Option<T>`, `Vec<T>` | `T \| null`, `T[]` |
| `Map<K, V>` | `Map<K, V>` |
| record | `interface` |
| unit enum, data enum | string-literal union, discriminated union on `kind` |
| error | a class extending `UndraError`, with subclasses per variant |

64-bit integers become `bigint` so no value is ever silently rounded; a 64-bit value outside the safe range is a decode error rather than a wrong number when you opt into `number`.

## Records and enums

ts

```ts
/** One item of the to-do list. */
export interface Todo { id: string; title: string; done: boolean }

export type Filter = "all" | "active" | "done";

export type Figure =
  | { kind: "circle"; radius: number }
  | { kind: "rect"; width: number; height: number }
  | { kind: "label"; value: string }
  | { kind: "empty" };
```

A `switch (figure.kind)` over the union is exhaustive under `strict`, so adding a variant in Rust breaks every `switch` that forgot it.

## Errors

A `#[undra::error]` becomes an abstract class with a `kind` and one subclass per variant, so you can branch with `instanceof` or on `kind`. A generated call that can fail rejects with exactly one of three things: its own error, as the typed class, not a string to parse; the `AbortSignal`'s reason (an `AbortError` by default), when the signal you passed cancelled the call; or `UndraCallError`, for anything else that went wrong with the call. The method's `@throws` documentation names its error.

ts

```ts
export abstract class TodoError extends UndraError {
  declare readonly kind: "emptyTitle";
}
export namespace TodoError {
  // message: "the title cannot be empty"
  export class EmptyTitle extends TodoError {}
}

import { UndraCallError } from "@undra/runtime";

try {
  await todos.add(draft, controller.signal);
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof TodoError) {
    setProblem("Give it a title first.");
  } else if (error instanceof UndraCallError) {
    setProblem(error.message);   // panicked, refused, unavailable, …
  } else {
    throw error;                 // the AbortError of controller.abort()
  }
}
```

`UndraCallError` extends `UndraError`, so one `error instanceof UndraError` shows either kind of failure to the user, and `message` reads well in an alert. Each case is a class in the `UndraCallError` namespace, `kind` is its discriminant, and `switch (error.kind)` over the `UndraCallFailure` union is exhaustive. Every failure of the call is a typed value: no reply status, lost connection or undecodable byte reaches you as a raw `UndraReplyError` or `UndraTransportError`.

| `kind` | When |
| --- | --- |
| `"cancelledByCore"` | The core cancelled the call: a restore replaced the object it ran on, or the core shut down. Not the `AbortSignal`'s reason, because your signal did not abort and the write did not land. |
| `"panicked"` (`panicMessage`, `backtrace`) | The core panicked while running the call. A native core catches the panic and keeps working; a wasm core traps instead, and the call fails as `"unavailable"` (reason `"trap"`). |
| `"refused"` (`reason`) | The core would not run the call: the object was closed or replaced by a restore, the call came from inside one of the core's callbacks (`E_REENTRANT`), or its arguments did not decode. |
| `"unavailable"` (`transport`) | The core cannot be reached: it was closed or never loaded, a wasm core trapped, or the remote connection closed or timed out. `transport` is an `UndraTransportError` and its `reason` says which (`"closed"`, `"timeout"`, `"trap"`, …). While `undra dev` is reconnecting, every call rejects with it at once (`"closed"`); so does every call on a core that a rebuild closed for good (`onClose` receives an `UndraSessionLostError`). |
| `"malformed"` (`detail`) | The core answered with something the bindings cannot read. After a successful schema check this is a bug in Undra; report it with the text. |

**In a production build, the runtime's own messages are codes.** `@undra/runtime` publishes a development build and a production build of the same code. `vite dev`, Vitest and React Native resolve the readable one; `vite build`, webpack in production mode and plain Node resolve the production one, whose `message` for what the runtime words itself is a code, its values and a link: `T0017: callSync, remote; see https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#T0017`. The [errors page](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html#runtime-messages) has every sentence. The class, `name`, `kind` and every typed field are the same in both, and an error from the core (a typed error of yours, a panic message, a refusal reason) travels as its own text in both, so branch on those, never on `message`. To read sentences in a production build, resolve the `development` condition (`resolve.conditions: ["development"]` in Vite).

**Commands report instead of rejecting.** A method that returns nothing and has no error type, such as `counter.increment()`, is a command. Its promise never rejects, so an event handler calls it with `void` and no `.catch`, and a failure is never an unhandled rejection. If it fails, the runtime logs the failure at error level, passes an `UndraUnhandledError` to `onError` and resolves. Awaiting a command tells you it was sent and answered, not that it succeeded: read the effect from the store, which changes only from the core's change-sets. A value the wire cannot represent is reported as `"malformed"`, not thrown. A store that cannot decode a change from the core skips it and reports it the same way, and so does a malformed change-set (dropped whole) or a port implementation that failed.

ts

```ts
await UndraPlaygroundCore.load({
  mode: "wasm-main",
  wasm: new URL(wasmUrl, location.href),
  onError: (unhandled) => {
    // unhandled.operation is "Todos.toggle", unhandled.error.kind is "refused"
    reportToSentry(unhandled);
  },
});
```

The handler runs synchronously where the failure was found, so keep it short, and it must not call into Undra. An exception it throws is logged and dropped.

**A lost connection is not an `onError` event.** Over `undra dev`, a command tapped while the dev server is away fails with `"unavailable"` too, and the connection state (`core.connection`, or `onConnectionChange`) already says so, once. A failure that is the connection being down is therefore logged at warning level and not handed to `onError`; a crash reporter would otherwise get one event per tap for as long as the laptop sleeps. Everything else `"unavailable"` is still reported: a command on a core you closed yourself, a timeout, and a wasm core that trapped.

## Objects and functions

An object is a class holding a handle. **Every method returns a `Promise`**, which keeps the API uniform across main-thread, worker and remote modes. A command's promise resolves even when the call fails (see [Errors](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-typescript.html#errors)), and a stream method returns an `AsyncIterable` that fails with the same errors while you iterate it. An async method takes an optional `AbortSignal` as its last argument to cancel the call in the core.

ts

```ts
export class Probe extends UndraObject {
  static create(core?: UndraCore): Promise<Probe>;
  counters(): Promise<ProbeCounters>;
  wait(ms: number, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<number>;
  ticks(count: number): AsyncIterable<number>;     // backpressure through stream credit
  reset(): Promise<void>;                          // a command: never rejects
}

export function add(a: number, b: number): Promise<number>;
```

Release an object with `close()` (idempotent) or with `using` where `Symbol.dispose` exists (Node 20+ and current browsers); a `FinalizationRegistry` is the backstop.

Objects also cross as parameters and results ([Objects and identity](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/objects.html)), and host callbacks as parameters ([Host callbacks](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/callbacks.html)): there is one wrapper per object, so `===` compares the core's objects, and an object of another core is refused with `UndraCallError.Refused` before anything is sent. The generated classes do this through **free functions of `@undra/runtime` that take the core first**, not methods of `UndraCore`, so a page that uses neither feature does not ship them (the size budget of the up-front chunk): `adopt(core, handle, Type)`, `adoptObject`, `adoptOptional`, `adoptList` and `requireOwn(core, object)` for objects; `lend(core, impl, callback)`, `lending(core, send, signal)` and `giveBack(core, instance)` for callbacks. App code does not call them. `callbacks(core)` is the registry of the callbacks the core holds (`liveCount`, `count(impl)`), which a test reads to check that nothing is left behind.

## Stores and signals

A store extends `UndraStore`. Every signal is a read-only `Signal<T>`: `get()` returns the current value, `peek()` reads without subscribing, and `subscribe(fn)` calls you on change and returns an unsubscribe function. Computed signals are written by the core.

ts

```ts
export class Todos extends UndraStore {
  readonly todos: Signal<Todo[]>;
  readonly filter: Signal<Filter>;
  readonly visible: Signal<Todo[]>;        // computed by the core
  readonly remaining: Signal<number>;      // computed by the core

  static create(core?: UndraCore): Promise<Todos>;
  setFilter(f: Filter): Promise<void>;                  // a command: never rejects
  add(title: string, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<Todo>;
}
```

Change-sets are batched with `queueMicrotask` into one flush per macrotask, so several signals that changed in one transaction update together and a component never renders a half-applied state.

## React and the other frameworks

`@undra/runtime/react` exports two hooks. `useSignal` is `useSyncExternalStore` over a signal, with a server snapshot. `useUndra` creates a store when the component mounts and closes it when it unmounts; it returns `undefined` until the store exists, and `useSignal` accepts an undefined signal.

tsx

```tsx
import { useUndra, useSignal } from "@undra/runtime/react";

export function CounterView() {
  const counter = useUndra(Counter);            // undefined until created
  const count = useSignal(counter?.count);
  const parity = useSignal(counter?.parity);   // computed in the core, same change-set
  if (counter === undefined) return null;
  return <button onClick={() => void counter.increment()}>{count} ({parity})</button>;
}
```

Adapters ship for the other frameworks as thin files, exported from `@undra/runtime/vue` (`useSignal` as a `shallowRef`, `useUndra`), `/svelte` (`signalStore`, a `Readable`) and `/solid` (`useSignal` as an `Accessor`, `useUndra`). The frameworks are optional peer dependencies; the core package imports none of them.

## Query handles

A `#[undra::query]` becomes a store with five signals (`data`, `status`, `error`, `fetching`, `updatedAt`) plus `refetch()` and `invalidate()`.

ts

```ts
const inbox = await RemoteTodosQueryHandle.create("inbox");
const items = useSignal(inbox.data);        // RemoteTodo[] | null
const busy = useSignal(inbox.fetching);
await inbox.refetch();
```

See [Queries & mutations](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/queries.html).

## Ports

The ten standard ports and their types are exported from `@undra/runtime` and are not generated into your package. The browser defaults use `fetch`, IndexedDB, OPFS, `setTimeout`, `navigator.onLine` and `visibilitychange`; Node uses `fetch` and files. Replace one with `adapters` in `UndraCore.load`. A port you define yourself becomes an interface:

ts

```ts
export interface Http extends UndraPort {
  request(req: HttpRequest): Promise<HttpResponse>;
}
```

See [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/ports.html).

## Testing

The runtime is testable without a browser: over the `remote` transport against a native core, and against a WAT stub of the wasm ABI. The contract suite runs the same scenarios as the Swift and Kotlin runners, against the real wasm module.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/reference/swift.html

Roadmap

# What is shipped, and what comes next.

Shipped is what is on `main`. Next, Later and Exploring come only from what the repository records as planned or open: plans, not promises. This page follows the project's working record, [.10x/status.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/status.md), and changes with it. Last updated 3 Oct 2026.

Shipped

## In 1.0

on main

What you can build on today, grouped. Each line has its page in the docs and its decision record in the repository.

### Core and bindings

- **Records, enums and typed errors**From one schema, written as each language writes them.
- **Stores, signals and computeds**Reactive state in the core; one change-set per transaction.
- **Keyed and derived lists (ADR-039)**A filtered view of 10,000 rows sends 158 bytes for one edit, not 353 KB.
- **Objects and host callbacks (ADR-040, ADR-041)**Classes cross as themselves; the core calls back through typed interfaces.
- **Newtypes, Decimal, generic types (ADR-042)**Read as native types on every platform.
- **Generic functions, objects and stores (ADR-058)**Declared instantiations arrive as overloads and ordinary classes.
- **One error channel (ADR-032)**Calls fail with a typed error; generated Swift never traps.
- **Several cores in one app (ADR-044)**Each core is self-contained, storage included.

### Platforms

- **SwiftUI, Compose and React**Plus Vue, Svelte and Solid adapters for the web runtime.
- **React Native (ADR-038)**A TurboModule over the C ABI under the same TypeScript mirror.
- **iOS 15 and 16 (ADR-045)**ObservableObject stores below iOS 17; proven by compilation and a probe on iOS 26.5.
- **No manual build step**A Gradle task, an Xcode build phase and a Vite plugin run undra build.
- **Bazel rules (ADR-061)**undra_core and undra_bindings, hermetic and offline; JVM, Node and Swift tested.
- **Everything from GitHub at one tag (ADR-063)**The crates, the Swift package, the Kotlin modules (JitPack) and the npm runtimes; no account needed.

### Data

- **Queries and mutations**Staleness, dedup, retry and optimistic updates with rollback.
- **Offline queue and persistence**Queued writes replay on reconnect and survive a restart.
- **Paged and lazy lists, polling (ADR-043)**A lazy list pages 10,000 rows on demand; polling pauses with the app.
- **Migrations and typed storage (ADR-037, ADR-049)**A changed schema still restores what the last version stored.
- **Snapshot, restore and web recovery**A crashed web core restarts from its last snapshot.

### Ports

- **Ten ports, with adapters and fakes**Http, Kv, SecureStore, Fs, Clock, Rng, Log, Timer, Connectivity, Lifecycle.
- **WebSocket, SSE and Db (ADR-047, ADR-048)**Streams with backpressure, and SQL over SQLite, each with a deterministic fake.
- **Your own network stack (ADR-060)**OkHttp, URLSession and fetch as the app configured them.
- **Android adapters**Backed by the platform, installed with one call.

### Dev loop and tooling

- **State-preserving reload (ADR-053, ADR-059)**undra dev rebuilds on save and keeps the state and query handles.
- **Devtools (ADR-054)**Live stores, a change-set timeline with time travel, port and query logs.
- **undra schema diff (ADR-062)**Each API change marked breaking or additive, for review and CI.
- **init, doctor and upgrade**A project with CI, every missing tool with its fix, pins moved in one step.
- **Teaching diagnostics**Every macro error says what, why and how to fix it.
- **Reconnect everywhere (ADR-051)**Apps on all three platforms reconnect to undra dev by themselves.

### Testing

- **A testing kit for apps (ADR-055)**Previews on the real core; recorded sessions replay in tests.
- **The contract grid**The same scenarios against the real core on Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript, every cell passing.
- **Adversarial reviews**Every core crate and every feature, reviewed by someone who did not write it.

### Size and speed

- **The JavaScript runtime at 16 KB (ADR-057)**What a page loads up front went from 22.1 KB to 15.8 KB gzipped.
- **The web core under 120 KB (ADR-052)**The hello-world wasm, measured and gated in CI.
- **Native size profile and gates (ADR-052)**Release builds tuned for size; opt_level chooses smaller or faster.
- **The web call path (ADR-056)**A generated TypeScript call went from 3.2–3.5 µs to 0.47–0.68 µs.
- **Frame-coalesced delivery (ADR-031)**Each mirror applies what arrived once per frame.
- **Harsh-conditions benchmarks**Firehose, churn, fan-out, backpressure and a soak, with CI gates.

### Production

- **Panic reports and symbols (ADR-046)**A contained panic reaches the app with frames undra symbolicate reads.
- **Background runs (ADR-046)**The offline queue drains under the OS's deadline.
- **A runtime ends when its owner lets go (ADR-034)**Off-core writes are refused; a panicking computed poisons only itself.

### Docs and samples

- **Cookbook and migration guides**Recipes, and the way over from Kotlin Multiplatform and UniFFI.
- **Fieldbook**A production-shaped sample beyond the playground.
- **API reference**Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript from the generated code; Rust from rustdoc.

Next

## Planned next

recorded as open

Each of these is recorded as open in the repository, with the work done around it. A plan, not a promise; the order may change.

- Benchmarks on physical phonesEvery device row so far is from a simulator, an emulator or headless Chromium. Real-phone rows next, then budgets for them and a CI job.
- Maven Central and the npm registryThe conventional registries, after launch, beside GitHub: the Kotlin runtime on Maven Central and the npm packages on the registry. undra upgrade moves a project over. crates.io follows, under a registry-safe prefix.
- Homebrew (brew install undra)Through homebrew-core, once the repository is 30 days old and notable (75 stars, or 30 forks or watchers). There is no tap at launch: the installer and cargo are the two ways to get the CLI.
- Android modules tested in CIundra-compose, android-adapters and android-work pass locally and on the emulator; an emulator job in CI runs them.
- Android under Bazel, verifiedThe rules declare Android; a build and a test run prove it.
- Byte-reproducible undra buildToday the same core built in two directories differs, because cargo hashes the absolute path into crate names.
- The examples on schema diffCommit each example's schema.json, so the repository reviews its own API changes the way it asks apps to.
- Cancelled port calls reach the platformA cancelled call is abandoned in the core today while the platform's request runs on. Its own decision record first.
- Your network stack, proved furtherCertificate pinning through OkHttp end to end, a build against OkHttp 5, and the iOS WebSocket adapter refusing a background session as the SSE adapter does.
- Smaller Android librariesRelocation packing saves about 3%, once a load test on API 23 passes.
- Windows CLIRelease binaries and docs for the undra command on Windows.
- A custom domainA home for the site and docs that is the project's own.

Later

## Later

approved, not started

Decided in direction and waiting their turn.

- Dart and Flutter bindingsA fourth host after React Native, which proved the pattern. Not started.
- Desktop as a first-class targetCompose Desktop and macOS samples built in CI over the runtimes that exist; Windows and Linux over the same C ABI.
- Xcode 27The Swift test target was reported not to build on Xcode 27. Our machines and CI run Xcode 26; it is fixed once it reproduces.

Exploring

## Exploring

ideas, not scheduled

Questions the project is asking, not plans.

- A GraphQL storyUndra has no GraphQL layer; an app built around Apollo keeps Apollo on the platform side.
- A sync engineIf it comes, a separate package, not part of the core.
- Compose Multiplatform interopAn Undra core under a Compose Multiplatform UI.

Not planned

## Not planned

Shared UI of any kind, and hosted services. Undra owns everything under the pixels and leaves the screens to SwiftUI, Compose, React and React Native.

> ## How to influence the roadmap
>
> Open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/issues) and describe the problem you have rather than the feature you want; real projects and real numbers move items up. Anything that touches the wire, the runtime model, the threading model or a generated public shape needs a decision record first, and those live in [.10x/adrs](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/tree/main/.10x/adrs).
>
> [Open an issue](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/issues)

Launch

# Undra 1.0: one Rust core under native apps

Undra is a Rust framework for the part of an app that is not pixels: its domain logic, reactive state, data layer and persistence. You write that part once, in Rust; Undra generates the Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript that SwiftUI, Compose, React and React Native use, and every screen stays the platform's own.

3 Oct 2026 · 5 min read · Undra team

## What it is

An Undra core is a Rust crate. You mark its records, enums, errors and stores with a handful of attributes; the macros describe them as a schema, and `undra bindgen` turns the schema into the API each platform would write itself: an `@Observable` class for SwiftUI, `StateFlow`s for Compose, hooks for React and React Native.

Each platform keeps a local mirror of the state its screens observe, so a read is a property access and never calls into Rust. A write crosses the boundary once per transaction, and the core answers with one binary change-set that patches every mirror. That is the diagram on the [home page](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/), and you can tap it. In a release build on the reference machine, an Apple M5 Pro and not a phone, a synchronous call into the core costs 49.8 ns on the core side, and a change-set of 100 signals 2.3 µs.

## Who it is for

Teams that ship on two or more platforms that must agree on logic, state and data rules: the same validation, the same offline queue, the same cache and when it goes stale, the same answer to "what does this list contain now" on an iPhone, an Android phone and a browser tab. Written three times, those rules drift apart a release at a time. Undra writes them once and leaves each screen as native as it was.

It assumes a team that can carry Rust, a real cost that the [default-choice post](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/why-undra-is-the-default-choice/) weighs against Kotlin Multiplatform, UniFFI and writing it three times.

## What is in 1.0

- **The core.** Records, enums and typed errors; stores of signals and computeds; keyed lists, and derived lists that send only what changed; objects and host callbacks; newtypes, decimals and declared generics.
- **The data layer.** Queries and mutations with staleness, retry and optimistic updates that roll back; an offline queue; persistence that migrates stored data across schema changes and refuses what it cannot convert; paged and lazy lists; polling.
- **Ports.** Ten platform services with adapters and deterministic fakes; WebSocket, server-sent events and SQLite; the app's own OkHttp, URLSession or fetch underneath.
- **The dev loop.** `undra dev` serves one core to every running app and keeps its state across a rebuild, except in a web page started with `npm run dev`, which reloads and starts fresh; devtools with a change-set timeline; `undra schema diff` marks each API change breaking or additive.
- **Platforms.** SwiftUI, Compose, React and React Native, built from Xcode, Gradle, Vite or Bazel. iOS 15 and 16 get `ObservableObject` stores, proven by compilation and a probe on iOS 26.5, not yet on an iOS 15 or 16 runtime, simulator or device.
- **Proof.** 35 contract scenarios against the real core on Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript (two run on TypeScript only), 101 of 101 cells passing; 7,770 tests at the 2 October count, with more added since; an adversarial review before every feature merged.

Sizes are gated in CI. The hello-world web core, a WebAssembly module, is 113.1 KB gzipped in the committed record, against a budget of 120 KB. The JavaScript runtime a hello page loads up front is 15.8 KB gzipped against 16 KB. The hello-world Android library for arm64-v8a is 898.2 KB, stripped and uncompressed, against 1.2 MB per ABI. The [roadmap](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/roadmap/) lists everything by group.

## Try it in five minutes

With Rust (and its `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target) and Node installed:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/install.sh | sh
undra init myapp
cd myapp/web && npm install && npm run dev
```

Cargo works too (`cargo install --git https://github.com/shreypdev/undra undra-cli`, built from source). `undra init` writes a core with a to-do store, its bindings and an app per platform, downloading nothing. `npm run dev` builds the core to WebAssembly (the first build compiles the Undra crates and takes a minute or two) and serves the app at `http://localhost:5173`. Edit `core/src/lib.rs` and save: the page is on the new core. `undra dev` serves one core to every app at once.

The iOS and Android apps get their runtimes from the same GitHub release, with no account: the Swift package at the repository's root and the Kotlin modules from JitPack. [Getting started](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/getting-started.html) has every step, as we ran it.

## What it is not

- **Not a UI toolkit.** No widgets, no layout, no shared screens, and none planned. [Why Undra keeps your UI native](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/why-undra-keeps-your-ui-native/) says who should share the UI instead.
- **Not for a single-platform app.** One platform has nothing to agree with; its logic belongs in that platform's language, without a boundary or a second toolchain.
- **Not proven on physical phones yet.** Every device number so far comes from the iPhone simulator, the Android emulator or headless Chromium, and says so.
- **Not widely used.** Undra is one team's work with no production users yet. The contract grid, the reviews and the records exist so you can check the claims instead of trusting them.

## Where to go next

The [playground](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/playground/) runs the real core in your browser. [Reads never cross the boundary](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/reads-never-cross-the-boundary/) explains the state model, and the comparisons with [Kotlin Multiplatform](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-kotlin-multiplatform/) and [UniFFI and Crux](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-uniffi-and-crux/) say where each tool is ahead. Questions go to [GitHub](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/issues).

Every claim and its source: [the claims ledger](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-1-0/claims.md).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/the-javascript-runtime-at-16-kb/

Performance

# Fifteen levers: the JavaScript runtime at 16 KB

What a hello-world page loads up front of `@undra/runtime` went from 22,100 to 15,774 bytes gzipped, under a 16,000-byte budget. No feature was removed: code a hello page does not use loads when something first needs it, and a production page reports an error as a code with a link instead of a sentence. Here are the fifteen levers, and the four defects the review caught.

3 Oct 2026 · 6 min read · Undra team

## Where the bytes were

The web size decision (ADR-052) asked for 16 KB of runtime up front. An earlier piece reached 21.2 KB and concluded that 16 KB would mean removing behaviour; five pieces then added 0.9 KB, and the gate stood at 22,100 bytes with no room. Instead we attributed every byte: a script charges each byte of the minified chunk, and each bit of its gzip stream, to its declaration.

Every size here is gzipped at zlib level 9. "Up front" is the first chunk of a production build of the `undra init` web template, made by Vite 8.3.1 (its bundler is Rolldown), counting the runtime's own code. Vite's preload helper, a snippet Vite adds to a chunk that loads another on demand, is 691 bytes and is reported beside the number. A share is what code costs in this chunk, not what removing it saves, so every lever below was measured by building. The nine largest of the 24 shares:

| Concern | gzipped bytes |
| --- | --- |
| wire format: reader, writer, codecs | 3,702 |
| the mirror (each platform's copy of the core's state) | 2,867 |
| the host that runs the core's WebAssembly in the page | 2,521 |
| error classes and their sentences | 2,038 |
| the call path | 1,889 |
| ports: dispatch, default ports, host events | 1,834 |
| core lifecycle: load, options, start, close | 1,805 |
| streams | 945 |
| the bundler's own helper and chunk table | 717 |

Four things stood out. A hello page shipped code it cannot run: streams the template does not have, reconnection for a core that is not remote, 20 of 24 codecs. Rolldown decides where a module goes by re-exports, not by use: a module the entry reaches statically through any file with code of its own lands in the first chunk, even if only an on-demand chunk uses it. Those are Rolldown's rules; another bundler may place modules differently and save less. The sentences of errors were about a tenth of the chunk. And 717 bytes were the bundler's: each on-demand chunk costs the first chunk 15 to 30 bytes of file name, so every lever that makes something lazy grows that share a little.

## The levers

Each landed with its measured number. gzip is not additive: a row is what it saved on top of the rows above. The table is as built, before the review's fixes below, whose cost of 131 bytes includes row 8's part.

| # | Lever | after | saved |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | `main` before | 22,100 |  |
| 1 | session payloads re-exported by the wire format's index file (a barrel) | 21,971 | 129 |
| 2 | nine port ids as literals, pinned by a test | 21,766 | 205 |
| 3, 11a | `codecs` as a module namespace; unnamed codecs in a module of their own | 20,799 | 967 |
| 4 | streams as a feature the generated entry passes | 20,152 | 647 |
| 5 | a typed channel to the in-process host | 19,458 | 694 |
| 6, 7 | observe waiters, and code only a core outside this thread needs, load with their transport | 18,942 | 516 |
| 8 | `stats`, `snapshot`, `restore`, `runInBackground` on first call; the review put `snapshot` and `restore` back up front | 18,580 | 362 |
| 9, 10a | each on-demand transport maps its own options; the sync-port refusal text | 18,311 | 269 |
| 11b | two rarely thrown error classes | 18,158 | 153 |
| 12 | trims | 18,079 | 79 |
| 13 | the production build says error codes, with a link | 16,763 | 1,316 |
| 14 | the production build renames private properties | 16,193 | 570 |
| 15 | Vite's preload helper reported beside the number | 15,679 | 514 |
| 4b | no bundler warning in an app with a stream | 15,680 | +1 |

Row 15 changes what is counted, not what is shipped, so the other reading has a gate of its own: with Vite's helper left in the chunk, the final record is 16,285 bytes against 16,600. Row 13 is the largest single lever. A production page carries an error's class, kind and fields, and its text is a code (`T` and a number), the values and a link to the [error codes](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/errors.html); the development build keeps the sentences.

## What left, and what stays

What left loads when it is first needed: stream support, the framed transports' codecs, reconnection, the observe waiters, `stats` and background runs, the codecs a schema does not name. What stays up front stays for a reason we measured:

- **Keyed-patch merging**, because read-your-writes drains are synchronous and could not wait for a chunk.
- **The mirror's compaction**, because its backlog bound must hold offline too.
- **Object identity**, because every app's first screen waits for it.
- **Connectivity and Lifecycle events**, about 530 bytes: a hello core listens to neither, but nothing tells the page so. That needs the core to say when it starts listening, which is an ABI decision with its own record. It is the next lever.

## What the review caught

The adversarial review reproduced the sizes to the byte and found four High defects at the levers' edges:

- **A stripped declaration.** `reclaim` was marked internal, so the published types dropped it, and generated bindings that import it failed `tsc` against the installed package. Every suite aliased the sources and stayed green. A test now asks the compiler about every name the generator imports.
- **Lost order.** `snapshot()` and `restore()` ran after an `await import()`, which yields even when the module is cached, so a call made after `restore()` reached the core first. They run at the call again.
- **A fetch at the wrong moment.** The background drain at `pagehide` needed a chunk fetched, when a page is being left or is offline and may not be able to fetch one. It calls the core directly now.
- **Codes where data was expected.** The production build had turned a WebSocket close reason, which reaches the server, and port errors, which reach the core, into codes. Text that leaves the runtime as data is a sentence in both builds.

The fixes cost 131 bytes, to 15,811; smaller fixes and a later merge left the record at 15,774.

## What it cost

On Node, an awaited call takes 325 to 333 nanoseconds where it took 313 to 316, about 4 to 5% more (four alternating runs on one machine); `callSync` did not move, at 162 to 168 nanoseconds before and 162 to 167 after. When the levers landed, the development build's first chunk was 21,151 bytes; it has not been re-measured since the review's fixes and is not gated, since a development page is served module by module. The page that uses every feature (in `wasm-main` mode, its first chunk plus every on-demand runtime chunk except the Worker script) loads 39,922 bytes, less than the 42,385 it loaded before.

The gate has three rows: the hello page (16,000 bytes), the hello page with Vite's helper counted (16,600) and the page that uses every feature (42,400, or 5% over its record, whichever is lower). A change that takes a row over its ceiling, or moves a runtime module into or out of the first chunk, fails the build; over a budget, the message names the levers left, the next being about 530 bytes of host events.

Every claim and its source: [the claims ledger](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/the-javascript-runtime-at-16-kb/claims.md). The full record is [ADR-057](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-057-js-runtime-16kb.md) and [its review](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/reviews/2026-10-02-ts-runtime-16k-review.md).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/a-week-of-outside-use/

Field notes

# A week of outside use: seven findings, five fixes

Before the release, a team tried Undra for a week, in a proof of concept, and sent us seven findings. Five are fixed and merged, each through a pull request with a decision record and an adversarial review. Two were not taken on. Here is each one, what we measured, and what changed.

3 Oct 2026 · 6 min read · Undra team

## The seven findings

| Finding | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Server-sent events are slow on iOS | Fixed: 7.8x on 4 KB events (release build, on a Mac) |
| The Swift tests do not build on Xcode 27 | Not taken on: no reproduction yet |
| No Bazel | Fixed: Bazel rules and an example workspace |
| A core is 1.6 MB per Android ABI | Fixed: a size profile, a setting and gates; the reported core is an estimated 1.42 MB by default |
| The Android adapter is not our network stack | Fixed: adapters over the app's own OkHttp |
| No GraphQL | Not taken on: Apollo stays on the platform side |
| Generated code is noise in review | Fixed: the schema is the API, and `undra schema diff` reads it |

## The SSE adapter read a byte at a time

The report measured the iOS ceiling for server-sent events 2.4x below what it should be. The code agreed: the Swift adapter pulled the response body from `URLSession.AsyncBytes` one byte at a time and handed the parser one byte per call. The Kotlin and TypeScript adapters already read chunks.

The adapter is now the delegate of a data task, and the parser gets whole chunks. Backpressure follows the Kotlin adapter's rule: the task is suspended while events wait for the core, so URLSession stops reading and TCP pushes back.

We measured on a Mac (Apple M5 Pro, macOS 26.5), not on an iPhone or the simulator: a release build of the adapter reading from a local test server. 4 KB events went from 12,600 to between 84,000 and 99,000 a second over three runs (7.8x is the middle run), and 512-byte events by 2.1x; 64-byte events did not move, because the limit there is URLSession's own receive path. A debug build gained 4.2x and 4.3x on the same two sizes, and the report's 2.4x falls inside that range. Separately, once the parser worked on bytes instead of characters, it alone went from 310 to 2,246 MB/s on 4 KB events, in a release harness fed 64 KiB chunks.

The review found two High defects in the fix itself: a cancelled waiter hung and left the request open, and a background URLSession, which takes no task delegate, aborted the app. A background session is now refused with a typed error. The old adapter streamed on one, so that is a behaviour change, stated in ADR-047.

## No Bazel

Undra's build was a command line that Xcode and Gradle call: a Bazel repository had nothing to put in its graph, and its lint rules flagged the generated Kotlin. The `bazel/` module adds `undra_core`, `undra_bindings` and a library rule per language, which run the CLI as a pinned, hermetic, offline tool. `examples/bazel` tests a core from Kotlin on the JVM, TypeScript on Node and, on macOS, Swift. Lint exclusions written beside every generated tree took ktlint 1.8 from 90 findings to none on the example's generated Kotlin. Android under Bazel is declared and not yet verified: the example's Android core stops at analysis for want of a C++ toolchain, and the roadmap says so.

## 1.6 MB per ABI

Nothing gated a native core's size. iOS and Android release builds now use a profile at `opt-level = "s"` that keeps the four crates of the call path at full speed, and three gates hold the hello world: 898,176 bytes for arm64-v8a and 960,776 for x86_64 (stripped, uncompressed) against 1.2 MB, and an iOS slice of 784,086 against 900 KB. For a team with a hard byte budget, `opt_level` in the `[android]` or `[ios]` table of `undra.toml` chooses `"s"` (the default), `"z"` (smallest) or `"3"` (fastest).

We did not have the reported core, so we estimated where it lands: the hello world's share plus the rest, scaled by how much the playground shrinks. It comes to about 1.42 MB per ABI with nothing changed (1.38 to 1.46 MB, since the tool rounds 1.55 to 1.65 million bytes to "1.6 MB") and about 1.18 MB at `opt_level = "z"` (1.14 to 1.21 MB), so `"z"` reaches 1.2 MB narrowly and not for every core of that size. `"z"` has a cost we measured on the playground's device benchmark, against `"3"`, which the default matches within noise: a synchronous call 1.33x slower on the iPhone simulator and 1.58x on the Android emulator, not on a phone. The answer is a setting with its price documented, not a promise.

## Inside the app's network stack

The default Android adapter used `HttpURLConnection`. An app's token refresh, interceptors, tracing and certificate pinning live in its own `OkHttpClient`, an object the platform's `HttpURLConnection` cannot reach, so a request from the core carried no token, appeared in no trace and was not pinned. The optional `okhttp-adapters` module puts Http, WebSocket and SSE over the app's own client with one call; on iOS the app's `URLSession` serves all three. Two limits remain. OkHttp itself leaves a client's network interceptors and event listener out of a WebSocket upgrade, so tracing written that way will not see the core's WebSockets; the docs say so. And the SSE adapter refuses a background `URLSession` while the WebSocket adapter does not yet, which is on the roadmap. The review's High: in the old install order, a queued offline request could leave through the default adapter, without the token and without the pin.

## Generated code in review

Two features had produced about 1,400 lines of bindings. The count was right: one feature of the playground is 130 to 250 generated lines per platform. We kept the code, since the project's rules require generated code to read as a platform engineer would write it, and moved review to the schema. Generated files are marked for GitHub to collapse, and `undra schema diff` prints one line per API change, breaking or additive. On the command line's test fixture, a to-do core with thirteen API changes, the generated bindings changed by 581 lines, the schema file by 77, and the diff printed 13.

## What we did not take on

**Xcode 27.** The Swift test target was reported not to build on it. Our machines and CI run Xcode 26, so we could not reproduce it; it needs the crash log. It stays on the roadmap until it reproduces.

**GraphQL.** Undra has no GraphQL layer, and an app built around Apollo keeps Apollo on the platform side. Whether Undra should have more is a question on the roadmap, not a plan.

## What a week taught us

Three of the five were places where our tests were green and a real app was not: a ceiling nobody had measured, a build system we did not use, a size we did not gate. What the five reviews left open is on the [roadmap](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/roadmap/): OkHttp pinning end to end, Android under Bazel, a byte-reproducible build.

Every claim and its source: [the claims ledger](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/a-week-of-outside-use/claims.md).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/why-undra-is-the-default-choice/

Overview

# Why Undra is the default choice

A team choosing how to share logic across iOS, Android and the web asks one question before any other: what will this stop me doing? We catalogued 68 limitations of Kotlin Multiplatform, UniFFI, Crux, React Native, Flutter, Capacitor and writing the logic three times, each dated and sourced where a source exists, and mapped every one to what Undra's repository does about it. This post is the result: what Undra solved and how, what it did not, and why a team can start from it by default.

2 Oct 2026 · 16 min read · Undra team

> **How to read this page.** We build Undra, so the page leans our way. Each statement about another tool links to the page it comes from, and we read every one of those pages again on 2 October 2026; where we are reading a page's silence, we write "its documentation describes no", and that reading is as of the same date. Statements about Undra link to a decision record, a docs page, a review or a benchmark file. Timings are measured on an Apple M5 Pro host, on its iPhone simulator, its Android emulator or in headless Chromium; none is from a physical device, and none compares Undra's speed with another tool's. Each claim has a row in the [claims ledger](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/site/blog/why-undra-is-the-default-choice/claims.md) with the fact-check's verdict, and the 68 limitations are in the [catalogue](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/specs/2026-10-01-competitive-limitations.md). If something is wrong or has moved, [open an issue](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/issues) and we will correct the page with a dated note.

## The matrix

The catalogue's matrix lists 36 things a team needs. On 1 October Undra was marked as having 10 of them, part of 9 and none of 16, with one not applicable. Since then every code piece of the v1.x program has merged, each feature after an adversarial review recorded in the repository. At the last merge the contract grid passed 101 of 101 cells over 35 scenarios, and the test suites ran 3,812 Rust, 2,043 TypeScript, 890 Kotlin, 914 Swift and 111 React Native tests. Counting again today: 28 solved, 5 partial, 2 open and 1 left out by decision. The count is ours, row by row in the ledger, and it is the part of this page we most want checked. The table groups the 36 rows into 12 classes. It leaves out Crux, which [its own post](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-uniffi-and-crux/) covers, and reads "Flutter / React Native" as those two with the logic written in the UI's language.

| Class | Kotlin Multiplatform | UniFFI | Flutter / React Native | Undra |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| State reaches the UIrows 3 to 6 | On iOS Swift [copies a Kotlin collection whole](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-objc-interop.html); observing a `Flow` takes [SKIE](https://skie.touchlab.co/) or [Swift export](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-swift-export.html), which is Alpha. | Its documentation describes no observable state; reading Rust state is [a call across the boundary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs/main/docs/manual/src/internals/lifting_and_lowering.md). | No language boundary. React Native [runs logic on the JS thread](https://reactnative.dev/docs/performance); a frame it misses is dropped. | **Solved.** Reads are local; a write crosses once; lists, and filtered or sorted views of them, cross as O(change); delivery is merged per frame. [Reads post](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/reads-never-cross-the-boundary/), [ADR-031](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-031-frame-coalesced-delivery.md), [039](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-039-derived-keyed-lists.md). |
| Errors and crashesrows 1, 2 | Only `@Throws` exceptions become Swift errors; [others end the program](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-objc-interop.html). | As we read its [Swift templates](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs/main/uniffi_bindgen/src/bindings/swift/templates/macros.swift), a Rust panic in a non-`Result` function stops the process. | Flutter [swaps a failed widget for a gray background](https://docs.flutter.dev/testing/errors) in release. Platform channels [answer with a code and a message](https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/platform-channels). | **Solved.** One closed `UndraCallError` set on every platform; panics are caught at the boundary and reach the app as a structured report; a trapped wasm core restarts from its snapshot. [ERRORS.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/ERRORS.md), [ADR-032](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-032-swift-error-channel.md), [046](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-046-production-operations.md), [049](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-049-storage-errors-worker-sync-ports-web-recovery.md). |
| What can crossrows 21 to 23 | Swift sees [an Objective-C header, or Swift export (Alpha)](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-swift-export.html), which erases generics. | [Objects and foreign traits](https://mozilla.github.io/uniffi-rs/latest/types/interfaces.html) cross; its documentation describes no [generic types](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs/main/docs/manual/src/types/builtin_types.md) of your own. | [flutter_rust_bridge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fzyzcjy/flutter_rust_bridge/master/README.md) takes arbitrary types and closures; React Native [native modules](https://reactnative.dev/docs/turbo-native-modules-introduction) need a spec and code per platform. | **Solved:** records, enums and errors become native sum types, no Objective-C; objects cross as parameters and returns; the core calls host callbacks; newtypes stay typed; generics cross as declared instantiations, functions as overloads and objects and stores as one class per alias. [Objects](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/objects.html), [callbacks](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/callbacks.html), [types](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/types.html), [generics](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/generics.html), [ADR-040](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-040-objects-as-parameters-and-returns.md) to [042](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-042-newtypes-generic-instantiations-and-leaf-types.md). |
| Data layerrows 7 to 10 | Libraries: [Room](https://developer.android.com/kotlin/multiplatform), [SQLDelight](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sqldelight/sqldelight/master/README.md) (compile-time migration checks), [Store](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MobileNativeFoundation/Store/main/README.md). | Its documentation [describes no](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs/main/README.md) cache, mutation, offline or persistence layer. | Libraries: [TanStack Query](https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/network-mode), [drift](https://pub.dev/packages/drift) (with migrations). | **Solved:** cache, dedup, retry, optimistic rollback, an offline queue that survives a restart, migrating persisted state, infinite queries, lazy lists, polling. **Not yet:** optimistic placeholders after a restart. [Queries](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/queries.html), [paging](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/paging.html), [ADR-037](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-037-persisted-state-migrations.md), [043](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-043-paged-queries-lazy-lists-and-polling.md). |
