| Storage, sockets, servicesrows 11, 12, 14 | Ktor, DataStore, Room, SQLDelight; many of Google's [Jetpack libraries](https://developer.android.com/kotlin/multiplatform) are KMP-ready. | Its documentation describes no adapters; SQL and sockets are Rust crates you bring. | React Native has [WebSocket](https://reactnative.dev/docs/network) and [expo-sqlite](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/latest/sdk/sqlite/); Flutter has [drift](https://pub.dev/packages/drift) and [web_socket_channel](https://pub.dev/packages/web_socket_channel). | **Solved:** default adapters for HTTP, storage, files and connectivity on iOS, Android, web and React Native; opt-in WebSocket, SSE and SQL ports. **Not yet:** the web database serves one tab per origin. [Ports](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/ports.html), [database](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/db.html), [real time](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/realtime.html). |
| Dev loop and toolingrows 15, 16 | [Compose Hot Reload needs a desktop JVM target](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/compose-hot-reload.html); JetBrains' 2025 roadmap calls [build speed](https://blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2025/08/kmp-roadmap-aug-2025/) "a common Kotlin/Native concern". | Each change rebuilds the library and the app; its documentation describes no dev server or devtools. | Both ship DevTools. Flutter [hot reload skips native code](https://docs.flutter.dev/tools/hot-reload); React Native [Fast Refresh can fall back to a full reload](https://reactnative.dev/docs/fast-refresh). | **Solved:** `undra dev` reconnects and keeps state across a rebuild, query handles included; devtools with time travel; Gradle, Xcode and Vite run `undra build`. [ADR-051](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-051-dev-client-reconnect-and-session-resume.md), [053](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-053-state-preserving-reload.md), [054](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-054-devtools.md), [059](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-059-transient-handles-across-restore.md). |
| Testing and previewsrows 18, 19 | [kotlinx-coroutines-test](https://kotlinlang.org/api/kotlinx.coroutines/kotlinx-coroutines-test/) gives virtual time in multiplatform tests. | Its documentation describes no fakes for platform I/O; you build the doubles. | Flutter's [widget previewer](https://docs.flutter.dev/tools/widget-previewer) supports no `dart:ffi` or native plugins. | **Solved:** `PreviewCore` runs your real core with fakes and a manual clock on Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript; a recorded session replays in tests. [Testing](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/testing.html), [ADR-055](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-055-testkit.md). |
| Compatibility and floorsrows 20, 24, 30 | Kotlin/Native targets [iOS 15.0 and later](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-target-support.html). Several KMP frameworks in one app [duplicate dependencies](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-project-configuration.html). | As we read its [Swift template](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs/main/uniffi_bindgen/src/bindings/swift/templates/wrapper.swift), a library and bindings that disagree stop the process. | React Native [iOS 15.1](https://github.com/react-native-community/discussions-and-proposals/discussions/812), Flutter [iOS 15](https://docs.flutter.dev/reference/supported-platforms). Flutter [does not support several Flutter libraries](https://docs.flutter.dev/add-to-app) in one app. | **Solved:** schema-hash gate at load; iOS 15 and 16 via `ObservableObject`; several cores side by side. **Caveat:** the iOS 15 and 16 mode has not run on an iOS 15 or 16 runtime. [Hash](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/reads-never-cross-the-boundary/#schema-hash), [iOS 15 and 16](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/ios-15-16.html), [cores](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/several-cores.html). |
| Platforms and UI frameworksrows 25 to 29, 36 | [Kotlin/Wasm is Beta](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/wasm-overview.html). Compose Multiplatform shares UI; [desktop is Stable](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/faq.html). | Python and Ruby are first-party; web comes [from a third-party generator](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs/main/README.md). | Flutter [paints one UI on six platforms](https://docs.flutter.dev/reference/supported-platforms), [not suited to text-rich static sites](https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/web/faq). React Native: [web, Windows and macOS out of tree](https://reactnative.dev/docs/out-of-tree-platforms). | **Solved:** web (wasm core; React, Vue, Svelte, Solid hooks) and React Native. **Not yet:** Flutter and Dart. **Partly:** desktop, and reuse on a server. **By decision:** no shared UI. [TypeScript](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/api-typescript.html), [React Native](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/REACT_NATIVE.md). |
| Adopting and buildingrows 31, 32 | [Several ways into Xcode](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-ios-integration-overview.html); its IDE plugin applies a build-phase script by default. | [No end-to-end packaging](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs/main/docs/manual/src/Motivation.md): no Rust for Android, no `.aar`. | React Native [joins an iOS app through CocoaPods](https://reactnative.dev/docs/integration-with-existing-apps); Flutter [add-to-app has limits](https://docs.flutter.dev/add-to-app). | **Solved:** `undra build` runs inside Gradle, Xcode and Vite; SwiftPM on native iOS, no CocoaPods. **Partly:** `undra adopt` edits none of your project files. [From KMP](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/from-kmp.html), [from UniFFI](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/from-uniffi.html), [CLI](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cli.html). |
| Running in productionrows 13, 17, 33, 34 | Background work is platform code ([WorkManager is Android-only](https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/background-tasks/persistent)). The [IDE plugin](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-plugin-releases.html) debugs across Swift and Kotlin. | Not assessed. | React Native [Headless JS is Android-only](https://reactnative.dev/docs/headless-js-android). Both debug in their own language with [DevTools](https://reactnative.dev/docs/react-native-devtools). | **Solved:** background runs in the window the OS grants; symbol files and `undra symbolicate`; a debugger path into Rust, documented for Xcode, Android Studio and Chrome and tested with LLDB on the iOS simulator. **Caveat:** iOS background tasks do not run in the simulator, so that handler is tested with fakes. **Not yet:** physical-device measurements. [Production](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/production.html), [ADR-046](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-046-production-operations.md), [device rows](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#device-numbers-ios-android-web). |
| Ecosystem and track recordrow 35 | JetBrains builds it; [Google states support](https://developer.android.com/kotlin/multiplatform). | [Used extensively in Firefox](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs/main/README.md); its README says it is a long way from 1.0. | Backed by Google, and by Meta and Expo. | **Not yet, and a post cannot fix it.** One team, no production users, nothing on a registry. [Roadmap](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/roadmap/). |

## What we solved, and how

Five classes carry most of the weight. Each gets one measured number and the file it came from.

### The boundary

A boundary costs twice: once per crossing, and once for what a crossing carries. Undra's rule is that [reads never cross](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/reads-never-cross-the-boundary/) and a write crosses once per transaction, returning one change-set for each store it touched. [ADR-031](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-031-frame-coalesced-delivery.md) adds the other half: the platform applies what has arrived once per frame, merged, with a bounded backlog.

The number: a burst of 1,667 one-row updates to a 10,000-row list, which is 100,000 a second at 60 Hz, reaches the iOS app as one drain that costs the main thread 787 µs at the median. Applying each update on its own is estimated at 3.4 to 3.94 ms, 20.4 to 23.7 percent of a frame, from the measured cost of one ([benchmark results](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#the-adr-031-drain-1667-one-update-keyed-patches-on-10000-rows-per-frame-100000-a-second-at-60-hz); iPhone 17 Pro simulator on an Apple M5 Pro, so not a device).

[ADR-044](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-044-per-core-symbol-namespacing.md) turned the C ABI into one function table per core, so two cores can share a process without sharing anything. What the table's indirection costs a call is not settled: the implementer measured +0.6 ns on quiet rounds whose load the record does not give, and the [reviewer](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/reviews/2026-10-02-abi-table-review.md), on a loaded machine, measured a median of −5.1 ns inside a spread of ±40 ns, which shows no regression above the noise and cannot confirm a figure that small. A re-measure on a quiet machine is owed.

What remains is the crossing itself: through the generated binding a call is about 300 ns on the iOS simulator and 0.47 to 0.68 µs in Chromium, against 44 ns for the core alone. [ADR-056](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-056-web-call-path.md) brought the Chromium call down from 3.2 to 3.5 µs by taking allocations and lowered private fields off the call path, and the same changes cut the React Native mirror's work at 100,000 keyed updates a second from 21.5 to 22.0 ms of a 16.7 ms frame to 5.0 to 5.4 ms, on the iPhone simulator under Hermes. The call is still over its targets, which is open work, below.

### State over the boundary

A filtered or sorted view of a big list used to cost the whole list. A `Computed<Vec<T>>` was recomputed at every commit and sent whole, so one edited row in a 10,000-row list shipped 352.6 KB and took 176.5 µs. A `DerivedList` ([ADR-039](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-039-derived-keyed-lists.md)) is kept from the source's recorded operations on two order-statistic trees and ships the change: 158 bytes for the same edit, in 333 ns measured on the signals crate directly and 392 ns through the runtime, which is the figure on our landing page; at 100,000 rows, 375 ns and 158 bytes ([finding 5](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#5-a-computed-list-over-a-keyed-list-cost-the-list-again-a-derived-list-costs-the-change-adr-039); best of three medians).

A contract scenario replays 60,000 seeded operations through the Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript runtimes and checks each view's hash after every change-set. What a platform still pays is its own list copy, once per drain: for a one-operation patch to a 100,000-row source, 47 µs in TypeScript and 7 µs in Kotlin. iOS 15 and 16 mode copies the list on every patch, 48 µs at 10,000 rows.

### The error channel

A call that fails does one of three things on every platform: it throws or rejects with the method's own error type, with the platform's cancellation, or with `UndraCallError`, a closed set of five cases (cancelled by the core, panicked, refused, unavailable, malformed). A command, which has no caller to throw to, reports through `onError`. No reply status, cancellation or lost connection reaches `fatalError`, an uncaught exception or an unhandled rejection ([docs/ERRORS.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/ERRORS.md), [ADR-032](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-032-swift-error-channel.md)).

A native panic is caught at the boundary and arrives as `panicked`, and the app's `onPanic` receives a structured report with frames its crash reporter can symbolicate ([ADR-046](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-046-production-operations.md)); a computed that panics poisons only itself ([ADR-019](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-019-signals-transactional-delivery.md)); a stream's failure is a typed item on the wire ([ADR-036](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-036-typed-stream-error-items.md)); a write from a thread the runtime does not own is refused in every build ([ADR-035](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-035-off-runtime-writes-are-typed-errors.md)). A wasm core cannot unwind, so it traps; with `crashRecovery()` the runtime restarts the same module and restores the last snapshot ([ADR-049](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-049-storage-errors-worker-sync-ports-web-recovery.md), [docs](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/web.html)). The number: 3.12 to 3.22 ms at the median from the trap to a running core, with a 100 KB state, over five runs in headless Chromium ([benchmark results](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#web-recovery-typescript-adr-049)). Recovery is opt-in, and a call in flight at the trap fails with `Unavailable`.

### The dev loop

Edit Rust, save, and the app on a simulator, an emulator or a page reconnects by itself, with exponential backoff from 250 ms to 5 s, and observes its stores again ([ADR-051](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-051-dev-client-reconnect-and-session-resume.md)). The core's state is snapshotted in memory before the rebuild and restored into the new core before it listens, so the app returns to the screen it was on, and the dev bar says "Reloaded, state kept" or why not ([ADR-053](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-053-state-preserving-reload.md)). A screen that shows a query is carried too: its query handle comes back on the same handle and fetches with the code that was just rebuilt, with no code in the app for the handle (a value the app set by a call outside its stores, such as a server&rsquo;s address, is told to the new core again; [ADR-059](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-059-transient-handles-across-restore.md)).

The number: the playground's 204 KiB snapshot restores in 1.6 ms inside `undra dev`, which runs a debug build of the core (189 µs in a release build), and 74 ms pass from suspending the old core to the new one listening ([the piece's record](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/decisions/sde/dev-reload.md)). A page served by `undra dev` shows every store's live value and a timeline of every change-set, and a scrubber restores the core to an earlier step while the app follows ([ADR-054](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-054-devtools.md), [docs/DEV_LOOP.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/DEV_LOOP.md)). It sits behind a per-run token.

### Shipping an update, and shipping the app

Persisted data records the structure it was written with, so a build that changed a type still reads what the last one stored: by name for free, through a `#[undra::migrate]` hook when a name changed, and never by discarding it silently ([ADR-037](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-037-persisted-state-migrations.md), [Shipping an update](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/updates.html)). A queued write the new build cannot carry over becomes a dead letter the app can show. Storage ports fail with typed errors (full, locked, corrupt, unavailable, io) on every platform instead of raw throws ([ADR-049](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-049-storage-errors-worker-sync-ports-web-recovery.md)).

The number: the hello-world web core is 113.1 KB gzipped against a 120 KB budget, and the JavaScript a hello-world page loads up front is 15.8 KB gzipped against a 16 KB budget, for the production build of the runtime as an app installs it, with Vite's own preload helper reported beside it and gated on its own. CI fails a change that exceeds either ([ADR-052](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-052-web-bundle-size.md), [size record](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/results/web-size.jsonl)). Opt-in pieces stay out of the hello world: the remote transport and the default ports load on first use, and the browser database adds about 299 KB gzipped, only to an app that imports it.

## What it costs to adopt

You do not move a domain on a Monday. The two migration guides describe three levels. **L1, side by side:** a few pure functions (from UniFFI, plain-data functions in a new crate beside yours) move first, and the rest of your stack stays. **L2, one feature:** one screen's state and requests become a store, a query and a mutation. **L3, the whole domain:** platform services become ports, and persistence and the offline queue move in ([from Kotlin Multiplatform](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/from-kmp.html), [from UniFFI](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/from-uniffi.html)).

The costs are real. The core is Rust, and for an Android-first team Rust is no longer the daily language. It is a second toolchain: Rust with the iOS, Android and wasm targets, Xcode, and the Android SDK and NDK; `undra doctor` checks each of them and prints the command that fixes what is missing. Generated Swift defaults to iOS 17, and an app that supports 15 and 16 takes the `ObservableObject` shape and its extra list copy. An observed keyed list exists three times: in the core, in a baseline copy the core keeps to build patches against, and in each platform's mirror. And `undra adopt` writes a core and the steps but edits none of your project files.

## What is still open

Plainly, in the order a team would meet it: the matrix's open and partial rows, then what the matrix does not show.

### Not built yet

- **Generics are declared, not open-ended.** Generic records, enums, functions, methods, objects and stores cross as the instantiations you list; a type parameter with no list, native generic types, and generic queries, ports and callbacks do not ([generics](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/generics.html), [the limits](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/types.html#generics-limits), [ADR-058](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-058-generic-functions-and-objects.md)).
- **Flutter and Dart.** Not started; the plan was to decide after React Native, which has shipped.
- **Desktop and Windows.** The Kotlin runtime is plain JVM, but no desktop target ships, and the CLI does not support Windows.
- **A server.** The TypeScript runtime needs Node 20 or later; there is no guide to sharing a core with a server.
- **Publishing.** Nothing is on crates.io, Maven Central, npm or Homebrew yet; the install channels go live with the first tagged release.

### Built, with a known limit

- A queued write's optimistic placeholder and its `invalidates` targets do not survive a restart: the write replays, and the screen refetches only the mutation's own key.
- The web database serves one tab per origin, and a migration that contains its own `COMMIT` is open.
- After an `undra dev` reload a query without `persist` shows loading once, because a snapshot carries no query data, and an object that is neither a store nor a query handle is not carried over.
- The binding call path is over its targets: about 300 ns on the iOS simulator against 60 ns, and 0.32 to 0.44 µs for the runtime's synchronous call in Chromium against 80 ns.
- iOS background tasks do not run in the simulator, so the iOS background handler is tested with fakes and has not run under the OS scheduler here.
- Every number here is from a host, a simulator, an emulator or Chromium. The iOS 15 and 16 mode is proven by compilation and a runtime probe on iOS 26.5, not on an older runtime.

### Where another tool is ahead, and stays ahead

- **Time and backing.** KMP has JetBrains and Google's stated support; UniFFI ships in Firefox. Undra is one team's work with no production users.
- **Android.** Shared Kotlin is plain Kotlin there, with no boundary. Undra crosses JNI.
- **Language.** For an Android-first team Kotlin is the daily language, and in our judgement Rust is the adoption wall.
- **Other hosts.** UniFFI serves Python and Ruby. Undra serves three UIs, and React Native on top.
- **Over-the-air logic.** Expo's [EAS Update](https://docs.expo.dev/eas-update/introduction/) ships JavaScript without a new binary. A native Undra core ships with the app; a web core updates with the site.
- **One UI.** Undra does not share UI, by decision. For one codebase on every screen, look at Flutter, React Native or Compose Multiplatform.
- **Writing it three times.** It needs no new language or toolchain and keeps the best native tooling, with no boundary to debug across.

## The default

Default is a claim about which question comes first, not about every team. If your logic is stateful (a cache, a queue, a session, lists that must agree across screens), your UI is native and your team can carry Rust, the open rows above are few enough to check against your own requirements in an afternoon. If one of the open rows is yours, use the tool that has it. If none is, start with L1: move one function, call it from Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript, and see what it costs you before you decide anything else.

Next: [why reads never cross the boundary](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/reads-never-cross-the-boundary/), [Undra vs Kotlin Multiplatform](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-kotlin-multiplatform/), [Undra vs UniFFI and Crux](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-uniffi-and-crux/), and [why Undra keeps your UI native](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/why-undra-keeps-your-ui-native/).

Every claim and its source: [the claims ledger](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/why-undra-is-the-default-choice/claims.md), where the fact-check of 2 October 2026 marked each row verified, corrected or removed.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-kotlin-multiplatform/

Comparison

# Undra vs Kotlin Multiplatform: sharing logic without leaving your platform

Undra and Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) both let you write your domain logic once and keep the screens in SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose and React. They bet on different languages, boundaries and toolchains. We build Undra, so read this with that in mind: every statement about KMP is dated to 30 September 2026 and linked to its source, and one section covers when KMP is the better choice.

30 Sep 2026 · 13 min read · Undra team

> **How to read this page.** Statements about KMP describe its state on 30 September 2026 and link to JetBrains' or Google's documentation where one exists. We have not benchmarked KMP and make no numeric claims about it. If something is wrong or has moved, [open an issue](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/issues) and we will correct the page with a dated note.

## The short version

KMP compiles Kotlin to each target: the JVM and Android, native code for iOS, JavaScript or WebAssembly for the web. Your shared code is Kotlin, it runs in a Kotlin runtime on every platform, and platform code calls into it. Undra compiles Rust to a C ABI library (iOS, and Android through JNI) and to a wasm module (web), and generates Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript from a schema extracted from the Rust. Platform code does not call into your logic to read state; it holds a local mirror.

Three differences follow:

- **Language.** Kotlin or Rust. For an Android-first team Kotlin is already the daily language. Rust gives you a borrow checker and no garbage collector, and asks more of the people learning it.
- **Boundary.** In KMP, platform code reads shared state by calling into the Kotlin runtime. In Undra, reads are local and only writes cross, once per transaction.
- **Scope.** KMP is broader: share only logic, or logic and UI with Compose Multiplatform. Undra never shares UI, and ships the state and data layer that KMP leaves to libraries.

## What each one shares

With KMP you write ordinary Kotlin in a common source set and the compiler produces a library per target. Anything Kotlin can express can be shared: models, networking, persistence, view models. Compose Multiplatform extends that to UI; JetBrains lists iOS as Stable and web as Beta ([Compose Multiplatform](https://kotlinlang.org/compose-multiplatform/)). A shared view model looks like this (illustrative, not from either repository):

Illustrative: a KMP shared view model (commonMain)

```kotlin
class TodosViewModel(private val repo: TodoRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(TodosState())
    val state: StateFlow<TodosState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun add(title: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.update { it.copy(todos = it.todos + repo.add(title)) }
    }
}
```

With Undra you write a Rust crate and mark what the platforms may see: `#[undra::store]` for state, `#[undra::api]` for records, enums and methods, `#[undra::query]` and `#[undra::mutation]` for server data, `#[undra::port]` for things the platform does for you. Undra shares everything under the pixels: stores of signals and computed values, typed errors, a query cache with staleness, deduplication, retry and optimistic updates, an offline queue, persistence, and ports for HTTP, storage, time and the rest. It does not share UI, now or later.

Undra v1 also has no sync engine, and persistence goes through a key-value port that each platform implements; there is no Rust-owned SQLite. If your shared layer needs a relational database today, KMP has more to offer.

## What Swift sees

On iOS, Kotlin/Native compiles a shared module into a framework that Swift reaches through an Objective-C header ([Kotlin docs](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-objc-interop.html)). JetBrains documents the consequences: generics map to Objective-C lightweight generics with limits, boxed primitives surface as `NSNumber` subclasses such as `KotlinInt`, and `suspend` functions appear as completion-handler functions, or as `async` functions in Swift, which the page calls experimental with limitations. `Flow` has no Swift counterpart in that mapping, which is why community tooling such as SKIE and KMP-NativeCoroutines exists.

JetBrains' answer is Swift export, which generates Swift directly and exports `suspend` functions as `async` and flows as `AsyncSequence`, which the Objective-C path does not. Its documentation calls it Alpha, on a page last modified 28 August 2026, lists limitations including generic type parameters being erased to their upper bounds, and says breaking changes are expected ([Swift export](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-swift-export.html)). In June 2026 Touchlab, the maker of SKIE, still called SKIE the choice for shipping KMP on iOS while describing Swift export's Objective-C-free architecture as "actively arriving" ([Touchlab](https://touchlab.co/the-future-of-kmps-ios-interop)). So as of September 2026 the mainstream path for a SwiftUI team is the Objective-C framework, usually with a community plugin. That is a moving target; treat it as a snapshot.

Undra emits Swift source. This is the real generated store for the playground's to-do list, abbreviated:

Generated by undra bindgen (abbreviated): examples/playground/generated/swift

```swift
@MainActor @Observable
public final class Todos: UndraStore, @unchecked Sendable {
    public private(set) var todos: [Todo] = []
    public private(set) var filter: Filter = .all
    /// Computed by the core; read-only.
    public private(set) var visible: [Todo] = []
    /// Computed by the core; read-only.
    public private(set) var remaining: UInt32 = 0

    /// Adds an item at the end of the list.
    /// - Throws: ``TodoError``, `CancellationError` if the task is cancelled, or ``UndraCallError``.
    public func add(title: String) async throws -> Todo { /* … */ }

    /// Chooses which items `visible` holds.
    /// - Note: A failure is logged and passed to `LoadOptions.onError`; the method does not throw.
    public func setFilter(_ filter: Filter) { /* … */ }
}
```

There is no Objective-C in the path. Records are `Sendable` structs, errors are enums thrown as themselves (`catch TodoError.emptyTitle`), and a SwiftUI view reads `todos.visible` like any other observable property. The price is a baseline of Swift 6 and, by default, iOS 17, which `@Observable` needs; an app that supports iOS 15 or 16 lowers its deployment target and gets `ObservableObject` stores ([supporting iOS 15 and 16](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/cookbook/ios-15-16.html)).

On Android the comparison inverts, in KMP's favour. Shared Kotlin is just Kotlin on Android's runtime, with no cross-language boundary. Undra's Android path crosses JNI into a Rust shared library and surfaces `StateFlow`s, `suspend` functions and sealed error classes that Compose reads with `collectAsState()`. That is idiomatic, but still a boundary.

## The read path

In KMP the shared state lives in the Kotlin runtime. On Android a read is a plain Kotlin read. On iOS, SwiftUI code reads Kotlin objects through the bridged API: an in-process call into the Kotlin/Native runtime, which is compiled into the framework your app links, with values bridged to Objective-C types rather than serialised. For a `Flow`, Swift needs something that collects it and feeds values into state SwiftUI observes; SKIE and KMP-NativeCoroutines expose a `Flow` as a Swift `AsyncSequence` for that. Whether that costs anything you can measure is a question for your app; we have not measured it and do not claim it is slow.

Undra's rule is that reads never cross the boundary (R5 in the project's constitution). Each platform runtime holds a mirror: store handle, then signal id, then the decoded value. The generated store exposes it in the platform's idiom, so a read is a property read on a Swift class, a `StateFlow.value` or a `Signal.peek()`. A write is a call in. The core runs it as one transaction and answers with one binary change-set per store touched, holding only the observed signals that changed, which the runtime applies on the main thread.

A contract test checks the rule: scenario S11 reads four signals 1,000 times and asserts the core's crossing counter did not move ([scenarios](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/contract-tests/scenarios.md)).

The trade is explicit. Undra pays a decode and a copy on every change, plus memory for the mirror. In exchange reads are ordinary native reads of native value types, and the same generated API works whether the core is in-process, in a web worker, or behind a WebSocket during `undra dev`: reads that crossed could not work over an asynchronous transport.

For scale: 49.8 ns for a synchronous call through the C ABI and 6.31 µs for one insert into an observed 10,000-row list, measured on an Apple M5 Pro. Both are the core's half only, excluding the Swift, JNI or JavaScript side, and neither is a device number ([benchmark results](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md)). That file lists a comparison against KMP and UniFFI baselines as not yet done, so this page makes no speed comparison.

## The web story

KMP has two web targets. Kotlin/JS compiles Kotlin to JavaScript ([docs](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/js-overview.html)). Kotlin/Wasm targets WebAssembly with garbage collection in the browser, and its documentation still calls it Beta ([docs](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/wasm-overview.html)). If your organisation writes Kotlin on the web, that is coherent. If your web team writes TypeScript and React, the questions are what the seam looks like and what the bundle carries.

Undra's web output is a wasm module built from your Rust core plus `@undra/runtime`, a TypeScript package with no runtime dependencies. Each store field becomes a `Signal<T>` with `get`, `peek` and `subscribe`; `@undra/runtime/react` exports `useUndra` and `useSignal` (built on `useSyncExternalStore`), and Vue, Svelte and Solid adapters exist too. The core can run on the main thread, in a worker, or remotely over a WebSocket. The repository measures 113.1 KB gzipped for the wasm module of Undra's runtime plus a hello-world core, against a budget of 120 KB that CI enforces; it grows with your code.

Playground code, abbreviated: examples/playground/web/src/views/TodosView.tsx

```tsx
const visible = useSignal(todos.visible);
const remaining = useSignal(todos.remaining);
// ...
<input type="checkbox" checked={todo.done} onChange={() => void todos.toggle(todo.id)} />
```

The web has its own costs. The shipped wasm profile aborts on a Rust panic, so a panic traps the module and the page recovers by reloading the core and restoring a snapshot (scenario S17 tests that). Every generated method returns a `Promise`, even ones that are synchronous in Swift and Kotlin. And 64-bit integers are `bigint` unless you opt into `number`.

## Tooling weight

KMP is one integrated toolchain: Kotlin and Gradle, with JetBrains' IDE support behind them. JetBrains documents several ways into Xcode: a build-phase script (the default with its IDE plugin), a local Swift package, CocoaPods, or a prebuilt XCFramework published through Swift Package Manager or CocoaPods ([integration overview](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-ios-integration-overview.html)). A team already running Gradle installs nothing new.

Undra is a second toolchain for most teams. The `undra` CLI scaffolds a project (`undra init`), generates bindings (`undra bindgen`), builds the core (`undra build` produces an XCFramework, 16 KB-aligned `.so` files per Android ABI and an optimised wasm module) and diagnoses your machine (`undra doctor`). You need Rust with the iOS, Android and wasm targets, Xcode, and the Android SDK and NDK. Rust builds are not quick, which is what `undra dev` is for: it runs the core on your machine behind a WebSocket and rebuilds on save, and the running iOS app, Android app or web page reconnects by itself and keeps its state, without rebuilding the app ([ADR-051](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-051-dev-client-reconnect-and-session-resume.md), [ADR-053](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-053-state-preserving-reload.md); corrected on 2 October 2026: when this post was first published the Android runtime had no remote transport).

The weight is roughly symmetrical. Either can be consumed as a prebuilt binary, so an iOS engineer who never edits the shared code takes an XCFramework built by Gradle or by Cargo. The second toolchain lands on whoever owns the shared code: usually the Android team with KMP, the Rust authors with Undra.

## Ecosystem and backing

This is KMP's largest advantage. Kotlin and KMP are developed by JetBrains, and Google's documentation states that KMP is officially supported for sharing business logic between Android and iOS and is stable and production-ready ([Android developers](https://developer.android.com/kotlin/multiplatform)). Google has made Jetpack libraries including ViewModel, lifecycle, DataStore, Room, Paging and SQLite KMP-ready. Around them sit Ktor for HTTP, SQLDelight for type-safe Kotlin generated from SQL, Koin for dependency injection, and the wider Kotlin ecosystem.

Undra 1.0 shipped on 30 September 2026, the date of this post. It is one team's project, dual-licensed MIT or Apache-2.0, with a reference app (the playground) in the repository and no third-party packages. Its evidence is its tests (more than 4,000 across five languages, 18 contract scenarios on three platforms) and four adversarial reviews of the core crates. That is evidence of care, not of years in production.

What Undra offers instead of a library ecosystem is a built-in data layer with the semantics of a server-state cache: staleness windows, request deduplication, retry with jitter, optimistic mutations with precise rollback, an offline queue and persistence. With KMP you would typically assemble that from HTTP and database libraries, often with a caching library on top, and your own glue.

## Team fit

If your mobile engineers are Android-first Kotlin developers and iOS is a second consumer of the same logic, KMP meets you where you are: the shared code is in a language the team writes daily.

Undra fits better when teams already maintain a Rust core, want memory safety without a garbage collector, or have iOS, Android and web engineers in separate groups who would rather consume a generated package than learn another platform's runtime. The cost is Rust. Undra's macros emit errors that say what, why, how to fix it and where to read more, and they keep lifetimes and threads off the common path, but the borrow checker is still there, and in our experience most mobile teams have few Rust engineers. Undra's adoption wall is hiring, not technology.

## Side by side

| Aspect | Kotlin Multiplatform | Undra |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared language | Kotlin | Rust |
| Runtime on iOS | Kotlin/Native, linked into the app | Rust static library in an XCFramework, C ABI |
| Swift surface (Sep 2026) | Objective-C header; Swift export in Alpha | Generated Swift, `@Observable` stores, typed throws |
| Android | Kotlin on Android's runtime, no boundary | Rust `.so` over JNI, `StateFlow` and `suspend` bindings |
| Web | Kotlin/JS; Kotlin/Wasm in Beta | Rust to wasm plus a TypeScript package with hooks |
| Read and write path | Calls into the Kotlin runtime | Reads local; one call in and one change-set per store out |
| State model | Bring your own (`Flow`, ViewModel) | Signals, computed values, keyed lists, built in |
| Data layer | Ktor, SQLDelight or Room, and your glue | Built-in queries, mutations, offline queue, persistence via a Kv port |
| Shared UI | Optional, Compose Multiplatform | Never |
| Dev loop | Gradle | `undra dev`: core on your machine, apps connect over WebSocket |
| Backing | JetBrains; Google support for shared logic | One team; v1.0 shipped 30 Sep 2026 |

## When Kotlin Multiplatform is the better choice

Choose KMP when any of these describes you.

- **You are an Android-first Kotlin organisation.** The shared code is in your language, it runs on Android with no boundary, and your hiring, reviews and tooling already fit.
- **You want to share UI, now or later.** Compose Multiplatform gives you a path from sharing logic to sharing screens, with iOS listed as Stable and interop with SwiftUI and UIKit where you want native parts. Undra will not share UI.
- **You need mature libraries today.** A shared relational database, a large HTTP and serialisation ecosystem, Jetpack libraries with Google behind them. Undra has a key-value port, a query layer and an opt-in SQL port over SQLite ([Db](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/db.html), added on 2 October 2026), not that ecosystem.
- **You want JetBrains and Google behind a long-lived app.** KMP has been Stable since Kotlin 1.9.20 in November 2023 ([release notes](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/whatsnew1920.html)), was in production before that, and has two large companies behind it. That is a lower-risk bet than a v1.0 from one team, and a legitimate reason to choose it.
- **You have to hire for it.** Kotlin engineers are plentiful on mobile teams and Rust engineers are not, and Undra's core has to be written in Rust.
- **You ship to desktop, or share code with a Kotlin backend.** KMP and Compose target desktop, and Kotlin on the server can share models with clients. Undra has no desktop targets yet.
- **Your shared logic is small.** A few models and validation functions do not justify a second toolchain.

## Where Undra fits

Choose Undra if what you keep rewriting three times is stateful and not visual: the cache, the retry policy, the offline queue, the session refresh, the list that must stay consistent across screens. Choose it if your UI engineers are happy in SwiftUI, Compose and React, and if Rust's guarantees are an asset for your domain and not a tax.

Next: the [core concepts](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/concepts.html), [why reads never cross the boundary](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/reads-never-cross-the-boundary/), and [why Undra keeps your UI native](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/why-undra-keeps-your-ui-native/).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/reads-never-cross-the-boundary/

Architecture

# Reads never cross the boundary: how Undra's state model works

Every cross-language framework has to decide what crosses the boundary, how often, and what it costs. Undra's answer fits in a sentence: reads never cross the boundary, and writes cross once per transaction. This post walks through the mechanism with real generated code from the playground app, the numbers we measured with links to the raw results, and an honest section on what the design costs you.

30 Sep 2026 · 14 min read · Undra team

## The rule

There are roughly three ways to keep native UI in step with state that lives in another language. The UI can ask for each value when it needs it, which costs a crossing per read per render. The core can send the whole state after every change, which costs a crossing proportional to the state. Or the UI can hold a copy, and the core can send only what changed. Undra does the third, and states it as the fifth rule of its constitution: **reads never cross the boundary; writes cross once per transaction; no generated getter calls into the core.** The [UniFFI and Crux comparison](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-uniffi-and-crux/) looks at how other tools place themselves among these options.

There is a second reason for the rule besides speed. If reads crossed, a core in a web worker or behind a WebSocket during `undra dev` would need every read to be asynchronous. Because reads are local, the same generated API works in-process, in a worker and over a socket.

## The mirror model

You declare state in Rust as a store of signals. Fields of type `Signal<T>`, `Computed<T>` and `DerivedList<T>` are the signals, numbered in declaration order; the rest is private:

Playground code, comments added: examples/playground/core/src/todos.rs

```rust
#[undra::store(restore = "Self::assemble")]
pub struct Todos {
    next: AtomicU64,                       // private state: not a signal
    #[undra(key = "id")]
    todos: Signal<Vec<Todo>>,              // signal 0
    filter: Signal<Filter>,                // signal 1
    #[undra(key = "id")]
    visible: DerivedList<Todo>,             // signal 2, derived in the core, sent as patches
    remaining: Computed<u32>,              // signal 3, derived in the core
}
```

The macros record this in a schema, and `undra bindgen` turns the schema into Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript. Each platform runtime holds a mirror, a map from store handle to signal id to decoded value, and the generated store exposes its slice of it in the platform's own idiom. This is the generated Swift, abbreviated:

Generated by undra bindgen (abbreviated): examples/playground/generated/swift

```swift
@MainActor @Observable
public final class Todos: UndraStore, @unchecked Sendable {
    public private(set) var todos: [Todo] = []
    public private(set) var filter: Filter = .all
    public private(set) var visible: [Todo] = []
    public private(set) var remaining: UInt32 = 0

    public override func apply(signal: UInt32, op: ChangeOp, reader: inout UndraReader) {
        do {
            switch signal {
            case 0:
                switch op {
                case .fullValue:
                    let value = try [Todo].undraDecode(&reader)
                    try reader.finish()
                    self.todos = value
                case .keyedPatch:
                    let ops: [PatchOp<Todo>] = try decodePatch(&reader)
                    try reader.finish()
                    try applyPatch(ops, to: &self.todos)
                case .lazyListInvalidated:
                    break
                }
            // ... cases 1 to 3 decode `filter`, `visible` and `remaining` ...
            default:
                break
            }
        } catch is PatchError {
            // The mirror diverged from the core: re-observe to receive a full value.
            self.core.observe(self.handle, signal: signal, on: false)
            self.core.observe(self.handle, signal: signal, on: true)
        } catch { /* ... */ }
    }
}
```

Kotlin exposes the same signals as `StateFlow`s and TypeScript as `Signal`s:

Generated by undra bindgen (abbreviated): examples/playground/generated/kotlin

```kotlin
class Todos private constructor(core: UndraCore, handle: Long) : UndraStore(core, handle) {
    private val _todos: MutableStateFlow<List<Todo>> = signal(emptyList())
    val todos: StateFlow<List<Todo>> = _todos.asStateFlow()
    private val _visible: MutableStateFlow<List<Todo>> = signal(emptyList())
    /** Derived by the core from another list; read-only. Changes arrive as keyed patches. */
    val visible: StateFlow<List<Todo>> = _visible.asStateFlow()
    // ...
}
```

Generated by undra bindgen (abbreviated): examples/playground/generated/ts

```ts
export class Todos extends UndraStore {
  readonly todos: Signal<Todo[]> = new Signal<Todo[]>([]);
  /** Derived by the core from another list; read-only. Changes arrive as keyed patches. */
  readonly visible: Signal<Todo[]> = new Signal<Todo[]>([]);
  // ...
}
```

A screen reads these like any other state: a SwiftUI view reads `todos.visible`, a Compose screen calls `store.visible.collectAsState()`, and a React component calls `useSignal(todos.visible)`, which is built on `useSyncExternalStore`. A contract test, scenario S11, reads four signals 1,000 times and asserts that the core's crossing counter did not change ([scenarios](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/contract-tests/scenarios.md)).

## A write crosses once

A write is a call. The runtime encodes the arguments, takes a call id, and crosses the boundary once. The core runs the method, and everything it writes inside one transaction is committed together. The counter store in the playground shows the idea:

Playground code, reformatted: examples/playground/core/src/counter.rs

```rust
pub fn add(&self, amount: i32) {
    self.ctx.txn(|| {
        self.count.update(|count| *count = count.saturating_add(amount));
        self.changes.update(|changes| *changes = changes.saturating_add(1));
    });   // one change-set carries count, changes and the computed parity
}
```

On commit the core recomputes the dirty computed values in dependency order, then builds one change-set for each store the transaction touched, containing only signals that the platform has observed and that changed. The layout is small:

ChangeSet payload (docs/SPEC.md section 3.5)

```text
txn_id   u64
count    u32
entries  count x { handle u64, signal_id u32, op u8, len u32, value bytes }
         op 0 = full value, 1 = keyed patch, 2 = lazy list invalidated
```

Scenario S09 pins the behaviour: `counter.add(5)` delivers three entries, for `count`, `changes` and `parity`, and the transaction counter grows by exactly one. Change-sets of one store reach the platform one at a time, in commit order, with strictly increasing transaction ids ([ADR-020](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-020-signals-delivery-order-and-round-cap.md)). Observing a signal sends its current value at once, so a store's initial state is just a change-set.

The platform runtime receives the payload on whatever thread produced it, possibly while a core lock is held, so it never calls back into the core from that callback. It takes the payload out and applies everything that has arrived in one hop to the main thread: the Swift runtime on the `MainActor`, Kotlin on `Dispatchers.Main.immediate`, TypeScript in one flush per macrotask. Applying means running the store's generated `apply`, which sets the `@Observable` property, the `StateFlow` value or the `Signal`. The UI framework does the rest.

## Keyed lists: recorded operations, not diffs

A list marked `#[undra(key = "id")]` sends patches made of insert, remove, update, move and clear operations instead of the whole list. The first version of this did not meet its own promise, and the story is in the repository because the benchmark caught it.

Originally the core found the patch by comparing the list as it is with a copy of the list as the host last saw it. That comparison hashes every key of both lists and compares surviving rows, so its cost was linear in the list and independent of the change. One insert into an observed 10,000-row list took 536.16 µs, and 85 percent of that was the diff ([Finding 1](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#1-a-keyed-patch-was-olist-not-ochange-with-recorded-list-operations-it-is-ochange-resolved-adr-027)). The store code had known exactly what it did, and that information was thrown away at the `Vec` and rediscovered at commit.

The fix, decided in [ADR-027](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-027-keyed-list-ops-are-recorded-not-diffed.md), records the operation instead. `Signal<Vec<T>>` has `push`, `insert`, `remove`, `update_at`, `move_item` and `clear`. Each mutates the list and appends the wire operation it performed to a log, and a commit sends the log as the patch. The wire did not change.

Playground code, abridged: examples/playground/core/src/biglist.rs

```rust
pub fn insert_at(&self, index: u32, label: String) -> Result<u32, ListError> {
    // ...check the index...
    let id = self.next_id.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
    // The recorded list ops keep the change-set O(change) (ADR-027).
    self.items.insert(index as usize, Item { id, label, version: 0 });
    Ok(id)
}
```

| One change, 10,000 observed rows | Diffed (before ADR-027) | Recorded operation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Insert | 536.16 µs | 6.31 µs |
| Update | 532.32 µs | 272.3 ns |
| Move | 702.95 µs | 9.74 µs |

These are host-measured, core-side medians on an Apple M5 Pro. The remaining 6.31 µs is mostly the `memmove` of the vector's tail, paid twice because the core keeps a baseline copy. Scenario S10 checks the wire: an insert into the 10,000-row list arrives as a single `Insert` operation in under 100 bytes. On the platform, the Swift runtime, for one, validates every index of a patch against the list as it will be at that point before it changes anything, so a bad patch cannot leave the list half changed. If a patch does not fit, the generated store treats the signal as out of sync and re-observes it, which delivers a full value.

The fast path is opt-in. A list written with `set`, `update` or `replace` is still found by diffing against what the host has, which is always correct and O(list): 528.7 µs for the same one-row edit in the benchmark gate's harness. The to-do store in the playground uses `update`, so it pays the diff. For a to-do list that is irrelevant. For the 10,000-row list it is the difference between microseconds and half a millisecond.

## The schema hash gate

Everything above assumes that the core and the generated code agree on the layout of every type. Undra makes that a checked property, not a convention. The macros emit a description of every public type and function, which is the schema. It is serialised canonically (lists sorted by name, no whitespace, doc comments excluded) and hashed with 64-bit FNV-1a ([SPEC section 2.3](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/SPEC.md)). Two cores with the same public surface have the same hash. Each generated package carries the hash it was generated from, and you pass it when loading the core:

Real playground code: examples/playground/ios/PlaygroundApp/UndraBootstrap.swift

```swift
try UndraCore.load(.inproc(adapters: adapters, expectedSchemaHash: UndraIds.schemaHash))
```

Playground code, abridged: examples/playground/android/.../UndraApp.kt

```kotlin
UndraCore.load(LoadOptions(expectedSchemaHash = UndraIds.SCHEMA_HASH, adapters = adapters))
```

Playground code, abridged: examples/playground/web/src/undra.ts

```ts
await UndraCore.load({ mode: "wasm-main", wasm, expectedSchemaHash: UndraIds.schemaHash, adapters });
```

If the hashes differ, loading fails before the core is initialised with a typed error carrying both hashes (`UndraSchemaMismatchError` in Swift and TypeScript, `UndraSchemaMismatchException` in Kotlin), and scenario S16 tests that on all three platforms. The remote and worker transports carry the hash in every message header. At build time `undra bindgen --check` exits non-zero when generated files are stale, so a stale binding fails in CI.

This is a hard gate and a blunt one. Any change to the public surface changes the hash, and v1 has no evolution across a mismatch. Breaking the wire is a major version and needs a decision record first. Other tools have comparable load-time checks, and we do not claim this one is unique.

## Typed errors and panic containment

An error in a `Result<T, E>` is a value of a `#[undra::error]` enum, and it arrives as the platform's natural typed error:

Generated by undra bindgen (abbreviated)

```swift
public enum TodoError: UndraError, Error, Sendable, Hashable {
    /// The title is empty once spaces are trimmed.
    case emptyTitle
}
// store.add(title:) is declared `async throws` and throws a TodoError as itself
```

Generated by undra bindgen (abbreviated)

```kotlin
sealed class TodoError(message: String) : UndraException(message) {
    data object EmptyTitle : TodoError("the title cannot be empty")
}
```

TypeScript gets `TodoError.EmptyTitle` as an `Error` subclass you can test with `instanceof`. Replies carry a status byte: ok, typed error, panic, cancelled, stream opened or bad request, and decoders return typed errors for malformed input and never panic.

A panic in the core is caught at the dispatch boundary on native targets and answered with a status that carries the panic message and a backtrace. The process is not aborted, the core keeps serving calls, and the log port receives a record at error level or above. Scenario S17 verifies this over JNI and the C ABI. What the host does with that reply is its own policy, and every platform turns it into a value the app can catch. Generated code turns a panic into `UndraCallError.Panicked` on every platform (Swift spells it `.panicked(message:backtrace:)`): a call fails with exactly one of three things, its own typed error (`TodoError`), the platform's cancellation (`CancellationError`, `CancellationException` or the `AbortSignal`'s reason) when the caller cancelled, or `UndraCallError` for a panic, a cancellation by the core, a refused call, an unreachable core or a reply it cannot read. A synchronous method that returns nothing, such as `todos.toggle(id:)`, is a command and never throws or rejects, so a SwiftUI button, a Compose `onClick` or a React handler can call it; if it fails, the runtime logs the failure, hands it to `onError` and returns. Nothing in the generated code stops the process or leaves an unhandled rejection ([ADR-032](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-032-swift-error-channel.md)), and S17 calls the generated `explode` on all three platforms.

On the web the shipped wasm profile is built with `panic=abort`, so a panic traps the module. Containment there means the page survives: the failing call rejects, the log adapter receives a fatal record first, and the page can load a fresh core and restore a snapshot of the stores, which S17 also tests. Snapshot and restore keep handles valid and cancel the calls that were running on the stores they replaced ([ADR-023](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-023-runtime-delivery-reentry-restore-and-shutdown.md)).

## Determinism

The core reads no clock and no random source and starts no thread outside the runtime. Time comes from the `Clock` port, delays from the `Timer` port, randomness from `Rng`, the network from `Http`. That is rule R12. The to-do store shows the discipline: its item identities come from a counter, not from a random source, and after a restore the counter continues above the largest identity in the snapshot.

The payoff is testability. In Rust, `TestRuntime` installs deterministic fakes for every port, including a `FakeClock` that fires timers when you advance it, and runs the executor on the test thread. On each platform, the contract tests supply a manual clock and an in-memory HTTP server. Scenario S12 advances the clock by 31 seconds to prove that a cached query becomes stale and refetches, without waiting 31 seconds. This is determinism of inputs. It does not make native thread scheduling deterministic, and we do not claim replayability beyond what the tests exercise.

## What we measured

Every number here comes from [bench/RESULTS.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md) or the README, measured on an Apple M5 Pro with release builds, on a machine that was sharing load with other builds.

| Operation | Median | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Synchronous call through the C ABI, core side | 49.8 ns | [C ABI table](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#c-abi-cratesundra-ffibenchesboundaryrs) |
| Same call without the allocation the ABI owes | 31.5 ns | [Dispatch table](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#dispatch) |
| 1 KB record, codec round trip | 228.0 ns | [Section 14 rows](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#section-14-rows-measured-on-the-host) |
| Change-set for 100 dirty signals, core side | 2.30 µs | [Signals and stores](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#signals-and-stores) |
| Decoding that change-set, borrowed | 253.9 ns | [Signals and stores](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#signals-and-stores) |
| Decoding and replaying a one-operation patch on 10,000 rows (Rust wire crate) | 2.57 µs | [Keyed patch](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#wire-keyed-patch-undra-wire) |
| Cold start, restoring 100 KB of state | 70.87 µs | [Snapshot](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#snapshot-and-restore) |
| Wasm runtime plus hello-world core, gzipped | 113.1 KB | [Size record](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/results/web-size.jsonl) |
| Android core, hello world, arm64-v8a, release | 898.2 KB | [Size record](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/results/native-size.jsonl) |

Read these for what they are. They are core-side, on a host faster than the phones the design targets, so within budget here is necessary and not sufficient. The per-device targets (an iPhone with an A15, a 2022 mid-range Android phone, Chromium) are measured in a later device phase, and the platform half of a crossing, meaning the Swift, JNI or JavaScript side and applying a change-set to a mirror, is not in these numbers. The 46 operations covered by the CI gate have budgets about five times what they measure, so the gate catches an operation that becomes several times slower, not a few percent ([the gate](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md#the-ci-gate)). We have not published a stress benchmark for sustained very high write rates, and we have not compared Undra against other tools, so this page makes no such comparison.

## What this costs

Every design has a price, and the honest version of this post lists it.

- **Memory for copies.** An observed keyed list exists in the core, in a baseline copy the core keeps to build patches against, and in the platform mirror. A computed value is sent whole and held in the mirror too. If you observe a large keyed list, you pay for three copies of it.
- **A computed list crosses whole.** A keyed `Signal<Vec<T>>` and a `DerivedList<T>` get patches. A `Computed<Vec<T>>` crosses as a full value whenever it changes, so declare a filtered or sorted view of a large list as a `DerivedList` ([ADR-039](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-039-derived-keyed-lists.md), added on 2 October 2026), which ships one edited row of a 10,000-row list in 158 bytes where the computed shipped 352.6 KB.
- **A crossing per write.** Writes are calls: they encode arguments, cross, and run under the core's single lock. A long synchronous method blocks other callers, so long work belongs in an async method. Every TypeScript method returns a `Promise`.
- **The O(change) path is opt-in.** The recorded list operations are what make patches cheap. A raw `update` closure is correct and O(list).
- **The discipline of a schema.** Every public type exists in the schema or it does not cross. Names become ids, so renaming a method changes the wire. Any public change changes the hash, bindings must be regenerated, and v1 has no version skew between a core and its UI. You get a build failure instead of a corrupt decode, and you pay for it in ceremony.
- **The host contract.** Callbacks can run on any thread, possibly with a core lock held. A host must not call back into the core from them; re-entry is refused with an error in every build instead of deadlocking, but the runtimes have to honour the rule.
- **Rust.** The core is Rust, with the learning curve that implies, and the wasm build aborts on panic.
- **Numbers that are not yet device numbers.** See above.

The [specification](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/docs/SPEC.md) is the binding description of everything in this post, and the [decision records](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/tree/main/.10x/adrs) say why each choice was made. To try it, start with the [getting started guide](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/getting-started.html), or read how Undra [compares with Kotlin Multiplatform](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-kotlin-multiplatform/) and [why it keeps your UI native](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/why-undra-keeps-your-ui-native/).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/why-undra-keeps-your-ui-native/

Thesis

# Why Undra keeps your UI native

Cross-platform tools fall into two camps. One shares the pixels: you write the UI once and a toolkit puts it on every platform. The other shares what is under the pixels and lets each platform draw its own screens. Undra is in the second camp, and this post explains why without pretending the first camp is wrong. Shared UI is the right answer for many products, and we say which.

30 Sep 2026 · 9 min read · Undra team

> **How to read this page.** We build Undra, a framework that shares logic and never UI, so we have a stake in this argument. Statements about Flutter, React Native and Compose Multiplatform describe them on 30 September 2026 and link to their own documentation. If you think we have misrepresented one, [open an issue](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/issues).

## Two bets on going cross-platform

The first bet is that the UI is the expensive part, so share it. Three mature tools make this bet in different ways.

- **Flutter** has its own rendering engine, Impeller, and its own implementations of each UI control rather than deferring to the system's ([architecture overview](https://docs.flutter.dev/resources/architectural-overview)). You write Dart, and Flutter paints its own widgets with its own engine.
- **React Native** turns a tree of React components into the platform's own views: a `UIView` on iOS, an `android.view.ViewGroup` or `android.widget.TextView` on Android ([render pipeline](https://reactnative.dev/architecture/render-pipeline)). You write JavaScript or TypeScript and the screen is made of host views. Its New Architecture has been the default since React Native 0.76 ([docs](https://reactnative.dev/docs/the-new-architecture/landing-page)).
- **Compose Multiplatform** takes Jetpack Compose to other platforms. JetBrains lists iOS as Stable and web as Beta and describes interop that lets you keep existing SwiftUI or Android View code ([product page](https://kotlinlang.org/compose-multiplatform/)). Its FAQ says the components are drawn on a canvas rather than being platform widgets ([FAQ](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/faq.html)).

The second bet is that the logic is the expensive part, so share that and keep the UI native. Undra, UniFFI, Crux and Kotlin Multiplatform used without Compose Multiplatform all make it, with different amounts of framework around the shared code. The [Kotlin Multiplatform comparison](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-kotlin-multiplatform/) and the [UniFFI and Crux comparison](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-uniffi-and-crux/) cover the differences among them.

## What shared UI buys

The benefits are large and we do not want to undersell them.

- **One UI codebase.** One set of screens, one set of UI tests, one design system implementation. A small team ships to several platforms with the headcount of one.
- **Consistency by construction.** The same screen behaves the same way everywhere, which matters when the product's identity is its own look and not the platform's.
- **Iteration speed.** These toolkits put a lot of effort into fast feedback loops for UI work, and a single codebase means a fix lands everywhere at once.
- **Fit with your existing skills.** A team that already writes React can reach mobile through React Native. A Kotlin team can reach iOS through Compose Multiplatform.

Shared UI is usually the right choice when any of these describes the product:

- A small team or a startup that needs to reach several platforms quickly.
- A brand-led or highly custom interface, where a bespoke look matters more than platform convention.
- An internal tool or a content app where the screens are simple and the platform's idioms are not a selling point.
- An app that is mostly UI with a thin logic layer, where there is little below the pixels worth sharing.

If that is you, use one of those toolkits. Undra will not help, and we do not plan to add shared UI.

## What shared UI trades away

The trade is not the same for each toolkit, and none of it is fatal. It is a set of costs that show up at the edges, and the costs are different if you start from a native app than if you start from nothing.

**Platform idioms.** Native controls bring platform behaviour with them: text selection, scroll physics, navigation transitions, keyboard handling, system sheets and menus. React Native inherits much of this because its screens are host views. Flutter and Compose Multiplatform draw their own controls, so matching a platform convention is the toolkit's work, or yours. Brand-led apps often do not want a match, which is the point of the first bet.

**Day-one OS features.** When a platform ships a new UI API, native code can adopt it with the new SDK. A shared toolkit adopts it on its own schedule, or you embed a native view. Flutter documents platform views for exactly this, and notes that synchronising them with Flutter's rendering carries overhead, so it recommends them for complex controls where reimplementing is impractical. Some surfaces are built in the platform's own UI framework regardless: iOS home-screen widgets, for example, are WidgetKit views written in SwiftUI ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/widgetkit)), so a shared-UI app writes those natively anyway.

**Accessibility fidelity.** With native UI, the platform's accessibility stack talks to platform views directly. A toolkit that draws its own controls must publish a semantics tree that the platform accessibility APIs can read. Flutter documents a semantics tree, built in its own pipeline phase and uploaded to the engine for assistive technology ([docs](https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/semantics/SemanticsNode-class.html)), and JetBrains documents that Compose semantics are mapped to native iOS accessibility objects and support VoiceOver ([docs](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/compose-ios-accessibility.html)). These work and are widely used. The cost is that keeping parity with each platform's accessibility behaviour is the toolkit's ongoing job, where with native UI it is the platform's.

**The hiring pool.** Platform teams hire SwiftUI, Compose and React specialists. A shared-UI toolkit has its own pool (Dart, React Native, Kotlin with Compose), and each of those is large. The cost appears when you already employ platform specialists: moving to shared UI re-skills or replaces them. Undra's version of this problem is Rust, which we come back to below.

## The line under the pixels

Undra draws the line exactly at the UI. Everything under it is shared: domain logic, reactive state, the data layer, persistence and the dev loop. Everything above it stays a hand-written SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose or React screen.

Our reasoning starts from where the work repeats. In our experience the code beneath the UI is where the three platforms disagree and where the subtle bugs live: the cache, the retry policy, the offline queue, pagination, the session refresh. Teams write these three times and get three slightly different answers. The screens, by contrast, are where platform expertise pays off. So Undra shares the part that must be identical and leaves the part that should feel native.

The bar is that a SwiftUI view bound to Undra state is indistinguishable from one bound to Swift state. That is achievable because the generated store is an ordinary `@Observable` class, a Kotlin `StateFlow` or a TypeScript `Signal`. The same store in the playground, in each platform's own UI code:

Playground code, abbreviated: examples/playground/ios/PlaygroundApp/Screens/TodosScreen.swift

```swift
ForEach(todos.visible, id: \.id) { todo in
    Button {
        todos.toggle(id: todo.id)
    } label: {
        Label(todo.title, systemImage: todo.done ? "checkmark.circle.fill" : "circle")
    }
    // ...
}
```

Playground code, abbreviated: examples/playground/android/.../ui/TodosScreen.kt

```kotlin
val visible by store.visible.collectAsState()
val remaining by store.remaining.collectAsState()
```

Playground code, abbreviated: examples/playground/web/src/views/TodosView.tsx

```tsx
const visible = useSignal(todos.visible);
const remaining = useSignal(todos.remaining);
```

Three screens, each written in its platform's idiom, reading one core's state. The consequence for day-one features is direct: because the UI is plain SwiftUI, Compose or React, a new platform API is available to you on the day it ships. Accessibility modifiers, previews, navigation, animation and the design system are the platform's own and stay yours. Undra's part is to keep what those screens show consistent with the logic, and it does that with a local mirror of the state, so reads from the UI never cross into the core.

Native tooling applies unchanged for the same reason. The playground's iOS screens carry accessibility identifiers and are driven by an XCUITest tour against the real core; its Compose screens use test tags; its web build is exercised by a Playwright smoke test in headless Chromium. Nothing in those tests knows Undra exists, because what they see is a SwiftUI, Compose or React UI.

## Why not share the UI too?

We considered it and rejected it, for a reason that is about focus more than principle. Flutter, React Native and Compose Multiplatform are whole-UI products, each maintained by a large team that chases every platform's new UI features, keeps accessibility in step and polishes rendering. An Undra UI toolkit would be a smaller and later version of one of them, and it would be the part of Undra most likely to age badly. The moment a framework paints pixels on three platforms it takes on that ongoing work, and it inherits the trade-offs listed above.

There is also a practical reason. If the UI stays native, Undra's generated code has a clear bar to meet: a Swift, Kotlin or TypeScript engineer who has never seen Rust must be able to review it and find it idiomatic. The golden files that lock the generated output are how the project holds itself to that bar.

## What the line costs

Drawing the line here has costs, and they are the mirror image of what shared UI buys.

- **You build three UIs.** That means three implementations of the design, three UI test suites, and keeping the screens from drifting apart. If your product needs pixel-identical screens, this is the wrong tool.
- **You need Rust.** The core is Rust. Undra's macros emit errors that say what, why, how to fix it and where to read more, and they keep lifetimes and threads off the common path, but the borrow checker remains, and in our experience most mobile teams have few Rust engineers. Only the people writing the core need it; the platform teams consume generated Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript.
- **Logic must be worth sharing.** If your app is mostly UI with little logic beneath it, sharing the logic buys little. The worst case for Undra is an app that is 90 percent UI and 10 percent logic.
- **It is a new framework.** Undra 1.0 shipped on 30 September 2026. Its reference app is the playground in the repository, and its evidence is its tests: more than 4,000 across five languages, and 18 contract scenarios run on iOS, Android and web. We are not claiming production mileage.
- **The scope is a choice.** Undra v1 has no sync engine, no hosted services and no shared UI. The last is a decision and not a backlog item.

## Choosing

| Your situation | A better fit |
| --- | --- |
| Small team, one UI codebase, brand-led custom interface | Shared UI: Flutter, React Native or Compose Multiplatform |
| An existing React team that wants mobile apps | React Native |
| A Kotlin team, Android first, wanting iOS screens too | Compose Multiplatform, which JetBrains lists as Stable on iOS |
| Existing native iOS and Android apps with platform teams and duplicated logic | Shared logic: Undra, Kotlin Multiplatform, UniFFI or Crux |
| Platform-idiomatic UI is a product requirement | Native UI with shared logic |
| A Rust library already exists and you need bindings | UniFFI |
| An app that is mostly UI with thin logic | Shared UI |
| Stateful, server-backed logic on three platforms that must stay consistent | Undra |

The two bets are not exclusive over time. Some teams share logic first and UI later, and a Kotlin team can do that inside one ecosystem. We have not built or tested Undra underneath a shared-UI toolkit, and Undra's generated bindings target SwiftUI, Compose and React idioms, so we make no claim there.

If the argument persuades you, the next question is how the state model works. [Reads never cross the boundary](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/reads-never-cross-the-boundary/) explains it in detail, and the [getting started guide](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/getting-started.html) gets a three-platform app running.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-uniffi-and-crux/

Comparison

# Undra vs UniFFI and Crux: three ways to put Rust under a native app

If you have decided your logic lives in Rust, there are at least three serious ways to get it under a SwiftUI, Compose or React app: UniFFI, which generates bindings and stops there; Crux, which adds an architecture; and Undra, which adds reactive state, a data layer and a dev loop. They are layers of one stack more than rivals, and the cheapest layer is sometimes the right one.

30 Sep 2026 · 11 min read · Undra team

> **How to read this page.** We build Undra. Statements about UniFFI and Crux describe them on 30 September 2026 and link to their own documentation. We have not benchmarked either and make no numeric claims about them. UniFFI and Crux are both pre-1.0, so details move; if something here is out of date, [open an issue](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/issues) and we will correct it with a dated note.

## Three layers, not three rivals

UniFFI owns the crossing: it generates the foreign-language side of a Rust library's API. Crux owns the shape of the app: an Elm-style core that never does I/O and a thin shell that does. Undra owns the state that sits between core and screen: signals the UI observes, a data layer, and the loop for developing both.

You can stop at any layer. A small Rust library with a handful of functions needs UniFFI and nothing else. An app whose state you want to reason about as a pure function of events may want Crux. Undra is for apps where the hard part is keeping native UI consistent with stateful, server-backed logic on three platforms. Undra does not build on UniFFI or Crux: it has its own wire format and a fixed 19-function C ABI, so nothing below is a statement that one is built on another.

## UniFFI: a binding generator

UniFFI is Mozilla's toolkit for generating foreign-language bindings for Rust libraries ([project](https://github.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs)). You describe the interface with proc-macros or a UDL file, build a shared library, and run the generator. It has first-party support for Kotlin, Swift and Python (with more limited Ruby support), and third-party bindings exist for others, including JavaScript and WebAssembly, Kotlin Multiplatform, Go and C#. Mozilla uses it extensively in Firefox on mobile and desktop, and describes it as ready for production but a long way from 1.0.

Illustrative: UniFFI proc-macro usage

```rust
uniffi::setup_scaffolding!();

#[derive(uniffi::Record)]
pub struct Todo { pub id: u64, pub title: String, pub done: bool }

#[uniffi::export]
pub fn add_todo(list: Vec<Todo>, title: String) -> Vec<Todo> { /* … */ }
```

The mechanics are the point. UniFFI generates a C-style FFI layer over primitive types. Simple values cross directly; strings, options and records are lowered into a byte buffer the project calls a `RustBuffer`, and lifted on the other side ([how it works](https://mozilla.github.io/uniffi-rs/latest/)). Every call your app makes is an FFI call. The generated Kotlin loads the library through JNA. It supports async functions, callback interfaces and foreign traits, and its Swift and Kotlin bindings check API checksums when the library initialises, which catches a binding and a library built from different interfaces. That last point is worth saying because Undra's schema-hash gate is not unique to Undra.

UniFFI is deliberately a lower layer. As far as its documentation goes it has no notion of observable state, a cache or a dev loop, and that documentation is candid that it offers no end-to-end packaging solution: it will not compile your Rust for Android or package the bindings into an `.aar`. That is a design choice, not a gap. But it means that if a SwiftUI screen must stay in sync with Rust state, you design the synchronisation: polling, or callback interfaces that push changes, and some representation of "what changed". Undra's mirror and change-sets are one answer to exactly that design problem.

## Crux: an architecture

Crux, maintained by Red Badger, splits an app into a Core in Rust and a Shell in the platform's language ([project](https://github.com/redbadger/crux)). The core follows the Elm architecture. You define an `Event` enum, a `Model`, a `ViewModel` and an `Effect` type, and an `update` function from event and model to a `Command` that requests effects. The core never performs I/O. It describes the work as data, the shell performs it and hands the outcome back, and the core continues. A shell is therefore a small loop: send an event, perform each requested effect and resolve it, and read the view model when a render is requested.
