Its README states that Crux is pre-1.0 and production-ready, with occasional breaking changes, and it links engineering write-ups from Proton and Photoroom.

Illustrative: the shape of a Crux app, not compilable as written

```rust
impl App for Todos {
    fn update(&self, event: Event, model: &mut Model) -> Command<Effect, Event> {
        match event {
            Event::Add(title) => { model.items.push(Item::new(title)); render() }
            Event::Refresh => Http::get(API_URL).expect_json().build().then_send(Event::Loaded),
            Event::Loaded(Ok(mut resp)) => { model.items = resp.take_body().unwrap(); render() }
            // ...
        }
    }
    fn view(&self, model: &Model) -> ViewModel { /* project the model for the UI */ }
}
```

The boundary is three calls on a bridge: `update` takes an event and returns effect requests, `resolve` hands an effect's output back, and `view` returns the current view model. All messages are serialised with Bincode; types for Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript are generated with facet-generate, and the README names BoltFFI as the generator of the FFI layer. Its published capabilities include Render, Http, KeyValue and Time, at what the README calls various stages of maturity. Shells can be SwiftUI, Compose, React or Vue, or Rust web frameworks such as Leptos and Yew, and a Rust shell can import the core directly.

## View models and change-sets

This is the deepest architectural difference between Crux and Undra, so it deserves care.

In Crux the shell renders a `ViewModel`. When the core asks for a render, the shell calls `view()` and receives the whole view model, serialised across the boundary. That is a clean contract: the UI is a function of one value, consistency is trivial, and the view model is easy to assert on in tests. The cost scales with the size of the view model, not the size of the change, and the shell must work out what changed, which SwiftUI and React already do by diffing. For a settings screen this is unremarkable. For a long list that changes one row at a time, the work per update is proportional to the list.

Crux is not stuck there. Photoroom's engineering blog describes running into this with a large view model, where the UI could not tell what had changed, and building patches on top: key-path changes generated by diffing view models before and after an update, and sending only those ([Photoroom, part 3](https://www.photoroom.com/inside-photoroom/building-live-collaboration-in-rust-for-millions-of-users-part-3)). In Crux that is something you build; in Undra it is the built-in model.

In Undra the state that crosses is per signal, and each platform observes the signals it renders. Changing the to-do filter ships the new filter and the recomputed `visible` list and nothing else, because the underlying `todos` did not change. A transaction commits one change-set per store it touched, holding only the observed signals that changed, each as a full value or, for a list with a key, as a patch of insert, remove, update and move operations that the core recorded as the store performed them ([decision record ADR-027](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-027-keyed-list-ops-are-recorded-not-diffed.md)). On a 10,000-row observed list, one insert measures 6.31 µs core-side as a recorded operation against 536.16 µs when the core had to diff, on an Apple M5 Pro ([benchmark results](https://github.com/shreypdev/undra/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md)). Those are Undra against an earlier Undra, not against Crux.

Undra's costs here are real. Computed lists cross as full values, because only a keyed `Signal<Vec<T>>` gets patches. The fast path is opt-in: a store must use operations like `insert` and `update_at` rather than an arbitrary `update` closure, which falls back to an O(list) diff. And the platform keeps a mirror, which is memory Crux does not need. If your view models are small, Crux's simplicity is the better trade.

## Effects as data, or ports

Crux's effects are data: the core requests, the shell performs, the result returns as an event. Its README highlights two consequences. The core stays sandboxed and portable, including inside wasm, and tests play the role of the shell, observing and resolving effects with no fakes, mocks or stubs. Commands can be written with async Rust, but the async block talks to the shell through a context rather than touching the model directly, so state changes live in `update`.

Undra takes the other road. Core code `await`s a port, an ordinary Rust trait that the platform implements, and continues in place:

Real playground code: examples/playground/core/src/remote.rs

```rust
#[undra::query(key = "remote-todos:{list}", stale = "30s", persist, retry = 1)]
pub async fn remote_todos(ctx: &Ctx, list: String) -> Result<Vec<RemoteTodo>, RemoteError> {
    let url = endpoint(ctx, &format!("/lists/{list}/todos"))?;
    parse(&send(ctx, HttpRequest::get(url)).await?)
}
```

Behind `send` is the `Http` port. There are ten standard ports (Http, Kv, SecureStore, Fs, Clock, Rng, Log, Timer, Connectivity, Lifecycle), with default adapters on each platform and deterministic fakes in Rust. The core reads no clock and no random source and starts no thread outside the runtime, so it is deterministic and testable, but through fakes you supply rather than through pure functions. The query macro then gives every platform the same staleness window, request deduplication, retry, optimistic updates with rollback, offline queue and persistence, where a Crux app builds its own caching on top of the Http capability (we found no cache in Crux's published capabilities or in `crux_http`'s documentation as of September 2026).

The trade is what you can reason about locally. A Crux `update` is a pure function you can read top to bottom. Undra's async methods are ordinary Rust that hold state across awaits, which is shorter to write and does more work for you, and harder to reason about exhaustively.

## What the UI code looks like

With UniFFI your SwiftUI or Compose code calls generated functions such as `addTodo(list:title:)` and gets values back. How those values reach a view, and how the view learns of later changes, is yours to build. With Crux the UI renders the latest view model and sends events; the shell's plumbing is the loop above. With Undra a view reads properties of a store, and the runtime has already put the current values there:

Playground code, abbreviated: examples/playground/ios/PlaygroundApp/Screens/TodosScreen.swift

```swift
ForEach(todos.visible, id: \.id) { todo in
    Button {
        todos.toggle(id: todo.id)
    } label: {
        Label(todo.title, systemImage: todo.done ? "checkmark.circle.fill" : "circle")
    }
    // ...
}
```

That is ordinary SwiftUI. `toggle` is a write that crosses once; `todos.visible` is a read that does not.

## Side by side

| Aspect | UniFFI | Crux | Undra |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | Binding generator for Rust libraries | Elm-style app architecture with a shell per platform | State, data layer and dev loop with generated bindings |
| Maintained by | Mozilla | Red Badger and contributors | The Undra team |
| What crosses | Function calls; complex values lowered to byte buffers | Serialised events, effect requests and responses in; the view model out | Calls in; binary change-sets out |
| Where state lives | Wherever you design it | `Model` in the core, projected to a `ViewModel` | Signals in stores, mirrored to each platform |
| How the UI reads | Calls you design | `view()` returns the whole view model | A local mirror; reads never cross |
| I/O | Your Rust calls out, or foreign callbacks | Effects as data, run by the shell | Ports answered by platform adapters |
| Data layer | None | Capabilities such as Http and KeyValue; caching is yours | Queries, mutations, offline queue, persistence |
| Web | Third-party bindings | Wasm core; React, Vue and Rust-based shells | Wasm core plus a TypeScript package with hooks |
| Generated code | Swift and Kotlin APIs mirroring your Rust interface | Types for events, effects and view models | Observable stores, typed errors, hooks, `StateFlow`s |
| Load-time check | Checksums at initialisation | Generated types that fail to compile on change | Schema-hash gate at load and at build |
| Status (Sep 2026) | Production use at Mozilla; pre-1.0 | Production-ready, pre-1.0 | v1.0 shipped 30 Sep 2026 |

## When UniFFI is the better choice

- **You want bindings, not a framework.** If you have a Rust library and need Swift and Kotlin callers, UniFFI is smaller and simpler to adopt than anything that also brings a runtime.
- **You already have state management on each platform.** If each app has its own architecture and you want to move only the computation, a generator of call bindings fits without asking you to adopt mirrors or signals.
- **Your API is objects and callbacks.** UniFFI exposes Rust objects with methods, supports callback interfaces and foreign traits, and maps async Rust functions to each language's native futures. Undra's surface is stores, records, methods and ports.
- **You need other languages.** Python and Ruby are in the tree and third-party generators cover Go, C# and more. Undra targets Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript.
- **You want the longer track record.** It is used extensively in Firefox and maintained by Mozilla. Undra is a new v1.0.
- **Your surface is small.** A few functions do not need schema-driven stores.

## When Crux is the better choice

- **You want Elm's discipline.** Every state change is an event, the core is a pure function of events and resolved effects, and tests are plain Rust with no fakes. Some teams find that the most maintainable way to build an app, and Undra does not impose it.
- **Your view models are small and whole-state updates are fine.** Then Crux's single-value contract is simpler than signals and patches.
- **You want Rust on the web side too.** Crux supports Rust web shells such as Leptos and Yew and lets a Rust shell import the core directly.
- **You need a C# shell.** Crux's README says its FFI layer is generated across native, web and C# shells. Undra targets Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript.
- **You want a community with production stories.** Crux's README links write-ups from Proton and Photoroom. Undra has a reference app and a test suite, not production mileage.
- **You do not need a built-in data layer.** If Http, KeyValue and Time capabilities are enough and you would rather own caching and sync yourself, Crux stays out of the way.

## Where Undra fits

Choose Undra when you want platform UIs to bind to Rust state directly, with lists that stay cheap as they grow, server data with the semantics of a cache, offline support that is tested on all three platforms, and a dev loop where the core runs on your machine. Read [why reads never cross the boundary](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/reads-never-cross-the-boundary/) for the model, [how Undra compares with Kotlin Multiplatform](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/blog/undra-vs-kotlin-multiplatform/), or start with the [getting started guide](https://shreypdev.github.io/undra/docs/getting-started.html).
